en: Regarding the Prologue to the *Lengyan jing lüeshu*:
I, being unworthy, have studied Chan at the gate of a Dharma teacher, yet I have not been able to gain even a single glance [of his insight].

When my formal practice concluded and I returned to the mountains of Min, finding myself with nothing to do, I took up the Great Canon and read it through extensively; regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I claimed to have uniquely grasped its essential pivot.

In the second volume of *Jiàn yīn zuò yì jiě* (Explanation of the Key Causes for Forming Wings), I have briefly set forth my humble views to supplement what has not yet been reached by other commentaries;
this was during the Jiǎzǐ year of the Tiānqǐ era. Upon reaching the Bǐnzǐ year of the Chóngzhēn era, I began teaching the Dharma at Kāiyuán Monastery in Quán.

It happened that Master Èryún, who held the office of Vice-Censor-in-Chief in the South of Quán, frequently ordered his carriage to visit me during the intervals of his official duties to discuss matters of great importance.

I once discussed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* with him, finding it vexing that the various commentaries were so disorganized and chaotic; I requested that he compose a summary of its essential meaning (*mahātmya*).
I remarked that while those who practice Chan often delight in contemplating the essential meaning, they frequently fail to clarify the intricate details.

Consequently, they are unable to completely dispel lingering doubts and instead hastily interpret the text according to their own views—a fault that is not minor. Therefore, I have composed this "Broad Wings" commentary (*Prajñāpakṣa*) to explain it.
In composing this brief commentary, I have also extensively gathered various interpretations to synthesize them into a single school of thought.

While I certainly do not hesitate to proclaim the general principles, I am likewise determined to clarify the subtle nuances, ensuring that readers may, upon seeing each point, attain a sudden and refreshing realization of the meaning, unobstructed by the literal text and undisturbed by the confusions of other commentaries.
Whether it be the Tiantai or the Huayan school, [the truth remains]—indeed, it has not yet... [text ends].
Xia inquired about its subsequent history: the first three fascicles were completed during the sweltering heat of the mid-autumn season in the Kaiyuan era;

subsequently, upon returning to Fuzhou, they completed another three fascicles at Gushan. In the spring of the following year, he traveled to Zhexi, where local gentry requested that he remain at Zhenji Temple in Xiaoxi;
it was only after this that the final four fascicles were finally accomplished. This was recorded by Cao Yu of Xianli after the Lantern Festival in the year Wuyin.
When the Honorable Attendant visited me, I could not help but gaze upon it for a moment in deep admiration; I have therefore commissioned artisans to carve this woodwork.
Once the work was completed, I have carefully recorded the date and month here, for the merit of this timely occasion must not be forgotten.
Written on the Mid-Autumn Day of the eighth month in the Wuyin year of the Chongzhen era by Shi Yuanyuan of Zhenji at Jiding Hall.
*A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Yuanyuan of Yongquan Chan Monastery, Gushan, Fuzhou.
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Mystical Crown*,
the first three characters of the title, "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Dàfódǐng*), refer to the wondrous mind that is our original nature. "Buddha-Crown" (佛頂) refers to this very point.

The character "Buddha" (佛) signifies the meaning of being most honored and most supreme; yet, fearing that these two meanings of "honored" and "supreme" might not fully exhaust its significance, the single character "Great" (大) is further added above the Buddha’s crown.

This reveals that this wondrous mind encompasses and gives forth the ten directions, pervading all existence, while its actual realm is transcendent, beyond the reach of words and the limits of thought; therefore, it is called the "Great Buddha."
The four lines below this heading all manifest the efficacy of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.

The first two lines are spoken from the perspective of the Buddha-stage, while the latter two lines are spoken from the perspective of the Bodhisattva-stage. "The secret cause of the Tathāgata" refers to taking this wondrous mind as the primary cause.
The Tathāgata represents the ultimate state of fruition; yet, at the very beginning of practice, one must first attain this [mind].
The wondrous mind serves as the cause, just as one must first obtain rice before steaming it into cooked grain, or gold before casting it into an image;

otherwise, even with skill and strength, there is no principle by which anything could be accomplished. To speak of "Esoteric" (Mikkyō) on account of this cause means that this mind transcends the realm of speech and thought, and is not comparable to the manifest causes of phenomenal appearances.
To speak of the "Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization" means to expound upon this wondrous mind.

This is the Great Teaching. All teachings spoken by the Buddhas are entirely based upon the revelation of this wondrous mind; those who practice do so by practicing this, and those who realize do so by realizing this.
Therefore, it is said that both practice and realization are ultimate and exhaustive, with no further meaning remaining beyond them.

If there were any proclamation made that did not rely on this wondrous mind, although it might not be the teaching of external paths, it would ultimately belong to the provisional and gradual, and would not be of definitive meaning. Thus, [the Buddha] said: "Bodhi..."
The practitioner of the *sārvakāra-caryā* says: "It is by relying on this wondrous mind that one performs the Great Practice (*mahācaryā*).

From the stage of the Ten Faiths up to Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*), the Bodhisattva aspires upward toward the fruit of Buddhahood and descends to transform sentient beings; thus, their practice is most vast. Nevertheless, it must rely upon this wondrous mind;

then, with every step taken and every foot placed down, all actions will be perfectly luminous, wondrous, and tranquil. If one does not rely upon this [mind], even if one were to cover the heavens with goodness, [it would be in vain].
Exerting effort throughout the ages, all such achievements belong merely to the realm of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) and are subject to the cycle of arising and ceasing.
*Śūraṅgama* is translated as "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena. This refers to the realization of this wondrous mind as the Great Samādhi.
All worldly phenomena are subject to arising and ceasing and are impermanent; they change and transform in an instant. How could there be anything therein that is ultimately solid?
It can be said that this mind alone fundamentally governs all affairs and encompasses all phenomena; in sum, it is the ultimate, solid, and perfect concentration.
Now that this has been realized, although one passes through ten thousand objects, one remains eternally tranquil, and although one responds to ten thousand conditions, one is never disturbed.
These four preceding lines clarify their essential meaning in full within the scripture; one should come to know them for oneself when encountering the text.
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying... up to "...returned to the place where the Buddha was.
This section is called the Introduction (*nidāna*), which provides the context for the preaching of the sutra.
From "Thus have I heard" up to "Mañjuśrī served as the leader" follows the general formula common to all sutras; whenever the Buddha preached a sutra, it invariably contained this.

Because there are six kinds [of introductory accounts], the commentators must recount them to provide evidence that the compilation of this sutra is not false, thereby causing people to have deep faith.
From the time King Prasenajit arrived until his return to the Buddha’s presence constitutes the introductory narrative of this sutra.
This introduction concerns Ānanda’s begging for alms, during which he mistakenly entered a brothel; it was then that the Buddha preached the Great Dhāraṇī of the Buddha-Usnīṣa.
He commanded Mañjuśrī to go and rescue [him]; within these words, there are many profound meanings that must not be overlooked.
Among all the disciples, Ānanda was foremost in his extensive learning; whatever the Buddha taught, he memorized and retained it without the slightest omission.
Thus, when he daily discussed the mind and nature, expounding the subtle and the profound, how could he have been unclear? Since he was already so learned...
Not being one who exclusively prizes learning based on words and ears, he resolved to take refuge in the Buddha’s teachings and study the Buddha’s practice;

thus, while entering the city to beg for alms, he recalled the Buddha’s reprimand of Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for their lack of impartiality, and immediately gave rise to a mind of equality and practiced equal compassion.
He begged for food without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy, maintaining a solemn and dignified demeanor at all times.
Gongzhai’s Dharma-straightness was truly such that he followed the rules and treaded the narrow path, contemplating at every step how to become a Buddha;
his extensive learning led him to resolve thus and to practice with such vigor that he ought to have traversed all circumstances with immunity from harm.
How is it that upon suddenly encountering Mātanga and the Brahma-mantra, he was immediately drawn into a brothel and completely lost his mastery? This was because—
Their so-called "awakening" is not true awakening, and their so-called "realization" is not true realization;
it is merely a matter of understanding within the faculty of the mind-root (*manas*), which they call "seeing one's nature. They arrange things within the mind-root, intending to become Buddhas.

Such people can be quite self-satisfied when they are at leisure and have no affairs, and they may even maintain their composure when encountering slight or trivial circumstances. However, when suddenly confronted with a situation that is difficult to maintain, they then—
The seven flowers have been split into eight; it is as the ancients said: "When mercury-silver encounters fire, it flies away.
Furthermore, there is a profound meaning in this sutra’s choice of sexual desire (*maithuna*) as the catalyst among all desires.
This is because, among all desires, sexual desire is the most fundamental; for as long as one possesses a body, it must necessarily arise from within sexual desire. This very desire is...
The life-vein (ming-di) that is most difficult to sever follows one through the cycles of the three realms, whether ascending or sinking;
it is largely determined by the gravity of this desire. If this desire is not severed, one will certainly not escape the cycle of rebirth.
To sever this desire, it cannot be said to be severed unless one has truly realized entry into one's original nature. It was for the sake of saving Ānanda that the World-Honored One [spoke thus].
The manifestation of a hundred jewel-lights from within the Great Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa symbolizes the light of supreme wisdom;
the manifestation of emanated Tathāgatas symbolizes the unconditioned Buddha of the mind; and the recitation of the mantra reveals the supreme Dharma of the mind.

All of these emerge from within that which is beyond thought and action, transcending emotion and escaping the realm of vision. Therefore, when the *Mārīcī-dhāraṇī* in Sanskrit encounters [the practitioner], it brings immediate liberation, just as hot water dissolves [impurities].

It is like ice melting under the sun or darkness being pierced by light such that it can never be recovered; yet, since the Buddha’s own power of incantation is sufficient to go and save [them], why must Mañjuśrī be sent with him?

This is because the unsurpassed, profound Dharma cannot be upheld without great wisdom, and a fundamental, grave illness cannot be eradicated without great wisdom; therefore, the specific command for Mañjuśrī serves to manifest the nature of great wisdom.

The meaning of the phrase "the causes and conditions have also arisen" is as follows: one now understands that the World-Honored One’s teaching is of an exceptionally profound flavor, unlike worldly treatises.

Regarding the two lines, "A lustful body came to caress him, nearly destroying the essence of his precepts," various commentaries claim that Ānanda was the lustful body that came to caress him and nearly destroyed the essence of his precepts. Only Wuxing held that Ānanda was a sage of the first fruit (srotāpanna).

When a person attains the Way, they share in the precepts such that there is absolutely no possibility of violation; thus, the two characters "will destroy" (*jiāng huǐ*) are attributed to Māra, meaning that Māra intends to destroy Ānanda’s *śīlaskandha* (precept-body).
This interpretation is extremely precise. What is meant by "following the *śīlaskandha*" refers to what the Sūtra calls the *avijñapti-śīla-skandha* (unmanifest precept-body);
when one maintains it as it is produced through the *jñapticaturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four proclamations), it becomes robust.

If one violates it, one becomes weak; therefore, it is called the "precept-essence" (*śīla-tattva*). Others further claim that since Ānanda was certainly free from any transgression, why did the World-Honored One need to recite mantras to go and protect him?
My humble opinion is that since the Sage manifested traces identical to those of ordinary people, the Dharma should have been such as this.
Ānanda saw the Buddha... [up to] ...it is impossible for one to know the mind through names.
When Ānanda returned and saw the Buddha, he regretted that his previous devotion to extensive learning had not perfected his power of the Way;
this was a major turning point for him. Having repented of his former errors, he sought the correctness of the present and requested the Buddhas to enable him to attain Bodhi.
The "wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna" requested in this Dharma are specific designations for the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
Being a single mind that is detached from all phenomena without leaving a trace is called *śamatha*;
being fully manifest within all phenomena is called *samādhi*; and being both detached and not detached is called *dhyāna*. These three—
It is called "wondrous" because it is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither identical nor distinct.

Furthermore, these three, when situated upon the fundamental substance of the original mind, are termed the "Three Tathāgatagarbhas," like gold within its ore, which is entirely the original substance before any effort has been applied.

When they are situated upon the cultivation and realization of the Bodhisattvas, they are termed the "Three Contemplations," like gold in the furnace, where the original substance gives rise to deliberate effort.
To cultivate one's efforts and return to the fundamental substance is what is termed the "Three Virtues" (triguṇa) upon the Buddhas' attainment of fruition;

it is like gold emerging from the furnace when the process of refinement is complete, its entire essence being pure and singular. When this sutra mentions *śamatha* and so forth, it specifically refers to the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) within the stages of the Bodhisattvas.
However, as these principles are expounded throughout the preceding and following sections, they naturally encompass the meanings of the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) and the Three Virtues.
The "initial expedient means" requested refers to the initial expedient means for practicing these three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

From this point down to the middle of the fourth fascicle, the opening and revealing of the single mind as the perfect fusion of the threefold treasury (*tripiṭaka*) constitutes the initial expedient means prior to contemplation.
From the middle of the fourth fascicle onward, the explanation of the two definitive meanings (*dviniścaya-artha*) represents the very first step for actually practicing contemplation.
The ten-fascicle text is skillfully composed with such meticulous detail that there is nothing within it that those who practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) should not know beforehand;

thus, all ten fascicles constitute the initial skillful means (*upāya*). Why did the Buddha, when Ānanda requested instruction on the initial skillful means for practicing the three contemplations, instead examine the nature of his initial resolve?
It is like a physician treating a patient, who must first diagnose the illness.
One must first identify the source of the illness before one can apply the medicine. It is like a journey of a thousand miles: caution lies in the very first step;

if this step is mistaken, there is no way to reach the destination. Ānanda himself confessed that he beheld the Tathāgata’s peerless and extraordinary marks with his own eyes, and because his heart gave rise to attachment and delight, he resolved to leave the household life. This was merely to pursue external appearances.
The arising of the mind belongs entirely to the realm of delusion; to seek the fruit of Buddhahood by means of this mind is like heading south when one intends to reach Yan.

For if one employs this mind, it matters not whether one gives rise to perverse emotions or commits evil deeds—even if one reaches the point of wearying of the mundane and tending toward the sacred, abandoning the defiled and grasping for the pure, or ultimately arrives at the state where both purity and defilement are discarded and both existence and non-existence are relinquished, one still does not transcend birth and death.
Ultimately, it belongs to saṃsāra; therefore, the World-Honored One urgently sought out and shattered it.

Yet, he did not directly refute its being "mind" but instead traced it circuitously to the place where it resides. This was because the deluded mind has no location; having no location, it has no substance.
Having no location and no substance—what else could it be but delusion? Ānanda’s initial attempt to identify the mind as being within the body was precisely this.
The common failing of ordinary people is that they assume the mind resides within the body; the World-Honored One refutes this by showing that the mind does not exist inside.

For if the mind were located within the body, it would necessarily perceive what occurs inside—just as a person standing in a hall must first see what is within the hall before seeing what is outside.
Since one is entirely unaware of or unable to see anything within the single membrane of the body, it is clear that the mind does not reside therein. (Second Section)
When he attempted to evade by claiming that the mind exists outside the body, the World-Honored One refuted this by means of the mutual awareness between body and mind.

For if the mind were outside the body, then the mind and body would have no connection whatsoever; the mind ought not to know what the eyes see. Yet, since the mind is able to discern what the eyes perceive, it is clear that the mind is certainly not outside.
When he evaded three times by asserting that the mind resides within the hidden sense organs, [the Buddha] stated that the mind does not reside within.
It does not abide externally but is hidden within the sense organs; just as when the eye is inside a crystal, it cannot see the interior yet can illuminate the exterior.
The World-Honored One refutes this by means of the mind not seeing the eye. For while a crystal encasing the eye enables one to see all objects, the eye also sees the crystal itself.
Now you claim that the mind is hidden within the eye and yet can see all things.
Yet, since he cannot see the eye itself, it is clear that the mind does not reside within the sense organs.

In four successive turns, he again flees back to the position that [the mind] is internal, claiming that when one closes the eyes and sees darkness, this constitutes seeing the interior; thus he attempts to resolve the difficulty regarding the inability to see the interior.

The World-Honored One refutes this by pointing out that seeing darkness is not "internal," for when one closes the eyes and sees darkness, the eye faces the darkness, and the darkness exists [outside].
If what is before your eyes is indeed before your eyes, it is not your internal viscera; how then can you say you see within?
If you claim that the object perceived does not exist outside but inside, then the eye must be able to look back upon itself—this error is even more extreme.

Five times he evaded the point by asserting "according to where there is conjunction," meaning that wherever there is conjunction, the mind exists there accordingly. The World-Honored One, however, [responded] that this mind is non-existent.
The refutation of its substance: if the mind possessed a substantial entity, it would necessarily have a point of origin.

Now, when we examine the nature of this cognizing mind through direct experience, we find that it does not emerge from within, nor does it enter from without; thus, it has no place from which it comes.

If the mind possessed a substantial entity, it would necessarily possess a fixed identity; yet this cognizing mind is neither a single entity nor a plurality of entities, nor is it... [it is not any such thing].

If the whole body is not the locus [of consciousness], then the locus itself is indeterminate. Since there is no point of origin from which it comes, how can there be a characteristic of "conjoining with" [the object]?
If the locus itself is indeterminate, how can the principle of "arising in accordance with" [conditions] be established?

You have evaded [this question] six times by claiming that consciousness arises in the "intermediate" space between the internal sense-faculties and external objects. The World-Honored One, however, refutes this by showing that such an intermediate state cannot be established.
If one takes both the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) together as the "middle," then half belongs to the organ and half belongs to the object;

these two stand in opposition, and there is ultimately no middle position. If, on the other hand, one takes that which dwells alone between the organ and the object—without including either—as the "middle," then since it is separate from the organ, it is not cognition, and since it is separate from the object, it is not non-cognition. What essential nature (*svabhāva*) could such a thing possess to constitute a "middle"? (7)
The opponent argues that because the preceding six bases have been refuted, the scriptural authority cited for establishing "non-attachment and no-mind" in all places is undermined;
the World-Honored One counters this by stating that having a mind yet being unattached is itself not non-attachment.

This is because when the World-Honored One extensively discourses on non-attachment within the Prajñāpāramitā assemblies, it is precisely because within the light of Prajñā, all phenomena are fundamentally empty and lack any oppositional counterparts. Now...
If one speaks in terms of the opposition between the two objects of existence and non-existence, then the meaning of "non-attachment" cannot be established.
If it is taken as non-existent, how could there be anything to which one might be attached such that one could speak of being unattached? If it is taken as existent, then one is already attached;

how then can one speak of non-attachment? According to the preceding seven refutations, the mind that was destroyed is precisely the mind that arises and ceases in dependence upon sensory objects. It is entirely...
The Buddha, Ānanda, provisionally demonstrated the deluded state by showing that the mind has no fixed location;
the World-Honored One then thoroughly analyzed and stripped away these views so that all false conceptualizations might be completely eliminated, thereby revealing the single True Reality alone.

If one recognizes this true mind, the minds of the seven locations will altogether become perfectly wondrous, with not a single part to be refuted—just as various images appear within a great round mirror, yet a deluded person grasps at those images as real.

Because it is a mirror, one must exert effort to shatter it; yet, if one recognizes the substance of the mirror, there is no reflection—how could it be a mirror, and what need would there be to shatter it?
Regarding the two lines, "The nails grow, the hair lengthens, the tendons turn, and the veins quiver," Changshui said: "The heart and stomach are set deep within;

even if one does not know them, how could the nails, hair, and skin—being superficial—possibly be difficult to perceive? This explanation is incorrect, for if the heart is already inside, it ought to be... [the text here appears to be truncated].
If the internal and secret [aspects] are already known, how can it be said that the internal and secret are difficult to know while the superficial is easy to understand?

Furthermore, although nails, hair, and so forth appear externally, they actually emerge from within; they are all substances of the body. In my humble opinion, regarding organs such as the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach, one may not perceive them when at rest;
yet when nails grow, hair lengthens, tendons shift, or vessels throb, they are active and thus easily perceived.
"How is it? At that time, Ānanda was among the great assembly... [up to] "...although he had attained much learning, he did not achieve the fruit of sainthood.
The previous section refuted the false mind by showing it has no location; this section directly refutes the false mind. Ānanda sequentially presented the seven locations.
Having already been refuted, they still do not realize that this mind has no location; thus they again inquire about the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because the World-Honored One intends to shatter their minds, he first manifests an auspicious omen to demonstrate it.

Generally, whenever the Buddhas are about to expound the Great Dharma, they invariably emit light and manifest omens as their regular practice, so that those of superior faculties within the Buddha’s assembly may perceive the light and receive its meaning.
The realization of the awakened one is manifested as the radiating of light from many gates, demonstrating that the wisdom-light shines brilliantly at the portals of the six sense faculties.
The sixfold trembling of all Buddha-worlds demonstrates that the ignorance accumulated over countless kalpas is overturned and shattered from this point onward.
The simultaneous manifestation of Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust demonstrates that the realm of wisdom is fully revealed, vast and perfectly luminous throughout the ten directions.
The merging of the various realms into a single realm demonstrates that delusory objects do not separate one from another, as both self and other are forgotten.

That all the great bodhisattvas within those worlds dwell in their own lands with palms joined in reverent listening demonstrates that the mind-measure (*cittamātra*) is fundamentally the original substance and that the hearing of the mind is fundamentally penetrating.
This is truly because, so long as the consciousness-mind has not been shattered, the fundamental light remains at the gateway of the six sense organs.
Obscured by afflictions and accumulated through the habituation of ignorance, it is firm and indestructible; the delusive objects are entirely clouded, creating a separation between self and other.

Only when the delusive consciousness is once shattered should it be understood in this way. Therefore, first a portent was manifested to show him this, and subsequently, for Ānanda, he pointed out the point of error:
that his cultivation would not result in Bodhi, but would instead lead to becoming a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, or an outsider.
The gods, Māras, and others all practice erroneously because they do not know the two kinds of fundamental roots.
These two kinds of fundamental roots are: first, the root of beginningless birth and death, which is this very攀緣心 (攀緣心;
*pán yuán xīn*, the mind that clings to objects) that you and all sentient beings currently take as your own nature; second, the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvāṇa. Then...

That which you now possess as the essential brightness of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-dhātu*), capable of giving rise to all conditions and yet remaining unaffected by those conditions, is precisely this.

The mind that clings to objects is merely consciousness, arising from the six sense organs clinging to the six sense objects. As for the "essential brightness of the consciousness-essence," it refers to the True Mind;
it is not something separate from consciousness, but is the very substance of primordial brightness inherent within this consciousness-essence itself.
The substance [of the Tathāgata] gives rise to all consciousnesses, yet it is truly beyond the reach of the discrimination of those consciousnesses.

Since both the true and the false have already been presented side by side, how is it that Ānanda still has not realized this? Thereupon, [the Buddha] raised his fist to demonstrate it, seeking to verify what Ānanda perceived.
He asked, "By means of whom do you see? To which he replied, "I and the great assembly all see with our eyes."
He asked, "What do you take to be the mind? He replied, "When I use the mind to investigate and pursue it, that which performs the investigation is the mind.
This was no different from what he had perceived at the very beginning when first generating the resolve for enlightenment;
in short, he had identified with the mind of discursive grasping and lost the essence of the primordial luminosity. The Buddha then rebuked him, saying, "This is not your mind. It is merely a guest."

The layered commentary and refutation states: "This is a false conceptualization of the characteristics of external objects (*pūrvadhātu*). Apart from the six external objects, it has no independent substance;

it is merely the cessation of all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. To inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness is still but a matter of the shadows of mental discrimination regarding the *dharmadhātu*.
Apart from these mental objects (*dharmadhātu*), it likewise has no independent substance. This [state of] inwardly maintaining profound stillness is where one is buried and killed.
The state of many sages and worthies—such as the Song dynasty Confucians observing the "vapor" (*qi*) when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused—is found precisely here;
the Laozi’s “attaining the utmost emptiness and maintaining profound stillness” is also found precisely here;
even the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) entered by Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas within Buddhism, and the fruits they realize, are all found precisely here. All of them.

Regarding the statement that when seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing have all ceased, this is the true realm: one fails to realize that there is a state of profound stillness (*youxian*) that can be maintained.
This profound stillness is itself an object of the mind (*dharmāyatana*). One who maintains profound stillness is engaging in discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Since the manifestation of objects through the discrimination of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is nothing other than a shadowy reflection, how much more so is profound stillness itself a shadowy reflection? Furthermore...
"All seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing arise and perish in an instant; how could they possibly produce a fruit that is eternally abiding?
Having heard this, Ānanda again shed tears of sorrow... [until] "...he himself undergoes the cycle of transmigration."
Although Ānanda knew that the deluded mind has no substance, he still did not yet know what constitutes the true [mind]; therefore, he now makes this inquiry.
The Tathāgata’s emission of light from the *svastika* on his chest signifies that the wondrously luminous true mind is fully endowed with myriad virtues;
its inherently existing wisdom-light does not arise from external objects. That the light is brilliant and radiant, manifesting hundreds of thousands of colors, signifies that it surpasses the sun.

The fact that it pervades all Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and as fine as motes of dust, symbolizes that the wondrous enlightened clarity alone perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm.

That it universally sprinkles the crowns of all Tathāgatas in all the precious lands of the ten directions symbolizes that the light of the unsurpassed mind is fundamentally identical for every Buddha. It then turns back to Ānanda and the great assembly.
This indicates that all sentient beings possess the potential for Buddhahood. If one can realize the true mind herein, the instruction is complete;
yet, since Ānanda remains deluded, I must address his specific points of confusion by manifesting the nature of seeing.
This has two purposes: first, because Ānanda initially resolved to seek enlightenment through the faculty of seeing; second, [to demonstrate that]... (the text continues).
All paths lead back to this point of seeing. It is difficult to describe the true mind through words; therefore, it is revealed by means of the nature of seeing.
Although this seeing still carries a trace of delusion, its nature is entirely true. Its essence is without birth or extinction and is not far removed from the true mind.
It is like taking out an ancient mirror and showing it to someone: although it may be slightly covered with dust and grime, it does not hinder its clarity.
In this regard, recognize that it is the mirror. Ānanda has always recognized the seeing as being in the eye;

by dividing seeing and the mind into two separate things, he says that when there are eyes one sees, and when there are no eyes one does not see. This seeing belongs entirely to the realm of arising and ceasing.

The World-Honored One, however, states that even when there are no eyes and one sees darkness, this too is seeing. Thus, one knows that while the external objects may themselves be dark, the seeing itself suffers no loss or impairment.
Distinguishing this from the view of arising and ceasing, and further because seeing occurs even when the eyes are absent, one knows that seeing is not the eye;

the eye merely manifests color, while seeing belongs entirely to the mind. Although Ānanda had reached this point and understood that seeing belongs entirely to the mind, he did not yet know why this mind should be considered true.
The World-Honored One then commanded Kauṇḍinya to explain it from a different perspective, using a peer of his own kind.

People say that the path one has personally practiced is easy to believe and enter. When Cunda received the transmission, he was commanded to recount the causes and conditions of his realization of the Way.
He realized that while "guest-dust" (āgantuka-rajas) comes and goes, the "host" has no place of going;

while dust is subject to movement and agitation, emptiness is fundamentally and eternally quiescent. Thus, he knew that that which moves is delusion, while that which does not move is the truth. From this...
The World-Honored One then opened and closed his hand to demonstrate to Ānanda, so that he might verify that while the hand has opening and closing, the seeing has neither.
This was an external test regarding objects, yet it remained somewhat remote rather than direct.
Thereupon, the Buddha emitted light from his palm which flew into the side of Ānanda’s head, causing him to look left and right; thus he verified that while the head moved, the seeing remained.
"Being unmoving" is the most intimate verification to be drawn from one's own person.
Since you have twice verified that while the body and its objects move, this seeing remains unmoving, you know that what moves is false and that what is unmoving is true.
It is clear that you should maintain the true and abandon the false. How can you clearly know that movement belongs to the body and its objects, yet from beginning to end [fail to realize this]?"

Chasing after delusions and losing the truth, one acts in a state of perversion; having lost that truth, one inevitably mistakes external objects for the self, causing the cycle of rebirth to continue without end.
This is nothing but what one has brought upon oneself—how lamentable it is!
A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll One;
A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánxián of Yǒngquán Chan Monastery at Gǔshān, Fúzhōu.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly (up to) attained what they had never experienced before.
The previous section revealed the stillness of the nature of seeing; this section reveals the permanence of the nature of seeing.

Although Ānanda had received the Buddha’s detailed instruction and understood that the nature of seeing was unmoving, he still feared that this seeing might arise and perish along with the body; therefore, he requested the Buddha to further elucidate it for him.

At that time, King Prasenajit, having previously heard the non-Buddhists claim that there is annihilation after death, and having now heard from the Buddha that there is no extinction after death, still harbored doubts and had not yet realized the nature of non-arising and non-extinction;
therefore, he also asked a question from the side. The Buddha first examined the transformation and decay of the body in order to reveal by contrast the unchanging nature of the self.
The King then said: "Although this body has never ceased to exist, one observes that it undergoes transformation and decay from moment to moment;
it is ever-new and does not abide, like fire burning wood that ultimately returns to ashes. One knows with certainty that this body must eventually perish through change.
Yet, because the Buddha still wishes to describe in detail the characteristics of this transformation and decay so as to enlighten the great assembly, he asks again about its facial features."
When you were a child, Your Majesty said to yourself: "From childhood I have grown to youth, and from youth to old age; what was once flourishing is now in decline—how can these be compared?

Yet even so, with the deluded mind of an ordinary person, you always presumed that youth and vigor could be relied upon, failing to perceive their transformation, and thus you asked why things do not suddenly decay.
Your Majesty then replied: "Change and transformation shift subtly and secretly; it is truly because one does not perceive them."

It is only by reflecting on the past through subsequent thought that one deeply realizes their difference; yet, if one observes according to coarse characteristics—taking even ten years as a measure—one perceives only aging and decay.
However, if one reflects with subtle discernment, it is clear that this is merely a matter of moment-to-moment, thought-to-thought continuity that never ceases, steadily tending toward exhaustion.
Thus, one knows that this body must inevitably undergo transformation and extinction. O King, regarding the arising and ceasing of this body:
Although you have already fully comprehended the characteristics of impermanence, you have not yet realized that within this very process there exists a nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.

Therefore, the Buddha used the witness of the Ganges to demonstrate this: consider whether the Ganges you saw at the age of three is in any way different from the Ganges you see now at the age of sixty-two; if it is not, then you shall know the nature of the body.
There is a difference between the old and the young in terms of their vision; there is no difference between the old and the young in terms of the body itself.

The body is that which undergoes transformation, whereas vision does not undergo transformation. Since that which undergoes transformation is subject to extinction, how could that which does not undergo transformation possibly have extinction?
Thus, after the body has perished, one abandons this life to move toward another life. Having already experienced such extinction, why should one harbor any doubt?
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat... [up to] ...the Tathāgata calls them those who are to be pitied.
Because Ānanda had previously stated that the mind does not undergo extinction, he then doubted: "Since it does not undergo extinction, there must be no loss;
for what reason does the World-Honored One reproach us for losing the true nature and acting in a perverted manner? The World-Honored One then took up [the matter].
The analogy of the upright and inverted hand means that when an upright hand is turned to become an inverted hand, it is merely a matter of exchanging the head for the tail;

the world then considers it inverted, yet has the hand actually lost anything? Know by this example that while the Tathāgata is called "Perfectly All-Knowing" (Samyak-saṃbuddha), you are called "inverted in nature";
this is because people themselves give rise to inversions, whereas the nature itself is not actually defective.
The following passage is the formal explanation of the point regarding inversion. It is because the measure of the true mind encompasses empty space and its function pervades the entire dharma-realm;
all phenomena, whether sentient or insentient, are without exception manifestations of this mind.

How can one lose this original mind, fail to recognize it, and instead recognize the mind as being confined within the physical body? This is to mistake delusion for enlightenment within the midst of enlightenment. Enlightenment.

This means that the wondrous mind is originally void and luminous; through delusion, it is falsely bound, and its mental characteristics become obscured and darkened, becoming what is called "emptiness.
This section now correctly elucidates this meaning: the single true Dharma-realm is entirely empty, which is awakening;

when ignorance suddenly arises, it becomes obscured and transforms into stubborn emptiness—this is the initial manifestation of empty space. Within the darkness of this obscured emptiness, as accumulated delusion becomes firm, it then forms [the world].

Darkness gives rise to form; this is the beginning of the establishment of this world. When deluded thoughts grasp at deluded forms, and deluded forms mingle with deluded thoughts, they bind together to form the sense organs; this is the beginning of the formation of this deluded body.
When external deluded conditions gather reflections within, there is arising and ceasing without end; when internal deluded consciousness discriminates the external, it rushes toward it.

To wander without ceasing in this state of murky confusion and agitation, and to falsely take this for the nature of the mind—once one is deluded into taking this as the mind, one will inevitably be confused by the thought that this mind resides within the physical body.
One fails to realize that everything outside the physical body—the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—is all an object within my wondrously luminous mind;
yet now, one instead identifies the mind as being inside the body. This is precisely [the error].
To abandon the ocean and recognize only the bubble is already delusion; how much more so to mistake the bubble for the ocean—is this not doubling one's delusion?

It is just like one who has fallen headlong and mistakes the head for the tail. Now, when the meanings of manifestation, stillness, and permanence are explained, they all rely upon the seeing-nature (*darśana-svabhāva*) for their expression.
Why is it that when explaining the meaning of perfect pervasiveness, the seeing-nature is not employed, but the mind-nature (*citta-svabhāva*) is directly cited instead?
Because the perception of the nature [of the mind] was still inverted and restricted to within the body, the meaning of the True Mind has been fully revealed here without remainder.
Below this, because Ānanda repeatedly gave rise to further doubts for the sake of future generations, there are six further rounds of discussion.
If this inversion involves the exchange of head and tail, some old commentaries may insist that the downward-pointing hand is correct, while the upward-pointing hand is not.

Whether one considers it inverted or upright depends on whether one holds the hand vertically as "upright" or hanging down as "inverted. The fool claims there is no fixed theory regarding the inversion or uprightness of the hand;
Ānanda merely defined inversion and uprightness according to worldly convention, and the Buddha likewise provisionally took this worldly inversion and uprightness as a metaphor.
The traditional interpretation uses the fact that worldly people do not recognize the inversion and uprightness of the hand as a metaphor for mental delusion.

Regarding the phrase "upside down yet not upside down," using the analogy of an inverted hand to illustrate perversion (*viparyāsa*) reveals an even greater error, as will be shown below in the passage beginning with "Just as when I hang my hand," where there is no difference between hanging [the hand] and being upside down;
this serves as particularly clear evidence. Why must one wait for a mistaken perception of the hand’s inversion or non-inversion before it can serve as an analogy for perversion?
As for these several lines concerning perversion, many of the ancient commentaries are unstable; I shall now offer my own interpretation.
When the Buddha raised his hand, he had already conformed to worldly convention by establishing what is correct; yet he then said that this "correct hand" was actually inverted and hanging downward.
This merely involves replacing the upward-pointing head with the downward-pointing tail and the downward-pointing tail with the upward-pointing head.
To the worldly eye, this differs from the "correct hand" by a factor of two, such that one considers it to be correct.
First, although inversion and correctness differ, how could there be any loss in the substance of the hand? That the hand does not lose its intended purpose means that correctness cannot be lacking;
this answers the question regarding what was omitted.
Ānanda received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue... (up to)... for this reason, the Tathāgata is named "The Compassionate One."

Although Ānanda was able to understand the Buddha’s teaching on the perfect and eternally abiding nature, he did so merely by using his conceptualizing mind to differentiate the sounds of the Dharma, thereby manifesting a shadowy reflection of that perfection and permanence;
it was not yet a realization of profound resonance with the true essence through the forgetting of emotions and the cessation of consciousness.
Having obtained only this state of mind, Ānanda mistakenly took it to be his original, fundamental ground of the mind.

Thus, since the Buddha has already deeply condemned desire and not recognized it as the fundamental source of the mind-ground, where then could that which is called "perfectly complete and eternally abiding" be?
This is why one seeks the Buddha to uproot the root of doubt. Ānanda, this question is most critical;
among those in the world who call themselves students of the Way, nine out of ten fall into this very error. Can anyone truly fail to recognize it?
Those who take this as the fundamental ground of the mind are rare. The Buddha told Ānanda: "What follows first breaks down the dharmas that serve as objects of perception.
This means that if one uses a perceiving mind to listen to the perfect and eternally abiding Dharma, then that perfect and eternally abiding state becomes merely an object of perception.

Since the Dharma has become an object, how can it be the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)? It is just like a person using a finger to point at the moon; if they grasp the finger instead of the moon, they will never see the moon.
One must look at the moon; if one mistakes the finger for the moon, the error is no small matter.

Here, by means of the Dharma-sound, the lower [teaching] breaks through the mind that acts as the perceiving subject. This is because this mind, apart from the Dharma-sound, possesses no inherent nature of discernment.
It is like a guest who comes and goes temporarily, not like a host who dwells permanently; how could it be real? Not only does it discern the sound of "self,"...
Apart from the sound of "self," there is a non-discriminative nature; even when one discriminates the appearance of "self," there is likewise a non-discriminative nature.

Even if all discrimination were entirely absent, this state would remain profound and obscure; therefore, it is not form (*rūpa*). If there were any essence within form, it would not be emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Externalists call this the "Primal Truth" (*tattva*), claiming that because it exists apart from sensory objects, it possesses a substantial body and should be recognized as the true nature.
Yet you do not realize that this is precisely the dharma-object within the mental faculty (*manas*). When the mental faculty encounters dharma-objects, there are two modes: arising and ceasing.
If one now discriminates but does not engage in activity, this is precisely the cessation of objects; it is the detachment from all dharma-objects.

Furthermore, there is no discriminating self-nature. Viewed from this perspective, that which you call "the nature of the mind" is merely the True Suchness (*tathatā*) returning to its original state.
How can that which is the master not returning be considered "true"? To "return" means, for example, that if a guest comes from another region, they may return to that other region;
however, because a host dwells permanently here, they cannot return.
All worldly conditions have their respective causes, and thus each has its own point of return; just as light comes from the solar orb, it may return to the sun.
"Darkness returns from the dark moon to the moon itself," and so forth; this alone refers to the essence of seeing, which possesses its own illuminating power and does not derive it from another.
Therefore, it cannot be returned. As for that which can be returned, it is naturally not the mind.
Since it cannot be returned, and yet it is neither you nor anyone else, it is for this reason designated as the fundamentally wondrous, pure, and luminous mind.
Ānanda said, "Although I recognize this nature of seeing [up to: 'your nature is not true; take mine to seek the reality.

Although Ānanda recognized that the nature of seeing has no place to return, he still doubted whether seeing must necessarily see objects. He thought that if one sets aside objects, there is no seeing;
thus, this seeing merely grasps the reflected images of external objects and is ultimately a mixture of delusion. How can it be called my true nature? The Buddha replied:

First, the five kinds of seeing are listed; although there is a distinction between the Buddhas and ordinary beings regarding the breadth or narrowness of their vision, they are all equally of the nature of that which is able to see.
Next, the objects seen by Ānanda are listed; although they differ in various ways, they are all equally things that are seen.
Within this context, one must discern who is the "self-substance" that is the seer, and who is [the object].

Is there not indeed a distinction between the objects perceived and their images? However, if one observes that while the objects and images have differences, the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) has no difference, then it becomes clear that seeing transcends objects and cannot be confused with them.

The subsequent lines, beginning with "If seeing were an object," further clarify that seeing is not an object by contrasting the visibility of objects with the invisibility of seeing itself. Thus, it is demonstrated that seeing is not an object.
If you claim that seeing must necessarily involve an object, then seeing itself would also be an object.
If seeing were an object, then seeing could itself be seen. If seeing could be seen, then you could see my seeing; yet how could my seeing ever be seen?
If you take the common perception of the objects I see to be my seeing itself, then when I—
When you do not see objects, how is it that you also do not see the place where I do not see?
If you claim that you can see the place where I do not see, then you must be generating false conceptualizations; this would naturally not be the characteristic of that "not seeing.
If you claim that you do not see the place where I do not see, then my seeing would ultimately remain invisible. If my seeing ultimately remains invisible, then...
Your seeing is also not something that can be seen; since seeing cannot be seen, it is naturally not a material thing. How could it not be your true nature?
Furthermore, the subsequent sentences below clarify that seeing is not a material thing by demonstrating that the categories of "self" and "other" (or "subject" and "object") are not established.
When you see a thing now, since you have seen the thing, the thing also sees you. Your seeing—[is thus mutual].

If your seeing were separate from objects, it would necessarily be mixed with them; you would then take yourself to be the object and the object to be yourself, such that your essential nature would become confused and intermingled.
How then could you, I, and all the world be established as distinct objects and selves?
Know therefore that your seeing must be you and not the object; thus, the nature of your seeing is all-pervasive and universal.
I am correcting your true nature; why do you doubt that it is not real and instead seek the truth by relying on my words?
Ānanda, your seeing of nature must be mine and no other—[it is] capable of universally containing the lands of the ten directions.

Because of the Buddha’s words that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive and is thus his own true nature, Ānanda became suspicious that the nature of seeing must have obstructions and therefore cannot be the true nature.
Consequently, he raised what he himself had witnessed to ask: "I once followed the Buddha to the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings and resided in the palaces of the sun and moon;
at those times, this seeing extended directly throughout the Sahā world, yet upon returning to the vihāra, it was restricted only to this place."
If one asks: within a single room, since this seeing is fundamentally pervasive by its very nature, why is it that what was previously seen as vast is now seen as small?
Is the vastness contracted into something small, or is it severed by walls and buildings? What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha’s intended answer is that it is not the seeing itself that has dimensions of large or small; rather, it is the fault of not having forgotten the external objects before one.
The ear is like the space seen within a square vessel appearing square, or the space seen within a round vessel appearing round.
It is not that space itself possesses a fixed squareness or roundness, nor is it indeterminate in its squareness or roundness; rather, it assumes squareness and roundness because of the vessels.
If one simply removes the vessels, the space naturally lacks any squareness or roundness. How could one further ask where the meaning of this space’s squareness or roundness resides? Now...
The perception of large and small arises from the objects with which it encounters; it is not that the seeing itself has a fixed largeness or smallness, nor is it indeterminate in size.
Rather, largeness and smallness are produced by virtue of external objects. If one simply removes those external objects, the seeing itself will naturally have no largeness or smallness.
How, then, could one further inquire as to where the meaning of this seeing’s largeness or smallness resides? If you believe that the essence of seeing...
When entering a room, can this vision be contracted and made small? When gazing at the sun, can this vision be drawn out and made large?
When walls and buildings stand, can this vision be split and severed? When pierced into a small hole, can this vision be joined and made to pass through?
How could such a principle possibly be so? Generally speaking, all sentient beings are simply because they do not... [text truncated]
To realize that all things are oneself, yet to be deluded by regarding oneself as a thing, is to lose the fundamental mind of the oneness of all things.
Since things are not the mind, not only do they fail to follow the turning of the mind, but they instead turn the mind itself.

Consequently, one is obstructed by things in movement, and whether viewing the great or the small, there is no portion of freedom. If one can realize that all things are one body, then [this is not so].

Only by not being turned by phenomena can one daily turn phenomena; if one can turn phenomena, then one’s body and mind will be as perfectly luminous as those of the Tathāgata, remaining unmoving within the site of enlightenment, and even upon the tip of a single hair, one can universally contain the lands of the ten directions.

"The tip of a hair" refers to the smallest unit of the primary retribution (the physical body), while "the lands of the ten directions" refers to the greatest extent of the secondary retribution (the environment).
The great containing the lands within a single hair-tip is the subsumption of the basis by the correct [phenomenon], which is also the small containing the great.

The ten directions existing within a hair-tip is the entry of the basis into the correct [phenomenon], which is also the great entering the small. When one views the lands within a hair-tip, the lands do not diminish;
this is the manifestation of the great within the small. When one views the hair-tip from outside the lands, the hair-tip does not expand; this is the manifestation of the small within the great.

This is indeed the ultimate point where the illumination and function of all Buddhas are perfectly interfused. According to this chapter, the power to transform objects depends entirely upon delusive sensory objects;

the efficacy of these delusive objects cannot be lightly estimated. This is because one must enter through deep cultivation of contemplative practice until the mind-ground suddenly opens up and the boundaries of body and world instantly vanish.
Only then does one reach the stage of "semblance non-obstruction," which extends even to the aggregate of form.

When all is exhausted throughout the ten directions and the void is opened so that there is no longer any darkness, and when the internal and external boundaries of the body are seen as clearly as fruit held in the palm, this is truly non-obstruction in its essence;

yet it is not yet non-obstruction in its function. Only when the primary and secondary, the large and the small, are entirely free of hindrance is it non-obstruction in function, and at that point, the Buddha’s work of capability is complete.
"If this essence of seeing is necessarily my luminous nature" (up to) "therefore it can cause you to distinguish between the finger and what is not the finger.
Ānanda, having heard the teaching that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive, then doubted: "If it is said to be all-pervasive, then it is not confined within the body or before the face;
there must be seeing everywhere. Furthermore, since I see objects, everything before me is nothing other than my own seeing."
Therefore it is said: "To see one's nature is to have it manifest before me. This may appear to be a shallow statement, yet it contains a profound meaning that must be understood.
For the measure of seeing one's nature encompasses the ten directions and its essence contains all phenomena; it is neither identical to nor separate from those phenomena.

Because it is not identical, the numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects, remaining unmixed with the physical body and the realms of existence, and untouched by birth and death.
If sentient beings are bound by not comprehending this principle, they will confuse the real with the false and sink into the cycle of saṃsāra;

since they lack the wisdom to distinguish them for themselves, how could they ever attain liberation? Precisely because it is not something separate, the dust-like lands and the myriad things are fused into a single body, its function pervading the entire dharma-realm, and its existence and disappearance are both free.
If sentient beings do not comprehend this principle, they will remain submerged in darkness and stagnate.
In the state of quiescent extinction where all entanglements are severed and emptiness prevails, one has already lost sight of the family treasure within; how, then, could it be put to use?

Since this sutra has, from the initial inquiry regarding the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment, consistently sought to shatter the false to reveal the true, it has deeply clarified the meaning that [the nature of mind] is not identical [to the physical senses], yet the principle that it is not separate from them remains unclarified.
For this reason, Ānanda feigned ignorance and dullness, specifically manifesting the nature of seeing before him.

Zhiwen’s intention was to prompt the World-Honored One to provide a teaching on returning to the True by means of the false, thereby clarifying the meaning that [the true] is not separate from [the false].
The Buddha replied: "Because you said you see me before you, I shall cause you to examine each and every thing within the field of vision before you:
is it truly seeing, or is it not seeing? If you consider it to be seeing, then everything pointed out would be a material object."
What does "seeing" refer to? If you consider it not to be seeing, then since you have already perceived an object, how can it not be seeing?

Ānanda, this matter is not fixed, yet the World-Honored One has validated both positions; where, then, lies his true intention? This principle is extremely profound, such that none but one of great wisdom can fathom it.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī specifically requested an explanation, and the Buddha then revealed to him the nature of seeing and non-seeing.
The objects seen and the characteristics conceived are like flowers in the sky; fundamentally they do not exist.
They are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi, which is but a single entity and inherently non-dual. How could one falsely distinguish between right and wrong?
Thus, Mañjuśrī is used as a metaphor to clarify the meaning that there can be no such distinction. It is said that Mañjuśrī is but a single person; how could there be another?
Can Mañjuśrī be divided into right and wrong? Yet it is not that there is no Mañjuśrī; only then can it be said that he cannot be judged as right or wrong.
By this analogy, one knows that there is only the single true mind—how could there be another thing that could be divided into right and wrong?
Yet it is not that there is no true mind at all; only then can it be said that it cannot be judged as right or wrong. Since there is only the single truth, and now...
To see that there is form and emptiness, as well as a seer and a hearer—how can this be anything other than the false perceptions clung to by sentient beings, like a second moon?
This second moon is seen only because of a diseased eye; it has no reality whatsoever, being nothing but the one moon.
How could one possibly debate right or wrong regarding that single moon? Therefore, what is seen through your own deluded thoughts cannot [be taken as real].
When one emerges from these notions of right and wrong, realizing that this is the single, true, subtle, wondrous, and luminous nature of awakening, then right and wrong naturally vanish;
there is nothing to point to, nor is there anything not to point to.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, it is truly as [you have said]... [until] one shall not grow weary on the sublime path to Bodhi."
Ānanda had already understood what was previously said, yet he remained concerned that the listeners might not grasp it clearly and could thus be confused with the teachings of external paths;
for a difference of a mere hair can lead to a separation of a thousand li. Therefore, he raised two further questions. His first question concerns "that which perceives conditions":

"perceives" refers to the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*), while "conditions" refers to the causal conditions of that nature of awakening. Since it was previously stated that all phenomena are entirely subsumed within the fundamental nature, this [nature] is not [a conditioned phenomenon].
They divide the nature of awakening and its conditions, and together regard them as pervading the ten directions, abiding eternally in stillness, neither arising nor ceasing.
There, among the non-Buddhists, there is one named Sāṃkhyakāra who establishes twenty-five principles (*tattva*);
the first principle is called *avyakta* (the Unmanifest), which he points to as the fundamental source of all phenomena and the eternally abiding substantial reality. This, however, is merely...
When seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving momentarily cease, a state of profound stillness appears; this is merely a reflection of mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*) and not the true nature.
Regarding the "true self" pointed out by various non-Buddhist outsiders, such as those who smear themselves with ashes, there are generally three types:
first, the vast self; second, the subtle self; and third, the self of indeterminate size. What I now refer to as "pervading the ten directions" refers to [the latter].
This is precisely the "vast self. These various so-called "selves" are all external to the elephant [the mind], grasping at emptiness as having a separate intrinsic nature;
furthermore, they possess dimensions of magnitude and trace the marks of coming and going. Therefore, they are all false teachings and do not constitute the true self.
The second question asks about "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*): because those non-Buddhists outside our tradition frequently speak of spontaneity, they refer to the internal nature of the mind as such.
Externally, all phenomena belong to the realm of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), yet the Buddha extensively taught the principle of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) to refute this view.

He maintained that just as internally, the spiritual capacities of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*) must take the seeds cultivated in previous lives as their cause and further rely on the auxiliary conditions of various teachings to finally achieve fruition;
so too externally, the hundred grains and other crops must have seeds as their cause and further rely on the auxiliary conditions of earth, water, and so forth.

It is like saying that conditions must first arise before sprouts and the like can be produced; yet now, hearing the Buddha’s teaching that the nature of awakening is neither born nor extinguished and is far removed from all false delusions, one concludes that the principle of causes and conditions does not apply at all. Thus, one again suspects that it is close to the doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
What is not understood is that the Buddha’s teaching on causes and conditions was intended to refute spontaneity; it is entirely a provisional teaching and not the ultimate truth.
For the sake of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the Buddha refuted this, saying: "Those who maintain the doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) must necessarily have a self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, regarding this perceived fruit, what constitutes its self-nature? If light were its self-nature, it should not perceive darkness;
if darkness were its self-nature, it should not perceive light, and so forth. Thus, one knows that self-nature lacks any fixed principle, and therefore [the concept of] spontaneity is untenable."
He refutes those who maintain that [the visual faculty] arises from causes and conditions, saying: "That which exists must necessarily have a cause before it comes to be.
Now, as for this seeing, by what cause does it exist? If it exists because of light, one should not see darkness; if it exists because of darkness, one should not see light.
From this, one knows that this seeing does not arise from a cause; thus, the doctrine of causes and conditions is incorrect. Regarding this cause, the Buddha...
If conditions arise spontaneously, whether they mutually negate or mutually establish one another, it is not that one intends to establish both, nor does one intend to negate both;

nor is it a case of negation and establishment being indeterminate. To speak at the ultimate level: there is neither dependence on causes and conditions nor spontaneity, neither non-dependence on causes and conditions nor non-spontaneity;
there is no "is" and no "is not," no "not-is" and no "not-not-is. For as soon as one enters the realm of emotional views, everything is but emptiness.
If one can merely contemplate the detachment from all marks of false conceptualization, then every phenomenon (*dharma*) will be entirely and perfectly true.

Ānanda, not yet having grasped the Buddha’s intention, again cited another teaching from the past to raise an objection: "In the past, the Buddha said that seeing must depend on space, light, the mind, and the eyes;
only when these four conditions are fulfilled does seeing come to be. This was a provisional [teaching] of the Hīnayāna."

Because this sutra explains the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it differs from that [previous teaching]. It does not simply claim that the essence of seeing (*darśana-essence*) does not depend on external conditions;

rather, it shows that just as worldly people only obtain the name "seeing" by means of the sun, moon, or lamps, they do not realize that even when the sun, moon, and lamps are absent, the dark appearance perceived at that time is also precisely seeing.
This is because the two objects—light and darkness—mutually overcome one another, yet seeing has never for a moment been non-existent. This is what is meant by "knowing-seeing."
Seeing in light is not seeing by means of light; seeing in darkness is not seeing by means of darkness; seeing through openness is not seeing by means of openness;
seeing through obstruction is not seeing by means of obstruction. Once these four principles are established, it is clear that the essence of seeing is definitively detached from conditions.

If even the essence of seeing is detached from conditions, how much more so the True Seeing that is able to see this essence of seeing? Thus, the True Seeing stands utterly apart from the essence of seeing.

It is not something that can be reached by the faculty of seeing; how could it be falsely conceptualized through the frivolous doctrines of cause and condition, spontaneity, or the harmonious and non-harmonious?
As for "true seeing," because it takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, wisdom and its object are of one essence, and subject and object are not divided;
therefore, it is called true seeing. As for the "faculty of seeing," it takes external, real objects as its domain, which are transformations produced by the karma-consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
Because that which has been traversed is thus [illusory], it is called "false. When the true seeing is manifest, there is absolutely no false seeing standing in opposition as its object.
It is simply like a person who, upon waking, realizes that what preceded was a dream; one who knows it is a dream—could that person be dreaming again?
Therefore it is said: "At the time of seeing the seeing, the seeing is not seeing; even seeing is detached from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it. (According to...)

In this sutra, because the true seeing was previously difficult to manifest, the "seeing-essence" (*jienjing*) was borrowed to reveal it; this was thus a case of revealing the true by means of the delusory.
Here, fearing that people might ultimately mistake the seeing-essence for the ultimate meaning and fail to accord with its principle, [the Buddha] further states: "The seeing of seeing is not seeing.
This is the stripping away of delusion to bring forth the truth, wherein the Buddha’s secret intent is fully exhausted without exception. Someone asked about this.
This chapter contains two questions in total. Why is it that all the Buddha’s answers now pertain only to the latter question, with not a single word regarding the former?

The answer is: there are two reasons for this. First, the "primordial darkness" (*ādikṛta*) and the "true self" (*ātman*) established by the non-Buddhists are both clung to as being spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, when the Buddha now refutes spontaneity, he simultaneously refutes primordial darkness and the true self. Furthermore, this...

Answer: It transcends the realm of emotion, is free from views, and all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are sublated within it; furthermore, how could there be any doctrine of a primordial darkness (*ādikṛta*) or a true self (*ātman*)?
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha [has taught], fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is eternally abiding."
Previously, the Buddha had consistently used the act of seeing to reveal the true nature, yet Ānanda failed to understand, mistaking the faculty of sight for the true nature itself.

Furthermore, he did not grasp the teaching that while the hearing-faculty can see, it is not the true seeing. Consequently, his confusion and distress increased even further. The World-Honored One then pointed out his ailment, stating:
"Although the nature of seeing is close to the truth, it still carries two kinds of delusion. Since there is this deluded seeing, it must reside within the locus of seeing."
Since afflictions and karma arise, once afflictions and karma exist, one must undergo the cycle of rebirth by drawing forth fruits within the sphere of karma;

this demonstrates that the nature of seeing is the root of the cycle of birth and death. Regarding what are called the "two kinds of false seeing," the first is termed "false seeing of individual karma.
This refers to the realm drawn by one's own karma, which is seen personally by a single individual as a realm of intimate proximity; as for the beauty or foulness of that realm—
That which one actually experiences for oneself has no relation to others, just as a person with cataracts sees a halo of five colors around a lamp that no one else perceives.
The first is called "common delusive vision," meaning that what is experienced is induced by shared karma;
it refers to distant objects perceived collectively by a multitude, where the beauty or ugliness of those objects is not for one's private enjoyment alone, but is common to all.
For example, when the people of a single country collectively encounter adverse conditions, they perceive various calamitous omens that do not exist in other countries.

Now, let us clarify this by examining it through two perspectives: the advancing and the retreating. Just as sentient beings, due to the deluded perceptions of their individual karma, see circular shadows when a diseased eye gazes at a lamp’s light;
although these appear to be external objects before them, they are ultimately produced by the eye's own cataracts and do not exist externally.

Just as the physical form produced by this cataract can only be seen by one who possesses it—and only such a person is free from the fault of the cataract—so too, when one person’s eye perceives mountains, rivers, nations, and all sentient beings, these are likewise formed by false perceptions.
These lands and sentient beings are originally my own enlightened awareness; because it is obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*), I myself see the shadows of that ignorance.
This shadow is entirely due to the cataract; only one who can perceive this cataract is the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) and is not the cataract itself.
Since one has momentarily perceived the cataract, one has already emerged from its exterior; how could one be called "seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing" again?
For that [awakening] is the true nature of seeing, and thus it is no longer termed "seeing. It is like the common deluded vision shared by all sentient beings.
The manifestations arising from miasmic evils, though appearing as present calamitous signs, are close to reality yet no different from the shadows of a lamp.
This is because both arise from the eye-disease of the observer and from miasmic evils respectively; neither is truly existent, being merely the product of a single deluded perception.
Now, using this as an analogy for the lands and sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm, these very lands and sentient beings [are likewise unreal].

Although these appear to be external objects, they are in fact identical to my own enlightened awareness—the pure, untainted, wondrous mind—from which seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing suddenly arise.

From this, delusions are produced, karma is created, and these illusory conditions of sickness emerge. They are born from the conjunction of the subjective support and the objective field, and they perish when that conjunction ends.
How could they possess any reality? If one can prevent such false perceptions from arising and remain far removed from them, [one attains liberation].
When the conditions for illusory affliction neither harmonize nor disharmonize, then it is not merely that karmic fruits cease to continue;
the very root of birth and death is likewise extinguished. By this, one can fulfill Bodhi and restore the original, pure, fundamental awakening (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-ālaya*).
These two matters—progress and retreat—are clearly elucidated together, just as they differ among those sentient beings.
From the delusive vision of karma up to the vision of the illness, these are formed by advancing the lamp’s shadow to conjoin with the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*).
Because one’s own vision and what is seen are taken as conditions, this is not called "vision"; rather, it is a regression of the environment and its inhabitants to conjoin with the lamp’s shadow.

This is like the common delusive vision shared by those sentient beings, extending to all other beings; this is advancing the calamitous phenomena to conjoin with the world, which is itself identical to awakening.

Clarifying that the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is eternally present, one observes that this world of decline is formed through the repeated and exhaustive investigation of calamitous phenomena;

it is seen to be composed solely of delusive vision. Since this delusive vision is none other than fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is not easily eradicated, the Buddha urgently designates "awakening free from eye-disease" within the context of individual karma, and profoundly clarifies the merit of distancing oneself from it within the context of commonality (*sabhāgatā*).
