It is truly because true awakening must manifest before deluded vision can be abandoned; and only when deluded vision is abandoned can true awakening be restored.
If one merely guards the nature of seeing without knowing how to abandon delusion, how could one possibly sever the cycle of saṃsāra and realize the eternally abiding?

Regarding the phrase "Just as those sentient beings share the same deluded vision," the ancient commentaries of the lower [tradition] point to this as an instance where advancing and retreating are combined for clarification;
however, this is not the case. Both the *Moxiang* (Feeling the Elephant) and the *Zhengmai* (Correct Pulse) do not accept this interpretation.

Nevertheless, because this section contains traces of a back-and-forth discussion, an error was consequently introduced. Yet, this section specifically cites the signs of calamity and must necessarily be treated as a distinct category of karmic retribution.

For what reason? Because these calamitous signs appear as if real, one must necessarily take the analogy of a lamp’s reflection to clarify their falsity; only then can they serve as a valid example. Question: This chapter states that the "sickness of seeing" is the most subtle. Seeing worlds and sentient beings is called false. If so, does it follow that one must not see worlds and sentient beings at all for it to be called "true seeing"? Answer: No. It is because one sees them as real that it is called false seeing. If one does not see them as real, then it is true seeing. Therefore, the sickness lies precisely in the act of seeing; it is not that there is no seeing at all. If one were entirely without seeing, who would then be able to perceive that this is true seeing? Thus, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is like a person with an eye disease who, upon being cured, no longer sees flowers in the sky; although they do not see flowers, they clearly know that those flowers were originally non-existent. If they did not see them at all, how could they know they were non-existent? True seeing is also like this. Although one does not see worlds and sentient beings, one clearly knows that they are originally non-existent. If one were entirely without seeing, how could one know that these worlds and sentient beings are originally non-existent? Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained true seeing. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained true seeing. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of all delusion. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has eradicated the root of delusion. If the root of delusion is eradicated, then one has attained true seeing. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained liberation. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained liberation. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of bondage. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has severed the root of bondage. If the root of bondage is severed, then one has attained liberation. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the Way. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the Way. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of the non-Way. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has eliminated the root of the non-Way. If the root of the non-Way is eliminated, then one has attained the Way. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the Buddha-way. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the Buddha-way. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of non-Buddhahood. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has destroyed the root of non-Buddhahood. If the root of non-Buddhahood is destroyed, then one has attained the Buddha-way. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the Tathāgata-way. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the Tathāgata-way. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of non-Tathāgatahood. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has removed the root of non-Tathāgatahood. If the root of non-Tathāgatahood is removed, then one has attained the Tathāgata-way. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has cut off the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. If the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas is cut off, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the ultimate Way. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the ultimate Way. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of the non-ultimate way. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has exhausted the root of the non-ultimate way. If the root of the non-ultimate way is exhausted, then one has attained the ultimate Way. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has severed the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times. If the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times is severed, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has eliminated the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions. If the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions is eliminated, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the ten directions. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times and ten directions. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times and ten directions. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times and ten directions. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has destroyed the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times and ten directions. If the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times and ten directions is destroyed, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the three times and ten directions. Therefore, the absence of the sickness of seeing is itself true seeing. It is not that there is no seeing at all. Furthermore, if one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future. If one still sees the sickness of seeing, then one has not yet attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future. Why? Because the sickness of seeing is the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future. If one does not see the sickness of seeing, then one has severed the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future. If the root of the non-way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future is severed, then one has attained the Way of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future. Therefore, the absence of the
Sentient beings in the world originally have neither beauty nor ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from their own minds.
The Buddhas see all phenomena as each and every one being empty, while sentient beings see all phenomena as each and every one being real.
Sentient beings see all phenomena as merely external objects, whereas the Buddhas see all phenomena as nothing but their own minds. This is the distinction between the true and the deluded.
"Ānanda, although you previously awakened to fundamental enlightenment... [omitted] ...the various obstructions are likewise so.
This was because Ānanda had previously stated that his mind regarding "all harmonious and disharmonious combinations" was still not yet opened;
therefore, [the Buddha] now specifically refutes it, saying: "If you suspect that the Bodhicitta arises through combination, then this pure and wondrous vision of yours—"
If you are so skilled as to claim that these four objects—light and darkness, penetration and obstruction—are not conjoined with anything, then with what would they be conjoined?

If they were conjoined with light, then at the time one perceives light, where would the perception itself be intermingled? If the perception and its object could be distinguished, then what form or image would the intermingling with light take?
Furthermore, when ordinary things know one another, they must first separate and then unite. Now, if you say that light is not the perception, then by what means can one perceive the light?
Since one can see that clarity is not separate from seeing, if you say that clarity is identical to seeing, then the act of seeing clarity would itself be the seeing of seeing;
how could this be? Seeing and seeing are not identical. Since they are neither separate nor identical, by what means could they achieve mutual harmony?
Furthermore, if clarity is not non-seeing, then the entire body is seeing, and seeing must therefore be all-pervasive. Moreover...
In what sense can it be called "harmony with clarity"? If clarity has already manifested, yet one does not immediately perceive it, then the whole body is entirely luminous;

this luminosity must be complete and cannot admit that perception (*darśana*) intermingles with it. Furthermore, if perception were distinct from clarity and were to blend with it, then clarity would be affected by the blending of perception and would lose its name.
Yet, you still call it "harmony with clarity"—how could this be the true meaning of the term? Thus, we know that perception...
The essence must certainly not be in harmony with light; rather, it is through its capacity for darkness and its susceptibility to obstruction that harmony can occur.

Furthermore, as for your pure and wondrous faculty of vision, with which of the four objects—light, darkness, penetration, or obstruction—does it harmonize? If it were to harmonize with light, it should perceive only light;
when it comes to darkness, it should be unable to see. How then could it still see darkness? If you claim that it sees darkness yet does not harmonize with darkness...

If seeing were conjoined with light, then that which is conjoined would not see; it should follow that one does not see light. Yet, how is it that by being conjoined with light, one further sees light?
Thus, we know that the essence of seeing is certainly not conjoined with light. From this, it can be understood that darkness and obstruction or penetration [of light] are likewise not conjoined.
Ānanda, having already had his theory of conjunction refuted, he again retreated to the position of non-conjunction. The Buddha spoke again: "You harbor doubts."

You have realized that they are not a composite; yet now, as for this pure and wondrous essence of your vision, among those four objects—light, darkness, penetration, and obstruction—which one is not a composite?
If it were not a composite with light, then vision and light would already not interpenetrate, and there would necessarily be distinct boundaries between them.
Observe this light and your vision: from where do their boundaries arise? Furthermore, within light there is no vision; [if there were], vision would not fail to know the characteristics of light.
From this, one knows that the essence of seeing must not be disunited from light; thus, its penetration by darkness and its obstruction can be understood.
Furthermore, as for your pure and wondrous essence of seeing, among those four objects—light, darkness, penetration, and obstruction—which is it that does not unite with it?
If it were not united with light, then light and the nature of seeing would necessarily be at odds, just as the ear encounters light.
Since it is like the ear encountering light yet being unable to know where the characteristic of light resides, how can one distinguish whether there is union or non-union?
Thus we know that the essence of seeing must not be non-united with light; otherwise, the penetration and obstruction of darkness could not be known.
To observe them through the lens of "union," their so-called harmony seems like disharmony; to speak of "non-union," their lack of harmony seems like harmony. These two—
Why is it that they cannot be fixed? It is simply because the true essence and wondrous awakening are fundamentally neither a combination nor a non-combination;

they truly transcend the reach of conceptual thought. To attempt to measure them with the conventional dharmas of worldly sophistry is just like trying to grasp empty space with one's hand—it only increases one's own fatigue. How could empty space ever conform to your grasping?
Caught! Ānanda, you still do not understand that all floating dust (up to: ... is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature).
As stated previously: "The seeing, the objects of seeing, and the perceived appearances are like flowers in the sky; they have never existed."
This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi;
having thus realized that all myriad delusions return to the single Truth, Ānanda still harbors doubts regarding "conjunction" and "non-conjunction.

This indicates he has not yet clarified this principle, for conjunction and non-conjunction can only be named when there are two distinct things; since there is now only the single Truth, how could there be...?

Is there not the doubt regarding the existence of combination and non-combination? Therefore, although the Buddha has already refuted combination, he further says, "You have not yet clearly understood all floating dust-like phenomena," and so on, up to "unifying the four categories and universally integrating the seven elements.
This is entirely a broad explanation of the teaching on returning to the truth by subsuming the false. "All floating dust and various illusory manifestations" collectively refers to all [phenomena].
Speaking of the Dharma in terms of arising and ceasing being entirely illusory, birth is itself cessation without waiting for time to pass; therefore it is said:
"It arises in this very place and perishes in that very place. Since arising and ceasing are simultaneous, it is merely a designation for illusory delusion and a manifestation of illusory delusion.
This manifestation of illusory delusion is like flowers in the sky—unreal, yet these very flowers are entirely empty space.

It is also like a reflection in a mirror; though the reflection is not real, the reflection as a whole is entirely the mirror. Therefore it is said that its nature is the true essence of wondrously enlightened clarity.

It is further said that arising and ceasing, going and coming, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously clear, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within this true and eternal nature, one cannot find going and coming, delusion and awakening, or birth and death; they are utterly unattainable.
This means that through the illusory and false, one penetrates the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) take the sense of "covering" the true nature as their meaning;
form (*rūpa*) is the foremost of the five aggregates. Whether internal, such as the physical body of the faculties, or external, such as the six objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*), all are termed "form.
It is most substantial and obstructive, such that no sentient being regards it as real rather than empty. Nevertheless, this form arises from conditions.
When conditions disperse, they cease; arising spontaneously, they move toward extinction without abiding for even a single moment.

Thus, that which arises in one moment is precisely that which ceases in that same moment—what is called "arising in this very place and perishing in that very place. Therefore, regarding form (*rūpa*), the Buddha said it is like seeing flowers in the sky with one's eyes:
these flowers do not come from the sky, nor do they emerge from the eyes; how could they be anything other than illusory? Form is likewise so.

The benefit of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness can thus be understood. "Feeling" (vedanā) is defined as the mind’s reception of external objects—be they painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Regarding this, the Buddha said: it is like a person rubbing two palms together, which falsely gives rise to sensations of roughness, smoothness, cold, or heat.
These sensations do not come from empty space, nor do they emerge from the palms; how could they be anything other than illusory?
The meaning of *saṃjñā* (perception) is the mental function of conceptualizing, recollecting, and maintaining external signs.

Regarding this, the Buddha said that it is like a person who, upon hearing the mention of sour plums, has saliva produced; or like one who, thinking of treading on a precipice, has their feet turn numb and sour.

This sourness is not produced from the plum, nor does it enter through the mouth. Why is it that upon hearing the word "sour" with the ear, saliva is produced? It is because of this [perception of] sourness.
Aching and numbness do not arise from the cliff, nor do they enter through the feet; how then can the mind conceive of treading upon them such that the feet ache and become numb?
This is merely a false manifestation arising from thought—how could it be anything other than illusory? "Walking" (cankrama) takes the sense of the constant flux of moment-to-moment consciousness.

Regarding walking, the Buddha said it is like a torrential stream where waves succeed one another; yet this nature of the flow does not arise because of space, nor does it arise because of... [the earth].

Water exists, yet it is not the nature of water; nor is it separate from space. The analogy of water illustrates that the fundamental nature of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) is originally without flow, yet they appear to flow—this too is merely a single instance of delusion.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*), which takes objects as its domain and functions through discrimination, is precisely that which discards one body and assumes another, acting as the master that migrates toward rebirth.
Regarding consciousness, the Buddha said it is like using a vessel to carry space far away to another country.

This emptiness does not come from that direction, nor does it enter here; it is like the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna-ātman*), which is fundamentally without transmigration yet appears to transmigrate—this too is merely a single instance of delusion.

In sum, all five are delusions; they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*) nor produced spontaneously, but constitute the wondrous True Suchness-nature (*tathatā-gotra*) of the Tathāgata-garbha. For were their essence not empty, then [they would not be as they are].
It is because they can be melted back into the true nature that they are entirely the true nature;
just as waves have no self-substance, so the waves are entirely water. The same principle applies to the six sense bases, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements discussed below.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánxián of Yǒngquán Chan Monastery at Gǔshān, Fúzhōu.
What are the six entrances (ṣaḍāyatana)? They are the essential nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous True Suchness (tathatā), up to [the point that they] are not of spontaneous nature.
The "six entrances" refer to the locations where the six objects enter, which are the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*).

When the sutra states that the six entrances are essentially the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous True Suchness, it is because they are illusory and false. As for the entrance of the eye, it is like a person gazing with wide-open eyes.
Yet you see flowers appear in the air; these flowers are certainly illusory, and the illusoriness of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is likewise so.

Since this nature of seeing arises entirely dependent upon the two sensory objects of light and darkness, if there were no light, nothing could be seen, and if there were no darkness, nothing could be seen—then where would the actual substance of seeing reside?
Since it has no substance of its own, one must surely suspect that it exists elsewhere.
From the beginning, one has considered whether [seeing] comes from light and darkness. If it came from light, one should not see darkness; if it came from darkness, one should not see light.
Thus, it cannot be said to come from light and darkness. One has also considered whether it emerges from the sense organ.

If it emerged from the organ, there would necessarily be neither light nor darkness. Since seeing is devoid of self-nature when both light and darkness are absent, it cannot be said to emerge from the organ.

If you consider that [the faculty] emerges from space, then since space encompasses both the sense objects (*viṣaya*) and the faculties (*indriya*), as you previously perceived the objects, you should now perceive the faculties.
Furthermore, since space itself possesses the capacity for seeing, what connection does it have with your eyes? Thus, one cannot say that it arises from space.

Since it has no inherent substance of its own, there is no place from which it comes. Therefore, you should know that the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is illusory; it is a deceptive manifestation of the single, wondrous nature.
Once the ear-faculty has entered [its object], it is like a person who blocks both ears with their hands and hears a sound within their head;

this sound is inherently false and illusory, and the falsity of the ear-faculty’s entry is likewise so. Thus, the nature of hearing entirely arises in dependence upon the two objects of movement and stillness.
If there were no movement to be heard and no stillness to be heard, then what would be the substantial reality of hearing?
Where, then, does the fruit reside? Since it possesses no inherent substance of its own, one must doubt whether it comes from elsewhere.
Does it arise from movement or stillness? If it arose from movement, one should not hear stillness; if it arose from stillness, one should not hear movement.
Thus, it cannot be said to arise from movement or stillness. Does it emerge from the sense organs? If it emerged from the sense organs, it would not involve movement or stillness.
Detached from both motion and stillness, hearing has no self-nature; it cannot be said to emerge from the sense organ. Could one say it arises from space?
Since space itself possesses hearing, how can it be called "empty space"? Furthermore, if space inherently possessed hearing, what would it have to do with your ears?
It cannot be said that it arises from space. Since it has no substance of its own, there is nowhere from which it comes. Therefore, you should know that the ear-entrance is empty.
Delusion is fundamentally nothing more than the false manifestation of the single wondrous nature. As for the sense-base of the nose:
it is like a person who suddenly pinches their nose and perceives a cold sensation within; this sensation is inherently illusory, and the illusoriness of the nasal sense-base is likewise so.
Thus, the nature of smelling arises entirely dependent upon the two conditions of openness and obstruction; if there were no openness, there would be nothing to smell.
When there is obstruction, hearing occurs; where, then, does the substantial entity of hearing reside? Since it has no inherent substance of its own, one must doubt from where it originates.
Does it arise from the state of being open or obstructed? If it arose from the state of being open, one should not hear when there is obstruction;

if it arose from the state of being obstructed, one should not hear when there is openness. It cannot be said that it arises from both openness and obstruction. Must it then be said that it arises from the sense organ itself?

If it emerged from the sense organ, it would not depend on the presence or absence of sound; since it is free from both, hearing has no inherent nature, and thus one cannot say it emerges from the organ.

Is it produced from space? Since hearing comes from the outside, you should turn back and smell your own nose. Furthermore, if space itself possessed hearing, what connection would it have with your nose?
Thus, one cannot say it is produced from space. Since it has no substance of its own, where does it come from?

Furthermore, since there is no fixed location for it, one should know that the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇāyatana*) is a false appearance, manifested merely through the deception of the single, wondrous nature.
As for the tongue-faculty (*jihvāyatana*), it is like a person using their own tongue to lick their lips; falsely, there arise tastes of bitter, sweet, and bland.
These tastes are inherently false, and the falsity of the tongue-faculty is likewise so. By this, one knows that the nature of taste is entirely [empty].

Based on the two kinds of false objects—sweetness, bitterness, and neutrality—if there were no bitterness, sweetness, and neutrality by which they could be known, then where would the reality of their substance be?
Since they themselves have no substance, one must doubt from where else they originate.
Is it that they come from bitterness, sweetness, and neutrality? If they came from bitterness and sweetness, one should not perceive neutrality; if they came from neutrality...
When it comes to respond to flavors, one does not know whether they are bitter or sweet; this cannot be said to come from bitterness, sweetness, or neutrality.

One might think they emerge from the tongue-root itself, yet if they emerged from the root, they would not depend on external flavors. If external flavors are without cognition and lack intrinsic nature, they cannot be said to emerge from the root.
One might think they are produced from space, but space has its own flavor; how then could your mouth perceive it?
Furthermore, knowing is itself empty; what concern is it to your mouth? It cannot be said that it arises from emptiness.

Since it has no self-substance, it likewise has no place of origin. Therefore, you should know that the tongue-faculty is illusory, being merely a deceptive manifestation of the single wondrous nature.
As for the body-faculty, it is like a person using both hands to touch one another and perceiving cold or heat, which ceases once they are separated.

This characteristic is inherently false and illusory, yet the body enters into it; thus, the illusion is likewise so. By this, one realizes that characteristics arise entirely dependent upon the two conditions of conjunction and separation.
If there were no conjunction to be perceived and no separation to be perceived, then where would the substantial reality of perception itself reside?
Since it has no substance of its own, one must doubt that it comes from elsewhere, and thus assume it originates from [the external object].

Does it arise from conjunction or separation? If it arose from conjunction, then when there is separation, one should not perceive it; if it arose from separation, then when there is conjunction, one should not perceive it.

Thus, it cannot be said to come from conjunction or separation. If one thinks it arises from the sense organs, if it were to arise from the organs without depending on conjunction or separation, then since conjunction and separation are absent, perception would have no inherent nature (svabhāva). Thus, it cannot be said to arise from the sense organs. If one thinks it arises from... [text fragment ends]
Does emptiness arise from emptiness? Since it possesses its own awareness, how could it be related to your body? It cannot be said that it arises from emptiness.

Since it has no intrinsic substance, it likewise has no place of origin; therefore, you should know that the body is an entry into delusion, merely a phantom manifestation of the single wondrous nature.
As for the entry of the mind: it is like a person who, when weary, falls asleep; when sleep is deep, one awakens. Within that sleep, one grasps...
Dust leads to recollection, and recollection leads to forgetting; these marks of inverted arising and ceasing do not cease for a moment.

This is the inhalation of past habitual tendencies that returns to the faculty of the mind (*manas*). These marks are the most illusory, and the illusoriness of the mental faculty (*manāyatana*) is likewise so.
By this, one knows that the nature [of consciousness] entirely depends on the two objects of arising and ceasing to be activated. If there were no arising and ceasing, [what would there be?]
If knowing is known, where then does the substantial reality of that knowing reside? Since it has no body of its own, one must surely suspect that it comes from elsewhere.
Does it come from waking and sleep, or from arising and ceasing? If it came from waking, what would become of the one who sleeps? If it came from arising, who would undergo cessation?
Thus, it cannot be said to come from waking and sleep, or from arising and ceasing. One must therefore suppose it comes from the sense-faculties (*indriya*).

It emerges as if from the sense organ, yet it does not depend on the organ; it arises neither during waking nor sleeping, and since external objects are entirely absent, it lacks both cognition and self-nature, such that one cannot say it emerges from the organ. Might one think it is born from space? Space itself possesses cognition;
what connection has it with your intention? Thus, one cannot say it is born from space. Since it has no substance of its own, there is nowhere from which it comes. Therefore, you should know this.
The mind-faculty is illusory, being merely a deceptive manifestation of the single, wondrous nature. ○ For example, when a person is weary, they fall asleep;
as detailed above, all these matters are merely provisional constructs that do not arise from external objects but are internally manifested by oneself.
Now, according to the preceding text, this "adornment" is likewise a provisional construct; falling asleep from weariness does not depend on external objects.
Yet, these inverted appearances manifest spontaneously within the dream to reveal the falsity of mental entry.

If the current commentator were to treat them as real dharmas, it would contradict the preceding example of provisional designation and would further confuse the subsequent passage concerning the collection of cognition abiding in the center. Consider this carefully.
What are the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as the fundamental Tathāgata-garbha (up to) "not of spontaneous nature"?
The twelve bases refer to the six sense organs (*indriya*) facing the six sense objects (*viṣaya*), each having its own fixed location; therefore, they are called "bases.

The Sūtra states that the twelve bases are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous True Suchness-nature (*tathatā-svabhāva*), because they are illusory and false. Regarding the three—roots, forms, and [consciousness]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Within the provisional teachings, there is the doctrine that the eye gives rise to the appearance of form; this has not yet reached the definitive meaning. The Buddha now refutes it:

if one claims that the eye can produce the appearance of form, then when the eye constantly perceives empty space, the interior of the eye should be of the nature of emptiness and devoid of the nature of form.
If the nature of form is eliminated, the appearance of form will naturally vanish entirely. When the appearance of form has completely vanished, what is there to manifest?
In this emptiness, the eye currently lacks the nature of form, yet the characteristic of form has not vanished; thus, one cannot say that form arises from the eye.
If you claim that form can produce the seeing of the eye, then when the eye contemplates emptiness, since no form is present to produce seeing, seeing should perish.
If seeing has perished, who would distinguish between emptiness and form? Since seeing is now able to distinguish between emptiness and form, one cannot say that seeing [arises from form].
It arises from form. Indeed, it is only when the eye and form have fixed locations that their mutual production occurs;

if they did not mutually produce one another, one should know they would lack fixed locations and would equally be mere empty falsehoods, being nothing more than what is falsely manifested by the single wondrous nature. Regarding sound, there are two locations.
The common people all say that the ear and the sound come and go before hearing is established. The Buddha now refutes this: if one were to claim that the sound comes...
If the sound were to reach the ear, it should reach only one person’s ear and not the ears of others;
how is it that the sound of a single bell is heard by the entire assembly? One cannot say that the sound comes to the ear.

If you claim that the ear travels to the place of the sound, it should travel only to one location and be unable to go elsewhere; yet now, while you hear the drum, you simultaneously hear [other sounds].

One cannot say that the ear travels to the location of the sound. If one were to claim that the two do not interact with one another, then each would remain fixed in its own position without any mutual engagement;

how, then, could hearing be established? Since the ear and the sound must have locations for there to be either interaction or non-interaction, yet neither interaction nor non-interaction can be definitively established, one should know that both lack a fixed location and are thus identical in this regard.

Falsehood and delusion are fundamentally one, being merely what the wondrous nature falsely manifests. Regarding the two locations of the nose and fragrance, the Buddha now refutes them by focusing solely on the location of fragrance.
If you claim that fragrance arises from the nose, then since the nose itself is not sandalwood, why does it produce the scent of sandalwood?
Furthermore, you say that smelling fragrance must involve it entering through the nose; yet if it exits through the nose, it does not fulfill the definition of "smelling. If you say:
If fragrance arises from emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is unchanging, then fragrance should be ever-present; why must one rely on burning this withered wood for fragrance to exist?
If you claim that fragrance arises from the wood—such as when sandalwood is burned—the smoke has not yet traveled far, yet within forty *li*, the nose perceives the fragrance.

Since the scent of the wood and the nose are distantly separated and do not interact, how can there be such perception? Thus, all three locations are thoroughly investigated and found to be untenable.
Since this fragrance has no place of origin, how could that which arises from the nose’s smelling of it have any reality?
You should know that these two [nose and fragrance] have no fixed location and are equally false, being merely manifestations conjured by the single wondrous nature.

Regarding the pair of tongue and taste, the Buddha now refutes them specifically at the level of taste. If one were to claim that taste arises in the tongue, and since the tongue is but a single entity, [how could there be various tastes?]
If it forms a single flavor, how can it change when encountering different objects? If there is no change, it cannot be called "knowing" the flavor.

If there is change, then you must have many tongues; how could a single tongue perceive many flavors? If you claim that the flavor arises from the food, then the food itself is not consciousness—how then could it have knowledge?
Furthermore, if the food knows for itself, what concern is that of yours? Why do you attribute it to your tongue?
If one were to say that flavor arises from emptiness, what flavor could emptiness possess? Suppose emptiness were to produce a salty taste;

then all people throughout the world would dwell within that salty taste, just like sea fish, suffering it forever without being able to escape it even slightly. By what means could they know the taste of the fresh?
Since they do not recognize the fresh, how could they know that their own [taste] is salty? If salt and fresh cannot be distinguished, how can there be knowledge?

When one examines the three locations associated with the perception of flavor to their conclusion, one finds that flavor has no place of origin; how then could that which arises dependent upon flavor possess any reality?
One should know that these two have no fixed location and are equally illusory, being merely manifested through deception by the single wondrous nature.

Regarding the body and the object of touch, the Buddha likewise refutes them by focusing solely on the locus of touch; as for the single element of touch— *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist commentary (likely concerning the *Awakening of Faith* or similar Mahāyāna treatises). The final sentence is incomplete, but the translation reflects the extant portion.*
External matter is called "touch" because it manifests as sensations such as cold, warmth, roughness, or smoothness when the body comes into contact with its object;

thus, that which touches possesses the faculty of cognition, while that which is touched is the objective realm of matter. Now, when one rubs the head with the hand, both possess cognition, making it impossible to distinguish between subject and object.
If the hand is the subject that touches, the head ought to lack cognition; how then can it constitute the "touch" of the head?
If the head is that which touches, the hand would be useless; how then could there be the touching of the hand?
If you claim that there is a separate touch for the head and a separate touch for the hand, then two sensations would arise, and one would consequently have two bodies.

If you claim that the head and hand together constitute a single touch, then the head and hand would merge into a single entity. If they were a single entity, touching would not occur, for touching necessarily requires the conjunction of two things.
Furthermore, if these two entities were to touch, where would the fruit of contact reside? If it resides in the agent of contact, then the object of contact is not touching;
if it resides in the object of contact, then the agent of contact is not touching. How can two distinct entities constitute a single act of contact?

Whether in the agent or in the object, both positions are untenable. It cannot be that empty space constitutes contact. When one investigates this repeatedly, contact ultimately remains indeterminate; thus, it is merely a perception of the body.

How could that which arises from contact with these [objects] have any reality? You should know that these two [the mind and mental objects] have no fixed location and are equally false, being merely manifested through deception by the single wondrous nature.
Regarding the two locations of mind and dharmas, the Buddha likewise refutes them specifically within the location of dharmas (*dharmāyatana*).
If one considers these dharmas to be identical to the mind, then since the mind is not an external object (*viṣaya*), how could the mind take it as an object and thereby constitute a "location"?
If you consider this to be separate from the mind, then is this dharma conscious or unconscious? If you consider it conscious, then it is simply the mind;

yet if it were different from your own mind, it would be the same as another person's mind. If it were identical to your own mind, how could the mind and its object stand in opposition to form two distinct aspects?
If you consider it unconscious, then since this dharma is not an external form, it should reside within [the body].
Beyond the emptiness of form, there is no place that is an object of the mind; from whom could it be established?
When one thoroughly investigates the dharmas until they have no fixed location, the mind realizes that those things which arise from dharmas—how could they possess any reality?

One should know that both [form and mind] lack a fixed location and are equally illusory, being merely manifested through deception by the single wondrous nature. The Sūtra says: "The nose knows through contact. This means...

The nose must be enveloped by the scent before one can perceive it; yet, the current claim that one perceives fragrance within forty *li* without waiting for the nose to be enveloped by the smoke contradicts the teachings.
Ancient commentators have offered two explanations: first, that this is due to the sharp and powerful faculties (*indriya-bala*) of a sage;

second, that it is due to the extraordinary power of a sublime fragrance. Neither of these two views is correct. I, the humble one, maintain that [the perception] occurs both through contact (*saṃyukta-jñāna*) and without contact (*asaṃyukta-jñāna*).
The Sarvāstivāda school’s provisional teaching on the characteristics of dharmas is not of definitive meaning; how could this present sutra, being of definitive meaning, be subject to such critique?
Now, the fact that this fragrance is known without waiting for contact precisely demonstrates that knowing it through contact does not exhaust the full principle.

Furthermore, while the ear is said to be a cognition occurring "outside" [the sense organ], this sutra also states that if there were no coming and going, there would likewise be no hearing; thus, it is not [merely] external.
Furthermore, how do we know this? We have observed that when the sound of a bell travels with the wind, it is heard from afar; when there is no wind, it is not heard.

This too seems to suggest that the sound reaches the vicinity of the ear before being heard. How could this be separate from the cognition itself? Therefore, we know that both the claim of separation and the claim of union are mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
Now, the profound purport of this sutra must be realized through silent insight.
What are the eighteen realms (dhātus) as the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, up to [the point that they are] not of spontaneous nature?
Regarding the eighteen realms: the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are each sixfold; when divided into internal, external, and intermediate, they constitute the realms.

Since the faculties and objects have already been thoroughly refuted previously, we shall here specifically refute the six consciousnesses. For instance, if visual consciousness arises from the eye and takes the eye as its realm...
If consciousness arises because of the eye, it does not depend on form; if there is no form, consciousness would have no object of discrimination—what use would it be?
Furthermore, the "elements" (dhātus) are established through mutual relativity. If there were only seeing without an object, internal and external could not be distinguished;
from what basis could one establish the "middle element"? If the element were produced from form and depended upon form, then when space is devoid of form, visual consciousness should cease.
If visual consciousness were to cease, how could one know emptiness? If visual consciousness does not cease, it exists alone without a counterpart;

from whom, then, could it be demarcated as a "middle realm"? Not only is there no basis for establishing a realm if consciousness does not cease, but even if consciousness were to transform and perish while form arises, both would be extinguished together—how then could the characteristic of a realm exist?
Not only is there no basis for knowing emptiness if consciousness transforms and perishes, [but the same applies to the existence of the realm].
Even if it does not undergo transformation or extinction, since consciousness arises from form, it should likewise be unable to know space.

If it were produced simultaneously with the eye and form, would it then rely on both the eye and form as its boundaries? If one claims that the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) merge into one, then the organ would cease to be the organ and the object would cease to be the object;

yet they remain distinct in between. If one claims that the organ and the object are divided into two, then the organ would be confused with the object and the object would be confused with the organ.

Furthermore, since the essential natures of both the sense organs and their objects are inherently chaotic and indeterminate from the outset, how could one establish a "middle realm" for consciousness?
Therefore, you should know that the triad of eye, form, and visual consciousness are all merely false manifestations of a single, wondrous fundamental nature.
If auditory consciousness were produced from the ear and the ear were its realm, then since there is no characteristic of sound [present in the ear itself], it would likewise be untenable.
How could the ear have cognition? If there is no cognition, then there is no consciousness (*vijñāna*). If one takes the ear as a physical form of flesh, it might still be able to hear;
yet, once the characteristic of sound has vanished, hearing itself cannot be established. How can you simply designate a non-cognizing form as the "element of consciousness" (*vijñānadhātu*)?
If [consciousness] arises from sound and you take sound as its element, then consciousness would have no relation to hearing; and if there is no hearing, then there is no sound.
Even if one were to falsely claim that sound exists because it is heard, consciousness would be produced by that sound; yet hearing sound necessarily involves hearing consciousness as well.
If one does not hear [consciousness], then sound is not the realm from which consciousness is produced. If one hears consciousness, then consciousness is identical to an external object.

Furthermore, since consciousness has already been heard, how could there be another knower who hears it? It must be like grass and trees, devoid of cognition. This is so even if one follows the position of the Ear.
Sound arises together with the two supports—the ear and sound—yet they constitute a realm (*dhātu*). Within the intermingling of sounds, no intermediate realm is established;
since there is no intermediate position, the distinction between internal and external also vanishes. From what, then, could a realm be further established?

Therefore, one should know that these three—the ear, sound, and consciousness—are all fundamentally non-existent, being merely the deceptive manifestations of a single wondrous nature. This is just as if olfactory consciousness were to arise from the nose.
If one considers the nose as a constituent element (*dhātu*), one does not know what constitutes the "nose. If one takes the physical form of flesh, it belongs to the body;

if there is cognition, that is contact (*spraṣṭavya*) and cannot be called the nose. If one takes the nature of the act of smelling, this nature is neither in the flesh, nor in space, nor in the fragrance—it cannot be called the nose in any case.
Since the nose itself cannot be found, how much less can it be established based upon it?
If it arises from fragrance, does it take fragrance as its realm? If consciousness were produced from fragrance, it should not know the fragrance;
if it can know it, then it was not produced from fragrance. If it does not know the fragrance, then it cannot even be called consciousness.

If it does not know the fragrance, then not only is there no consciousness, but the fragrance itself cannot be established. If it arises from both the nose and fragrance together, taking both the nose and fragrance as its realm?
If both the nose and the fragrance are destroyed, then that which is between them cannot be found; if the intermediate realm is not established, how can the internal and external realms stand?
Therefore, one should know that these three—the nose, the fragrance, and consciousness—are all without fundamental substance, being merely the deceptive manifestations of a single, wondrous nature.
If tongue-consciousness were to arise from the tongue and take the tongue as its realm, it would not depend on external flavors, for the tongue would possess flavor of its own accord.
Furthermore, if the tongue has flavor, who comes to taste it? If the tongue has no flavor, how can the realm [of taste] be established?

If it arises because of flavor and takes flavor as its realm, then consciousness itself would be the flavor; it should not be aware of itself. Moreover, since flavor is not a single entity, consciousness should have multiple bodies.
If consciousness were one, then flavors should all be identical. Since there is no such discrimination, how can it be called "consciousness"?

Since neither the tongue nor flavors exist independently, how could empty space produce consciousness? If it arises because of the tongue and flavors, would the tongue and flavors serve as its dual bases?
If these two were to merge into one, then both the internal and external would lack self-nature; furthermore, how could a realm of consciousness arise from that which is in between?
Therefore, you should know that the three—the tongue, flavors, and consciousness—are all fundamentally non-existent, being but a single wondrous essence.

It is merely that the nature [of things] manifests through deception, just as with body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*). If body-consciousness arises because of the body, does it take the body as its sphere (*dhātu*)?
Since there is no separation or union [of the body], how could body-consciousness exist? If it arises because of contact (*spraṣṭavya*), does it take contact as its sphere?

If there were no body, how could one perceive contact through separation or union? If it arises from both the body and contact together, taking both the body and contact as its sphere—surely, things do not... [The text ends here].

If one can have cognition through mere contact, it must necessarily depend upon the body before contact is known; thus, bodily cognition is itself contact, for there is no difference between contact and cognition.
Contact-cognition is itself the body, for there is no difference between the body and cognition.

Furthermore, your body is certainly not the body, because it is the cognition that is immediate to contact. Your contact is certainly not contact, because it is the cognition that is immediate to the body.
Furthermore, when contact joins with the body, they form a single entity without two distinct characteristics;

when contact separates from the body, both are equal to empty space, likewise without two distinct characteristics. Viewed from this perspective, since the interior and exterior are already void, how could a middle exist?
Since the middle is void, the interior and exterior are likewise non-existent. From whom, then, could one establish the boundaries? This is so.
Therefore, one should know that the triad of body, touch, and consciousness is merely a deceptive manifestation of a single, wondrous nature that originally has no basis.

If it were like the mental consciousness, which arises from the mind and takes the mind as its realm—wherein the mind must depend upon dharmas before it can exist—if those prior dharmas did not exist, from what would the mind arise?
Since the mind has no form, both the sense faculty and the object would be extinguished; even if consciousness were present, it would have no support.

Why do you again ask whether the consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the mental faculty (*manas*) are the same or different? If you say that consciousness is the same as the mental faculty, why speak further of "consciousness arising from the mind"?
If you say that consciousness is different from the mental faculty, since the mental faculty already possesses consciousness, there would be no separate consciousness;

if there were no separate consciousness, it would not be of the same category as the mind—how then could it be said to be produced by the mind? If there is a separate consciousness, then it would constitute a duality with the consciousness [of the mind].
One must certainly transform this consciousness and investigate it thoroughly; when neither similarity nor difference can be distinguished, upon what basis is the "consciousness-element" established?

Is it because it arises from dharmas that the dharmas constitute its element? Yet these dharmas have no substantial reality at all; they are merely external objects grasped by the mental faculty (*manas*), arising and ceasing as mere external reflections.
Since the dharmas that serve as their cause are already void, the [consciousness] produced from them— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

How could consciousness be real? Furthermore, from which realm could its arising be obtained? Therefore, you should know that the mind (*manas*), phenomena (*dharma*), and consciousness—these three locations—are all devoid of intrinsic substance;

they are merely the deceptive manifestations of a single, wondrous nature. Furthermore, as for your conscious mind and its various powers of deliberation and discrimination—is it identical to or different from [the true nature]?
There have been many interpretations in the past, yet none were thorough. Now, let us examine the Sūtra in detail.
The two characters "wen" (text/pattern) and "shi" (consciousness) closely follow upon the preceding "yi-shi" (mental consciousness); it is undoubtedly the mental consciousness.
The phrase "the nature of constant deliberation and simultaneous discernment" refers to the faculty of mind (*manas*). This faculty of mind is precisely the seventh consciousness;

it is able to constantly and critically deliberate, and it also largely possesses the nature of discernment. This is where the Buddha examines whether this mental consciousness and the faculty of mind are identical or distinct.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "If the intention is the same, then the intentions are equal," and so forth.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One" (up to) "...there is no real meaning at all.

Regarding the previous four sections, which all state that [the elements] are neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously, Ānanda, seizing upon this, gave rise to a doubt, saying: "One..."
The true nature can be said not to involve causes and conditions; yet, as for the myriad phenomena, they must necessarily be formed through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
How can these two be the same as spontaneity (*svabhāva*)? Since neither [of these views] is correct, this meaning is profound and far-reaching, and its location is unknown;
therefore, I request that the Buddha deign to provide instruction. Having deeply rebuked his delusion, the Buddha further established a parable to clarify it, saying: "All..."

If the essential nature of the great elements were inherently established and fixed from the beginning, such that it did not harmonize with other conditions, then it would be like empty space, which does not harmonize with forms.
However, the nature of the great elements can manifest characteristics by relying on conditions; thus, it is not the case that they do not harmonize.

This is because the natures of the great elements lack any self-substance whatsoever and must depend upon the harmony of various conditions to be formed; in this regard, they are like a whirling firebrand.
The wheel shifts according to its appearances, yet the nature of the great [wheel] does not shift along with those appearances;
this is not a matter of conjunction. It is neither like space, which lacks conjunction, nor like a fire-wheel, which is a conjunction.

If one asks what it is then like, it should be understood as water forming ice and ice returning to water. The arising and ceasing of the ice is a metaphor for the function of following conditions (*pratyaya*).

The fact that the substance of water remains as it was is a metaphor for the unchanging essence. This means that while the nature is complete within the characteristics and remains unchanged as it follows conditions, the characteristics themselves are the nature;
and while the nature fully follows conditions, it does not change. Thus, although "nature" and "characteristics" have two names, they in reality possess no two distinct substances.
How could one then cling to them as being either combined or not combined? Now, let us clarify this by means of the nature of earth. That which is coarse...

The earth is extremely subtle, bordering upon the infinitesimal particle (*paramāṇu*). According to conventional perception, when one analyzes the infinitesimal particle, it dissolves into empty space;

thus, one calculates that by accumulating empty space, the characteristics of form and matter arise. Yet, when forming an infinitesimal particle, one does not know how many instances of empty space combine to constitute it;
and when analyzing it back into empty space, one likewise does not know how many characteristics of form and matter combine to constitute that emptiness.

If space were to combine with form, it would not constitute space; yet if it combines with space, how could it constitute form? Moreover, while form may still be analyzed, space cannot be combined [with anything].
Therefore, know that those who claim the earth-element is produced through combination are merely engaging in conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
You fundamentally do not understand the source and course of this earth-nature; it issues directly from the *tathāgatagarbha*, wherein the nature of form is inherently complete within the mind.
The emptiness that possesses the reality of all phenomena is precisely the color of their true substance;

because it does not involve phenomenal characteristics, it is called "pure and fundamental. Because this one is the entire whole, it can pervade the Dharma-realm—this is what is meant by the "unchanging substance.
Yet how could this substance be limited to being unchanging? It is further able to...
The minds of sentient beings correspond to the measure of what they know, manifesting according to their karma.

Since the minds of sentient beings have degrees of superiority and inferiority, and the measure of what they know has breadth and narrowness, their karma varies in magnitude, being neither uniform nor consistent in its purity or defilement.

This nature follows what it is moved by, each forming its own manifestation; from the supreme Buddhas above to the three miserable realms below, although there are ten thousand differences in their gradations, [the principle remains the same].
These distinctions and the general unity are all manifestations that arise according to karma; this is precisely what is called "the function of following conditions.
That which is unchanging is not due to causes and conditions, and that which follows conditions is not something self-existent (*svabhāva*).

Those who reckon them as being either caused by conditions or self-existent are merely making false assertions based on the discriminations of the conscious mind; how could these be the true meaning? The six great meanings below are all... [text continues]

Following this model, this section elucidates the profound meaning of the reality of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*), all of which have never before been revealed.

While the preceding four sections necessarily involve the destruction of delusive appearances (*lakṣaṇa*) before one can realize the single truth, here the nature-body (*dharmatā-kāya*) is inherently endowed with the seven great elements (*saptamahābhūta*), each of which is itself true.
Whereas previously the entire substance of the mind was described as pervading the *dharmadhātu*, here each of the seven great elements is individually [pervasive].
Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, the previous section on "shattering the false to return to the true" (po-wàng guī-zhēn) was like a *tathāgatagarbha* resembling emptiness;
now, however, the whole essence is the function, and the whole function returns to the essence—the perfect fusion of the threefold treasury (*trikāya*) is seen herein.

Therefore, this section is truly the ultimate discourse in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*). The two lines, "Essential form is true emptiness; essential emptiness is true form," reside within the *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
Because these two meanings are mutually fused and identical in their own nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), both are termed "nature" (*dhātu*) and "truth" (*tattva*);

this is not like the sense of the mutual identity of truth and delusion found in the Prajñā school. This applies to all six elements below as well. Furthermore, regarding the three great elements—space, consciousness, and cognition—the phrasing varies slightly, yet the meaning remains no different.
For instance, regarding the element of space, it says: "The nature-awareness is true emptiness; the nature-emptiness is true awareness. This refers merely to...
The "Greatness of the Element" (mahābhūta) is emptiness; it cannot be called "emptiness of nature," for it is "true emptiness.
Therefore, it is easily said to be the "true awakening of the nature. Regarding the "Greatness of Seeing": "the seeing of the nature" refers to the luminosity of the essence of awakening;
the "essence of awakening" refers to the seeing of the luminosity of the nature. Regarding the "Greatness of Cognition": "the cognition of the nature" refers to knowing through clarity.
Regarding the phrase "the awakened clarity of true consciousness" (*jue-ming zhen-shi*): it means that the consciousness of the true nature is precisely the wondrously luminous knowledge;
the clarity of original awakening (*ben-ju*) is precisely the consciousness of the true substance. These all refer to the principle of the mutual fusion of the nature and its manifestations.

One should know that regarding the two phrases "discriminating, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing," Wenglun says they specifically point to the various consciousnesses (*vijñānas*), which is difficult to reconcile with the preceding two [sections on] the Great [Elements]. One should examine this in detail.

If this assembly were previously composed of the four roots and later became the seven great elements, it would not be so; otherwise, there would merely be six elements. Why then speak of seven great elements?
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [remained] until their minds were unmoving and unshakable.
This is Ānanda and the great assembly realizing and praising the Buddha.
From the initial fascicle’s discernment of mind and views, through to the four divisions and seven major sections, he extensively elucidates the illusory attachments to body and mind;
all biased and provisional polemics are discarded, causing them to realize that this single mind transcends the myriad dharmas and is entirely unfathomable, fusing the myriad [dharmas] into one.
The Dharma encompasses all without exception; its true essence is perfect and wondrous, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. This subtle and profound revelation reaches its ultimate limit here.
Thus, those whose body and mind become vast and serene, attaining freedom from all hindrances, have their deluded emotions suddenly emptied.

Each person comes to know for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions; this is the total manifestation of the awakened essence. This awakening is limpid and all-pervasive, encompassing and containing the ten voids.

Therefore, one sees the emptiness of the ten directions as leaves in the palm of one's hand; since the true nature of all phenomena is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, all things are the wondrous mind of Bodhi.
Having thus awakened to the vastness of the mind’s measure, one looks back upon the body born of one’s parents:
it is as minute as a speck of dust and as illusory as a bubble, suddenly becoming nothing at all—only then does one truly arrive at this realization.
Having attained this fundamental, wondrous, and eternally abiding mind, he was deeply moved by his own good fortune and spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha:
"Wondrously profound" refers to the ocean of awakening, perfectly clear and unmuddied by external things; this is the essence of the contemplation of *śamatha*.

"Total retention" (*dhāraṇī*) refers to the treasury-mind, which is perfectly pervasive and encompasses the ten directions; this is the essence of the contemplation of *samādhi*. "Immovable" refers to the constant nature of the wondrous essence.
That quiescence is fundamentally without arising or ceasing is the very essence of the contemplation of *dhyāna*. These three are all unsurpassed and most honored dharmas;
taken together as one, they constitute the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. The Buddha’s preceding detailed and exhaustive explanations were none other than this meaning;
therefore, Ānanda praised it here. If one attains this Great Samādhi, the inverted perceptions from beginningless time will be instantly eliminated. Their root—
Because the Dharmakāya of existing reality is suddenly attained, one makes the vow to achieve Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings in order to repay the Buddha’s grace.
However, since the subtle afflictions have not yet been exhausted when the Dharmakāya is first established, how could one ascend to supreme enlightenment?

Therefore, one further hopes that the Buddha will thoroughly eliminate them. According to this sutra, Ānanda initially requested instruction on the three contemplations; therefore, the expounder follows [this sequence].
Prior to this, most [commentators] have judged [the text] to belong primarily to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*); yet there are also differing judgments:
some judge that from the section on "The Mind-View" up to the end of the "Seven Great Elements" it is entirely the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*);

some judge that the four categories prior to this belong to the contemplation of emptiness, the four categories belong to the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*), and the seven great elements belong to the contemplation of the middle way (*madhyamā-vipaśyanā*); and some judge that the four categories and the seven...

The *Da jipian* (Great Collection of Judgments) classifies [the three truths] as belonging to the provisional (*prajñapti*), while the *Zhongguan* (Madhyamaka) is placed in the subsequent section; however, upon careful examination of the intent of the sūtra, neither interpretation can be fully sustained.
In my humble opinion, this sūtra is perfectly subtle and wondrous: to mention one is to encompass all three.

How much less could it be that the Buddha’s teaching rigidly fixed where emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is spoken of, where the provisional is spoken of, or where the middle (*madhyama*) is spoken of? It is merely a matter of responding to questions as they arise, in order to open [the understanding of beings].
By revealing the wondrous nature of the one mind, the meaning of the three contemplations naturally becomes manifest.

If one were first to establish the three contemplations as fixed, dead laws and then dissect the Buddha’s words to conform to them, how could such a person be considered skilled in interpreting the sutras?
A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Three;
A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánxián of Yongquan Chan Monastery at Gǔshān, Fúzhōu.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra... [up to] "truly there are conditioned dharmas.

This Pūrṇa raises two doubts based on the preceding passage concerning the seven great elements: first, because the preceding passage on the seven great elements states that they are all "pure and originally so," he doubts, saying:
"If they are pure and originally so, it should not be possible for them to exist [as they do]."
The mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena may exist for a time, yet they must also swiftly perish;

how then can they successively flow on, ending and beginning again with no period of rest? Since the preceding section on the seven elements all stated that they pervade the entire Dharma-realm, one might doubt:
"If the natures of these various elements each individually pervade [the realm], then as for the nature of earth..."

If the nature of water obstructs the nature of water, and the nature of fire obstructs the nature of earth, while the nature of space further congeals them—then when this pervasiveness exists here, that must perish elsewhere.
How can both be omnipresent? These two doubts are both instances of clinging to characteristics while challenging the nature;

they fail to realize that delusive appearances are fundamentally empty and that there is only the single awakened nature (buddha-nature), which arises specifically from false conceptualization. Thus, the Buddha...

In response to the first question, [the Buddha] first raises the meaning of "the wondrous luminosity of the nature-awakening" (*xing-jue miao-ming*) and "the fundamental awakening that is luminous and wondrous" (*ben-jue ming-miao*) to demonstrate it.

The nature-awakening and the fundamental awakening are not two; they are revealed as not being dependent on another, hence they are called "nature" (*xing*). They are self-awakened, hence they are called "fundamental" (*ben*).
They are fundamentally self-awakened, hence they are "wondrous" (*miao*). "Wondrous" means that its essence and characteristics are quiescent and extinguished, beyond the reach of mind or speech.
The "luminous" (ming) refers to the spiritual mirror that is never obscured; it cannot be darkened by afflictions or delusions.
"Wondrous luminosity" (miaoming ming) is spoken of in inverted terms to manifest their mutual fusion and non-duality.

If Purna could understand this meaning, he would know that true awakening is wondrously luminous, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm, transcending both subject and object, and being only a single characteristic—how then could mountains and rivers suddenly arise?
Is it because of this that there is transmigration? Because he had not yet understood, [the Buddha] again posed two questions to examine him, saying:

"When you speak of 'awakened clarity' (*jue-ming*), is it because its nature is inherently clear that you name it 'awakening,' or is it because there was previously a lack of clarity that you suddenly designate it as 'clear awakening'?
Purna then replied: "If it were such that there was no clarity and one suddenly named it 'awakening'..."
If you say that awakening is "that which has nothing to illuminate," my meaning is that it must necessarily have something to illuminate before it can be called awakening.
To take illumination as having an object is to recognize the delusory; to take awakening as being non-illuminating is to lose the truth.
To insist on adding illumination to awakening is to increase the delusory within the true. This is the foundation for infinite suffering. Therefore, the Buddha explained [this] in detail.

He showed it to him and said: "Do you mean that if there is nothing to be illuminated, then there can be no so-called 'illuminating awareness' (*prabhāsvara-vijñāna*), and only when there is something to be illuminated can it be called 'illuminating awareness'?
To be entirely unaware of anything to be illuminated is deluded discrimination; therefore, it is not awakening (*bodhi*).
To have nothing to be illuminated is to be shrouded in darkness and lose one's clarity; therefore, it is not illumination. This is because [in either case] there is something to be illuminated."
That which has no object of illumination is, in sum, the self-arising and ceasing of deluded illumination; this is nothing but ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, ignorance is not the nature of the profound clarity of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*); how could it be grasped as true illumination? Indeed, the nature of enlightenment inherently possesses its own luminosity;
it cannot be said that enlightenment is originally non-luminous and must wait for illumination. Now, to falsely add illumination where there is none—this is [the error].

Awakened clarity becomes fundamental ignorance. For true awakening is fundamentally not something that can be made an object of illumination; yet because one stubbornly desires to illuminate it, it transforms into an objective correlate (*lakṣya*).
Once the objective has been falsely established, it in turn manifests as a false movement. This false illumination and false capacity become increasingly manifest;

once the false capacity is manifest, the false object becomes increasingly coarse. Within the state where there is neither identity nor difference, the characteristics of objective realms appear, and a blazing diversity is formed.
Difference is the characteristic of form; because there is the characteristic of difference, one perceives non-identity.
That difference manifests identity. Identity is the characteristic of the formless; because of identity, difference is manifested, and because of difference, identity is manifested.

As identity and difference manifest each other, they further manifest that which is neither identical nor different. Because this resembles having a form and appearance, it is not the case that it is formless.
This sameness also possesses a semblance of cognition; furthermore, it is not different from that insentient color. Therefore, it is said that there is neither sameness nor difference.
These three characteristics are precisely what is later referred to as empty space, the world, and sentient beings.

However, as they still reside within the fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), they are hazy and indeterminate, lacking any names; thus, they are merely called "sameness and difference" and "neither sameness nor difference."
It acts as the embryo for the sentient beings within those empty space-worlds. Since there are realms, deluded appearances manifest;
struck by the winds of these objects, the waves of consciousness arise in chaos. Thus it is said: "Such disturbances interact to give rise to weariness;

when this weariness persists without interruption, it inevitably gives rise to deluded dust, which becomes turbid within itself. From this, the afflictions of worldly toil are incited—greed, anger, and so forth."
Through false views, one creates various kinds of karma; once the causal conditions of karma exist, one consequently experiences the fruit of suffering.
That which arises is the world, like bubbles arising upon the sea; that which remains still becomes empty space, like the sea being without bubbles.

This empty space is precisely the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) within the aforementioned consciousness, while this world is precisely the "particular characteristic" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) within the aforementioned consciousness. Thus it is.
Within the preceding consciousness, there is again that which is neither identical nor different; this concludes the point that these are the truly conditioned phenomena of sentient beings.
This above serves as a general answer to the cause by which all conditioned phenomena—the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—suddenly arise:
it is simply because of a single moment of deluded luminosity acting as their root.
"Awakened clarity and empty dullness" (extending to) "ending and beginning again.
This is the specific answer regarding the causes and conditions for the threefold generation and continuity [of the world]. The world first arises from delusive existence;
from awakened clarity, once it arises, one immediately perceives empty dullness. Thus, clarity and dullness alternate and interact with one another.

Because one is unaware that the mind is moving, it is said that they depend on one another to become unsteady; because this can generate wind, there is a wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) that supports the world.
Due to movement arising from space, this deluded awareness of movement clings to what is perceived as luminous, grasping at it tenaciously and refusing to let go;
thus, it solidifies into something obstructive, and so there is a gold-circle (*kāñcana-maṇḍala*) that sustains the lands. When firm awareness becomes gold, it is hard and solid.

The wind of unimpeded luminosity arises and moves, never remaining still; this alternation of movement and rigidity, their mutual friction and agitation, is just like the worldly method of drilling wood for fire.
Thus, there is the light of fire, which is the nature of transformation. The precious clarity produces moisture, just as the luster of a pearl can produce water.
The fire-light steams upward, like hot vapors rising and flowing as sweat. Therefore, there is...
