The water-wheel encompasses the realms of the ten directions; its proximate cause above is the deluded mind, by which the four great elements are formed.

Once the four great elements have been formed, each possesses the function of generation and completion. Thereupon, fire ascends and water descends; as these two join together, they transform into the great earth.
That which sinks becomes the vast oceans, and that which floats becomes the continents and sandbars. Thus, within the vast oceans, fire...
Light constantly arises within the sandbanks and shoals, and rivers and streams constantly flow through them, so as not to forget the vital energy derived from one's parents.
When these sandbanks possess high mountains, it is because the power of the water is weaker than that of fire; thus, the upward-tending intention is predominant.
If the mountain rocks strike [the flames], they form flames, and if they melt, they become water. As for the vegetation found upon these sandbanks:
Thus, although the power of earth is inferior to that of water, its function of providing nourishment is superior;
for when forests and marshes are burned, they become earth, yet when compressed, they become water. Reaching this point, the support for all living beings is fully provided.

In sum, they mutually arise from delusion and take delusion as their seed, one birth following another in succession, each life cutting off the previous while various forms entangle one another—this is the nature of this world.

Because of this continuity, the beginning of sentient beings also originates from false existence. Because of the clarity of awareness, and because that clarity of awareness becomes a fault, one establishes what is "illuminated.
Once the object of delusion is established, the principle of the illuminating subject becomes restricted by it;

thus, hearing does not transcend sound, and seeing does not surpass form. This is because the six sense objects falsely manifest externally, causing the six sense organs to be partitioned horizontally.
Internally, when the sense organs and their objects stand in opposition, consciousness necessarily arises and karma increases; this constitutes the cause of the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
Alternatively, when parents and offspring share the same karma and are bound together, the two modes of birth—womb-born (*jarāyu-ja*) and egg-born (*aṇḍa-ja*)—are formed.

Or, when not depending on parents but arising through the union or separation of conditions and environments, the two modes of birth—moisture-born (*saṃsveda-ja*) and transformation-born (*upapāduka*)—are formed. Now, regarding the womb-born:
The beginning of clarity arises from deluded clarity as it manifests forms; this is when the intermediate state being sees its parents. Next, because of seeing these forms, conceptualization arises;
this is when the intermediate state being sees its parents and is moved by emotion. Seeing adverse conditions, one perceives them as different; difference leads to aversion.
Seeing favorable conditions, one perceives them as the same; sameness leads to attachment. This is how the intermediate state being relates to its parents.
Love and hatred arise; that upon which love is focused becomes the seed, and that which is received becomes the womb.
Furthermore, one relies on the attraction of the parents' union as the necessary condition through shared karma (*sabhāga-karma*). This is the beginning of taking form through birth from a womb.
As for the differences among the four modes of birth: birth from an egg arises from thought (*saṃjñā*), due to disordered thinking; birth from a womb arises from emotion (*vedanā*).

Birth arises from craving; moisture-born beings arise through union, being produced by clinging to moist vapors; transformation-born beings arise through separation, being produced by detached imagination of an object.
Although these births—born of thought, born of passion, born of union, or born of separation—all possess these characteristics, each is designated according to its predominant factor.
Therefore, it is said that they arise "according to what is appropriate. As for the fourth [type], which involves mutual transformation, this refers to the karma received.
The body of retribution follows the four modes of birth, rising and sinking without fixed substance; this is how sentient beings continue their succession.

The beginning of karmic fruition starts with craving (*tṛṣṇā*). When the affection of craving becomes deep and binds one so that it cannot be relinquished, parents and children give birth to one another in an uninterrupted cycle.
Such karmic fruits take sensual craving as their root; each cherishes [their own].
If each takes from the other to satisfy their greed without ceasing, they will inevitably come to devour one another;
thus, among the four modes of birth, the strong oppress the weak and prey upon one another in succession. Such karmic results have greed for killing as their root.
Since you eat them and they in turn eat you, this irrational mutual plundering continues without end, and as these evil karmas arise together, they are never exhausted.
Regarding the future limit, these karmic fruits have greed and theft as their root. "You owe me my life" further explains and establishes the meaning of continuity;

in brief, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the three fundamental roots of these karmic fruits, which is why they remain inexhaustible throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Thus ends the third section, which specifically clarifies the karmic fruits of the world, sentient beings, and karma itself.
Although the continuities of these seeds differ from one another, they all arise from awakened clarity (*bodha-vidyā*), because it possesses the nature of clear and knowing awareness.
Through this act of knowing, false appearances are manifested; from these false appearances, further false views are produced.
Thus, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) undergo successive transitions, all collectively accomplished by what is entirely illusory.

Ending and beginning again, it ultimately has no exhaustion. Regarding the section on "Awakened clarity, emptiness, and dullness," it should simply be explained according to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Wēn-líng’s interpretation—using the Five Elements (*pañcabhūta*) theory of mutual overcoming and mutual production, such as the metaphors of husband and wife or mother and son—is erroneous in more than one way.
For instance, in the formation of earth from water and fire, water overcomes fire, which constitutes the relationship of husband and wife; yet fire...

That earth gives birth to soil as mother and child, and water produces grasses and trees—this is earth overcoming water as husband and wife; yet water gives birth to wood as mother and child—these explanations seem plausible.

However, when it comes to the claim that from the awakening of light and the dullness of emptiness wind arises, and from the establishment of bright awareness and solidity gold is formed, and that wind and gold rubbing against each other produce fire and light, such an explanation is difficult to reconcile; thus, [the author] forcibly [applies...]
Awakened clarity is water; the dullness of space is earth; the wind-wheel is wood. By combining these explanations:
the earth of spatial dullness overcomes the water of awakened clarity, forming a husband-and-wife relationship, while water gives rise to wind-wood as mother and son.
Metal overcomes wind-wood, which constitutes losing one's wife; yet wind-wood gives rise to fire as mother and son, for metal itself arises from space.

That which is produced through the solidification of the "shaking" and the manifestation of "clarity," thereby establishing obstruction, is formed by the union of the clarity of awareness (*jue-ming*) and empty wind.

Why, then, do you now omit the water of the clarity of awareness and speak only of "earth producing wood" and "wood producing metal"? Furthermore, upon what basis does the clarity of awareness rely to be paired with water?
The clarity of awareness belongs to the mind (*xin*), while the five phases (*wu-xing*) belong to form (*se*); how can that which belongs to the mind be listed alongside that which belongs to form?
If one enumerates emptiness (*ākāśa*) as one of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*), it would not be the "Great Radiance" (*Mahāprabhā*).

Even if one were to examine exhaustively the books of this land [China], there is none that treats emptiness as earth; how much less so when, if emptiness belonged to earth, it would fall within the numerical category of the five elements—how then could it be called the "Great Void"?
As for wind belonging to wood, although this land has such a theory, the Buddha [regards] wind...
To claim that a single great tree belongs to the element of earth (*pṛthivīdhātu*), yet now treat wind as wood, contradicts the Buddha’s teachings;

how could such an annotation of the Buddhist scriptures not be erroneous? Furthermore, the assertion that when the female element is inferior, the yin and yang harmonize to produce offspring is also mistaken.
It is like claiming that water and fire combine to form the great earth; according to the intent of the sūtras, it is when the force of water is inferior to that of fire [that such a result occurs].
Based on this reasoning by Gao Shan, since the power of fire is inferior to that of water, it should form the great oceans; where fire and water are equal, they should form islands and ponds.

If one insists that a son can only be born when the husband is inferior to the wife, then it would follow that only when the power of water is inferior to fire could it produce the great oceans and islands—rather than forming high mountains alone. Is such indeed the Buddha’s intention? Let the observer examine this in detail.
Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous clarity... is also like this.
This represents Pūrṇa’s arising of doubt upon hearing what was previously stated:

that since the essence of awakening of sentient beings is no different from that of the Tathāgata, yet they can suddenly give rise to all conditioned phenomena, then after the Tathāgata has attained Buddhahood, all conditioned [phenomena]...
One should further give rise to this realization: because sentient beings doubt that they have a beginning, they consequently doubt that the Buddha-fruit has an end.
Little do they know that sentient beings have never awakened from the outset, and that all delusions have no beginning.

Although the Buddha spoke of "establishing objects based on consciousness" and so forth, this was merely to cut off idle talk in order to clarify that the myriad dharmas are delusory, and that even the clarity regarding these delusions is itself delusory. Now...
The Buddha merely answered the difficult question regarding the end of Buddhahood by specifically establishing four parables in detail.

First, the parable of one who has lost their way illustrates the fundamental emptiness of that which has no locus. A person who has lost their way mistakes south for north; yet this delusion does not arise from delusion, nor does it arise from awakening.
Since it has no cause, one knows it has no substantial reality; therefore, upon encountering someone who points out the direction, [the error is corrected].
Thus, one clearly knows the direction; how could one possibly be deluded again? One should understand that ignorance has no inherent nature and is ultimately empty.

Originally there was truly no delusion; it only appeared to exist because one was in a state of delusion. If even before awakening it was not existent, how much less so once awakened—how could one be deluded again?
The metaphor of flowers in the sky illustrates that all phenomena are not real. Space originally has no flowers; they are seen falsely due to an ocular affliction.
If the disease of cataracts is removed, the flowers in the sky vanish; yet their vanishing was originally non-existent, so how could that which has vanished be born again?
One should understand that all phenomena have no substance and are fundamentally unborn; they arise only through the delusions of ignorance.

Since ignorance is shattered, how could there be any phenomena, let alone the appearance of their cessation? Furthermore, since the mark of cessation cannot even be apprehended, how much less could it cause them to be born again after having ceased?
The analogy of gold ore illustrates that the fruition of awakening is free from admixture;

when the wisdom of bodhi illuminates and afflictions are forever extinguished, it is like ore being exhausted so that the gold is pure—how could the ore ever arise again? The analogy of wood and ash illustrates that the fruition of virtue is non-arising;
when nirvana is attained and quiescence is reached, the two deaths are both exhausted, just as wood is burned into ash—how could the wood ever arise again?

Regarding the four metaphors for the arising of wood from a Buddha: the first two concern the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), explaining that the wondrous substance is fundamentally quiescent and all delusions are fundamentally empty;
the latter two concern the gate of Arising and Ceasing, explaining that habitual outflows and delusions arise, and can only be severed through realization.

If one were to cite only the former metaphors, there might be the fear that delusions do not obstruct the Truth and that afflictions could extinguish themselves spontaneously, thereby negating cause and effect and falling into false views.

If one were to cite only the latter analogy, there might be the fear that awakening is not the pure nature, that it is fundamentally produced from delusion, or that it deviates from the principle of true permanence;
thus, all four analogies are presented together, each illustrating a specific dharma, so as to exhaustively clarify the underlying principles.

"Pūrṇa, furthermore, as for your question [extending to] 'being content with a little,' this answers Pūrṇa’s subsequent inquiry regarding the doubt that the various great elements obstruct one another. The Buddha establishes a metaphor to clarify it:
Now, the essence of space is not itself any of the manifold phenomena, yet it is able to allow all phenomena to manifest without resistance; since this is its very essence..."
Fundamentally there are no marks; why then do all these various marks suddenly appear? It is because when the sun shines, it is bright, and when clouds darken it, it is dim.
With the sun, the clouds, and so forth as conditions, the seven kinds of marks such as brightness and darkness simply manifest.

Yet how could these marks possess any reality? Observe this brightness: although it appears because of the sun, it is not actually the sun; although it appears because of space, it is not actually space.
In reality, it is not empty. If you consider it to be the light of the sun, then this sun should pervade the entire ten-directional world for it to be called the light of the sun;
yet within space there is another round sun, and since that which lies outside this sun is the very substance of space, how can it be called the light of the sun?
If you consider it to be the light of space, then space should be able to illuminate itself for it to be called space.
When light does not produce radiance during the time of clouds and mist at midnight, how can it be called "empty"?
Although one says it is neither the sun nor emptiness, it manifests in dependence upon both the sky and the sun;

yet, since it is not different from the sky and the sun, it can be known that light itself has no substantial reality. Since light lacks substantial reality, it can also be known that all phenomena are equally illusory.

Now, applying this to the Dharma: the essence of empty space is not the various phenomena; it serves as a metaphor for the fact that the fundamental nature is originally not the seven elements (*mahābhūta*).

That it does not reject the manifestation of these phenomena serves as a metaphor for how the seven elements appear according to karma. Appearing according to karma is like a small well being dug until it becomes empty space, or like drilling wood to produce fire;
yet on a large scale, the empty realm of the great trichiliocosm remains as it is even through the fires at the end of the kalpa.
The power of karma—that which is manifested through the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the various sages—is likewise the sovereign power of karma.
Whether they manifest individually, they appear individually; whether they manifest together, they appear together. All are entirely illusory and lack any substantial reality.
To observe them as they appear together: it is like the reflection of the sun in water; when two people view it simultaneously and walk off in opposite directions, east and west, it becomes two suns.
One to the east and one to the west—both are difficult to verify as to which is one and which is two;
they cannot withstand scrutiny. Since a single reflection is already illusory, how much more so when two appear? Such circular delusions are utterly unreliable.

Viewed from this perspective, their nature is fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out; what, then, could there be to suppress or destroy? If you seek further to find something to suppress or destroy, [you will find nothing].

This is like seeking flowers in the sky to produce fruit from the void; their nature is fundamentally true, being solely wondrously enlightened and luminous, and was originally neither water nor fire—how could there be any further mutual incompatibility?
Having thus answered Pūrṇa’s question exhaustively, the Buddha further feared that people might harbor doubts, thinking:
"While it may be unimpeded to speak according to principle, what can be done about the phenomena before one's eyes—the water..."
Fire ultimately obstructs one another; that you do not realize this is the fault of sentient beings' deluded attachments.

Therefore, I shall now distinguish between them by means of the deluded and awakened mind. When sentient beings give rise within the *tathāgatagarbha* to views of form and emptiness as mutually opposing and mutually usurping, the *tathāgatagarbha* follows what you grasp and becomes form and emptiness, yet it remains all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.

When there is wind, there is movement; when empty, there is stillness; with the sun, there is brightness; with clouds, there is darkness. These various characteristics obstruct one another and cannot coexist.
What is the reason for this? It is because they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust, thereby giving rise to these signs of worldly affliction.
When I employ my wondrously luminous wisdom—neither arising nor ceasing—to accord with the Tathāgatagarbha, then it is the Tathāgatagarbha.
The arising, abiding, and ceasing of delusive appearances are utterly unobtainable; there is only the wondrous clarity that perfectly illuminates the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within this, great functions manifest before one’s eyes: the many and the one can be mutually identical, and the large and the small can appear interchangeably.

Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the following eight lines correctly demonstrate these characteristics: "Without moving from the site of enlightenment, pervading the worlds of the ten directions"—this "one" is...
The immeasurable pervades the worlds of the ten directions, yet all are the immovable site of enlightenment; this immeasurability is one.
The body contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions; this one is immeasurable. The voids of the ten directions enter into the form of a single body;
this immeasurability is one. Within the tip of a single hair, a jeweled king-land is manifested; this is the manifestation of the great within the small.
Manifesting a Jewel King land upon the tip of a single hair while the appearance of the hair does not enlarge—this is the manifestation of the large within the small.
Sitting within a minute speck of dust while turning the Great Dharma Wheel—this is the manifestation of the large within the small.

Turning the Great Dharma Wheel within a single minute speck of dust while the speck of dust does not enlarge—this is the manifestation of the small within the large. This is the ultimate limit of the function of perfect interfusion and non-obstruction.
What is the reason for this? It is because by extinguishing dust and following awakening, one brings forth this wondrously enlightened nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, the Buddha now fears that people might doubt this, thinking that while unimpeded wondrous function is achieved through the Buddha’s cultivation, it must ultimately remain obstructed within the realm of sentient beings.
Therefore, he once again explains it in terms of the original mind to perfectly manifest the Threefold Treasury (*tripiṭaka*), so as to cause people to...

Know that this wondrous nature is fundamentally and inherently interfused; it is unrelated to delusion or enlightenment, being originally possessed by every person, yet only manifested upon reaching the stage of fruition.

In the phrase "the fundamentally wondrous, perfect mind" (*ben miao yuan xin*), the character "wondrous" (*miao*) is emphasized; this refers to the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, which is the essence of eternal quiescence.

Therefore, all worldly and world-transcending phenomena are entirely non-existent [in themselves]. In the phrase "the originally luminous, wondrous mind" (*yuan ming xin miao*), the character "luminous" (*ming*) is emphasized.
The "Word" (字) is the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, which is the function of constant illumination.

Therefore, all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds are simultaneously identical to the wondrously luminous primordial mind. Regarding the double occurrence of the two characters "wondrously luminous" (妙明):

this refers to the empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha, which is the essence where stillness and illumination are non-dual and where substance and function are inseparable. Thus, it is simultaneously free from both "identical" and "not identical," and it is simultaneously both.

This is not the Three Piṭakas; it is neither sequential nor simultaneous, neither identical nor distinct, but perfectly interfused and wondrously sublime, beyond all description—the so-called Unsurpassed Bodhi, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
How could it be conceived by means of the mind one currently possesses or through worldly language? It must be through wondrous wisdom that one can truly enter into accord with it.
Just as lutes, zithers, and other instruments possess exquisite sounds yet cannot produce them without skillful fingers,
so too sentient beings possess true nature yet cannot manifest that nature without sublime wisdom. Although I now press my fingers to demonstrate the ocean of nature,
making it as clearly revealed as the light emitted by the Ocean-Seal Samādhi, what could possibly be hidden from you, such that you grasp its meaning the very moment you raise your mind?
Briefly stated, this very mind that grasps and comprehends is precisely what gives rise to worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) and creates obstacles early on. Why is this so?
It is because you are unable to diligently seek the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, but instead cherish the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), considering a small attainment sufficient.

Consequently, wondrous wisdom does not manifest, and wondrous function remains unrevealed. The twelve phrases beginning with "Observing appearances as fundamentally false" are as follows: [text omitted].
The direct explanation of Pūrṇa’s doubts follows the analogy and precedes the application to the dharma (*dharmasaṃkramaṇa*); thus, the textual sequence is highly discordant.
Jiaoguang and Zhengmai maintain that this is a misplaced interpolation and that it should be moved to follow the application to the dharma, as this arrangement renders the meaning appropriate;

therefore, I now rely upon their view. It is not that the two phrases "clarifying non-illumination" and "the exhaustion of non-illumination" require the addition of the character "illumination" (*ming*) before "non-illumination."

Regarding the various explanations of the phrase "the superior clarity" (*shàng míng*), my humble opinion is as follows: the character *míng* (clarity) above refers to the act of clarifying—that is, the contemplation (*guān*) of the twelve links of dependent origination.
To clarify ignorance (*wú míng*) means to contemplate the arising of this ignorance; to clarify the exhaustion of ignorance means to contemplate the cessation of this ignorance.
Since such contemplative wisdom does not originally exist within the Tathāgatagarbha, both [ignorance and its exhaustion] are negated.
Pūrṇa said, "I and the Tathāgata [up to] 'it is not obtained from without.
This Pūrṇa had previously heard the Buddha say that the world and its sentient beings all give rise to deluded illumination;
because he harbored doubts as to what cause this deluded illumination arises from and wished to exhaust its root cause in order to decisively sever it, the Buddha then [acted for him].
To clarify this by means of an analogy: it is like the case of Yanruo, who upon looking into a mirror suddenly became deranged in mind and went about frantically searching for his own head.

How could this have had a cause? It was merely the delusion of his own mind. One should know that the essence of this awareness is fundamentally perfect, luminous, and wondrous, such that no delusion can be found therein.
If one now labels it "delusion," it is entirely without reality; how then could there be a cause? If there were, [it would not be delusion].
Since its cause must necessarily be real, how can it be called delusory?
It is merely because one's own various deluded thoughts take each other as causes that, from confusion to accumulated confusion, one passes through distant kalpas.

Although Buddhas appear in the world to reveal this delusion, the wheel of confusion can never be turned back. Thus, although the cause of delusion blazes forth as something existent, it is actually due to that very delusion.
Thus, one considers that what exists is not a substantial reality of the present;

if one realizes that this delusion is fundamentally without cause, then the essence of the false has no basis and lacks even birth—what, then, would there be to extinguish? Yet you speak of the "universal extinction" of all things.
This is because those who have attained Bodhi, though able to describe the appearances within delusion, cannot actually find anything to sever, just as [one cannot grasp the reflection in a mirror].
A person who has awakened can speak of the objects within a dream, yet they cannot actually be obtained or grasped;
how much more so this delusion, which is without cause and fundamentally non-existent—how could it wait until after awakening to cease?
It is just like Yajñadatta, who, fearing he had lost his head, ran about in a frenzy: from what cause did this madness arise? When the madness subsides, the head is not found outside.
Even if you have not yet ceased this madness, your head is nonetheless not lost; know that fundamentally there is no real substance.
How could there be a causal basis for the nature of this delusion? Its very essence is precisely like this—how could one possibly investigate what its cause might be?

If you now wish to reverse this wheel of delusion, it is not necessary to exhaustively seek out the cause of the delusion to sever it; you need only [focus] upon the world, sentient beings, and the fruits of their karma.
If one does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the objects of the threefold continuity, then the mind ceases and the objects naturally vanish;
thus, the three conditions are severed. Since the three conditions are severed, the objects vanish and the mind naturally ceases; thus, the three causes do not arise.

Because the three kinds of objects serve as the conditions for the conceptualization of the deluded mind, it is said that these three kinds of objects are the conditions for this discriminating mind, which is itself [the deluded mind].

Because it is the cause for the arising of the three kinds of delusory objects, it is called the "cause. Since neither cause nor condition can be established independently, how could fundamental ignorance exist alone?
Therefore, it too subsides and ceases. When ignorance has ceased, the originally inherent true essence fully manifests as the supreme, pure, and luminous mind.
This mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm and is not obtained from others; thus, one knows that there is no [ignorance].
The fundamental emptiness is revealed not through annihilation; the true essence is immovable and is not established by artificial power.

What need is there for the toil of cultivation and realization? It is like cutting away a mere sinew. This is just like the story of the poor man with the jewel in his garment: the jewel was always present, yet there was no gain or loss.
That he was poor before and rich now was not due to seeking it from without. According to this, ignorance arises directly dependent upon the True [Essence]. Thus...
If the Real is itself the cause of the delusive, why do you say it is without cause? One must know that the essence of Reality is eternally quiescent and fundamentally unborn;
one may only say that the delusive arises in dependence upon the Real, but one cannot say that the Real can produce the delusive. It is like the moon appearing in water:
one may only say that the moon appears in dependence on the water, but one cannot say that the water can produce the moon. Furthermore, this is discussed solely in terms of the objects of delusion.
Though these words may seem concise, if one speaks from the perspective of the realized state, ignorance is fundamentally empty; how, then, could there be arising?
It is just as the reflection of the moon is fundamentally void—how could it be said that it arises?
At that moment, Ānanda remained among the great assembly (until... still lingering to observe and listen.
This Ānanda again harbors doubts regarding causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). First, he doubted that the nature of seeing does not belong to causes and conditions;
next, he doubted that the myriad dharmas do not belong to causes and conditions; now, he doubts that the realization of the fruit does not belong to causes and conditions. This is because...
I have heard the Buddha say that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise; this does not discard the principle of causes and conditions.
Yet, you also say that delusion has no cause and what need is there for cultivation or realization? This seems to be an abrupt abandonment of causes and conditions.

Not having grasped the Buddha’s intent, it appears as though your choices are inconsistent and your own words contradict one another; therefore, I ask this question. The Buddha, intending to refute this view, first establishes the correct position.
That view says: "You think that if the causal conditions for the madness of the youth Rāvaṇa in the city were to be eliminated, then the state of non-madness would naturally emerge;
you hold that what was previously latent due to causes and conditions is suddenly manifested as something natural.
Your reckoning does not go beyond this principle. If this view were true, it would be ignorance and not the fundamental [nature]."

The emptiness of *bodhi* is neither inherently existent nor entirely established; these two constitute dualistic deluded attachments. Furthermore, if these two attachments were produced by causes and conditions, they would necessarily not be spontaneous;
if they were spontaneous, they would necessarily not be produced by causes and conditions. Now, Ānanda intended to negate both [extremes], yet instead he ended up negating both.
Therefore, the following text refutes them simultaneously by taking the confusion regarding the head as the point of departure—just as the head is originally...
If that were so, there would be nothing that is not natural. Why, then, on account of the causes and conditions of madness, does one run about frantically for fear of losing one's head?

Such a calculation of "naturalness" is delusory. If the head were fundamentally natural, yet one runs madly and frantically for fear of losing it due to causes and conditions, then it would follow that the head has truly been lost.
However, since the head has never actually moved, what need is there for such [fear]? What reliance can there be upon it?
To regard causes and conditions as such is the delusion of one who calculates causes and conditions; this refers to using the head to refute the dualistic calculation regarding Bodhi.

Alternatively, some may say that madness originally arises from spontaneity (*ziran*); if that were so, then prior to being mad, there ought to have been madness. Where would this madness be stored beforehand?
Since there was originally no madness, one cannot claim that madness arises from spontaneity. Or it may be said that madness does not...

If this [madness] arises from spontaneity (*svabhāva*), it would belong to the category of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). Now, since the head was originally not lost, why run about in a frenzy?

This madness is merely a false fabrication; furthermore, one cannot say that madness arises from causes and conditions. This uses the example of madness to refute the two non-dualistic views regarding ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since both awakening (*bodhi*) and ignorance are neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous, these two views [of spontaneity and causality] are likewise untenable.
Thus, both false consciousness and conceptual discrimination are merely frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and entirely devoid of real meaning.
It should be understood that my previous statement—that because the three conditions are severed, it is the bodhicitta—precisely refers to the cessation of frivolous proliferation.

For it is within these three types of continuity that one falsely gives rise to discrimination, which constitutes frivolous proliferation; now, by not following them, frivolous proliferation is cut off and ignorance ceases.
If there is no basis, what else could it be but bodhicitta? However, you must not say that there is a bodhicitta that arises.
If you say that bodhicitta arises and the arising-and-ceasing mind ceases, this is merely arising and ceasing; it is not bodhicitta.
When both cessation and arising are exhausted, one does not see the arising of bodhicitta, nor does one see the cessation of arising and ceasing. This is precisely non-effort (*anābhoga*).
If the Way were to take this as having a "naturalness," then that naturalness would mean the arising of the mind and the ceasing of the mind;
this, too, is arising and ceasing, and is not Bodhi. Why is this naturalness also not Bodhi?

Because it is called "unborn and unceasing" (anutpāda-aniruddha) by virtue of being the opposite of arising and ceasing—it is a name established through relative opposition; therefore, both are [conditioned].
Conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is just like the various characteristics of the world that combine into a single entity, which is termed "the nature of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-dharmatā*).
Consequently, that which is not so conjoined is termed "the original nature" (*prakṛti*). This name "original nature" is established based upon conjunction;
how could it be real? If one can remain utterly detached from both the original and the non-original, as well as from conjunction and non-conjunction, [one attains liberation].

Furthermore, when there is neither a mind of detachment nor a mind of non-detachment, this is the true bodhicitta; only then is it called the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).

From "From the arising of bodhicitta" up to this point, [the text] utterly sweeps away the two extremes of dualistic calculation, correctly refuting the previous notion that the extinction of the causes and conditions of madness results in the natural emergence of a non-mad state. In the section following "Bodhi and Nirvana," [the text] deeply rebukes Ānanda.
It is difficult and requires radical effort. Awakening and Nirvana are far removed from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);

as the fruit, they still lie at a great distance and cannot be realized through your diligent toil over kalpas. Even if you were to memorize many sutras, it would only serve to increase your conceptual proliferation.
Therefore, although you are now foremost in erudition and have practiced for accumulated kalpas, in the end you will be unable to achieve it.
To escape the perils of Māraṇḍa, one must rely on my Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī to attain liberation.

Thus we know that cultivation over kalpas is not equal to cultivating untainted karma for a single day. If even a woman of inferior faculties like Māraṇḍa or Yaśodharā could transcend entanglements and receive a prediction of enlightenment through a single moment of cultivating untainted wholesome karma, how much more so for you, who possess the faculties of a man?
How can you willingly deceive yourselves with frivolous discourse, lingering in the traces of what you have seen and heard, unable to emerge on your own?
From the first fascicle’s discernment of mind and views that illuminates the nature of awakening, down to the profound investigation of all phenomena that resolves doubts and obstructions—
all of this constitutes the initial expedient means to ensure that one's faith and understanding are authentic, serving as the causal ground for the mind of practice.
Since this is the reality, one can perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition; therefore, the following text separately opens the gate of cultivation.

Regarding the World-Honored One’s present teaching on the three conditions for severing the karma of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, Tianru [Zongyi] briefly cites the results of such karma, while his underlying intent includes the world and its sentient beings;
this interpretation is excellent. As for Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, whose three types of karma have already ceased to exist—how could the Buddha further instruct him to sever them?

Moreover, since one has merely ceased coarse karma, how can it be said that one has suddenly attained Bodhi? If one asks where madness could have been latent prior to its onset, it is difficult to find a corresponding state of conformity.
If one were to say that delusion was latent prior to becoming confused, then sentient beings would have a time before they were confused, and ignorance would have a day of its initial arising;
this would greatly contradict the Buddha’s intent. Now, taking this from the perspective of principle, it is appropriate [to consider it as follows]:...
If one were to say that delusion occurs within the fundamental spontaneity, then within that which is fundamentally pure and quiescent, wherein could delusion possibly lurk?
This is what the Chan school refers to as "prior to the time of Vīryasvara.
Ānanda and the great assembly heard the Buddha [speak of] his pure and wondrous virtue.

At the end of the third fascicle, Ānanda had already declared his realization; however, he had only realized its general essence of pervasiveness and permanence, while subtle delusions had not yet been dispelled.
For this reason, Pūrṇa specifically requested further instruction to resolve his remaining doubts.

The Buddha then elucidated each point for him, fully revealing the entire substance and great function of this mind—its pervasive, perfect, and harmonious nature—which was precisely what Ānanda [had been seeking].
It is vast and open, free from delusion; yet, if one possesses knowledge but lacks practice, it will ultimately be difficult to enter into realization.

Therefore, at the conclusion of the preceding section, the Buddha rebuked him for his many learnings being of no merit and failing to reach the level of cultivation. Consequently, after Ānanda had expressed his gratitude, he requested instruction on the gateway to attaining the Way.
Thus, there arose the analogy of the celestial king granting a house that must be entered through a door, which the Buddha then demonstrated.
Regarding the two principles of certainty for awakening the initial mind, this is precisely the gateway for entering samādhi, known as the primary expedient means.
As for the first principle of certainty: one must carefully examine whether the mind of the causal stage and the enlightenment of the resultant stage are identical or different;
one must take the non-arising, non-perishing mind as the cause in order to seek the non-arising, non-perishing fruit.

When cause and effect are identical, that constitutes true cultivation. If one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the cause while seeking a fruit that is non-arising and non-ceasing, then cause and effect are disparate; how could such a thing ever be accomplished?

For this reason, you should clearly illuminate that all conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) are necessarily subject to destruction; only space, being unconditioned, is not subject to creation. Thus it begins.

By this irrefutable analogy, one may know that it is difficult for a mind characterized by conditioned activity—subject to arising and ceasing—to produce a result that is eternally abiding and indestructible.
What is meant by the "conditioned mind"? It is the four great elements (mahābhūta) that entwine within your body;

from these four entanglements, they divide your profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, and luminous mind into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. From beginning to end, these constitute five layers of turbidity.
To lose the true source is precisely what practitioners of cultivation must urgently eliminate; how could one rely upon it further as the fundamental cause for practice?
Why is it called "turbidity"? It is like water, which is fundamentally clear and pure, and earth, which is fundamentally obstructive;
these two natures originally do not follow one another. If earth is thrown into water, the earth loses its obstruction and the water perishes [its clarity].
That which is pure and clear yet has a turbid appearance is called "turbidity. The five layers of the present [world] are also like this.

Regarding the first layer, when one speaks of the initial state of dark obscurity as emptiness, it refers to a single thought of non-awakening that falsely perceives empty space pervading the ten directions.
Here, emptiness and seeing merge without distinction; there is emptiness, yet there is no substance with form or material quality.
Seeing [objects] without the perception of either opposition or compliance, this empty vision interweaves with delusion to form the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

At the very moment when ignorance first arises in the state of chaotic vastness, that is precisely the kalpa-turbidity. The second stage concerns the formation of the sense organs from the aggregation of matter:
after darkness is formed from within space to become matter, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) then coalesce, and these four great elements form the body.
Internally, the four natures of seeing, hearing, smelling, and cognizing are obstructed by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), resulting in stagnation and hindrance;

conversely, the four great elements are moved by these four natures, resulting in cognition. Through the interweaving of these natures and elements, delusion gives rise to the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Because the faculty of the body exists, there arises the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). This third stage involves the arising of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) through the opposition between the faculties and their objects.

At that time, when there is recollection, cognition, chanting, or study within the mind, the internal nature gives rise to deluded awareness, and external appearances manifest as the six sense-objects.

Awareness is without characteristics apart from the objects, and the objects are without substance apart from awareness. Because this nature and these phenomena are interwoven, they falsely constitute the turbidity of afflictions;
as the objects condition the mind until it is filled with thoughts, there is never a moment free from weariness and disturbance. However—
The fourth point concerns the transition from death to rebirth. This illusory body arises and perishes morning and night without ceasing for even a moment;
yet, through perception and attachment to a self, one constantly yearns for this world. As the momentum of karma does not cease, one is perpetually transferred to other lands.
Thus, the interweaving of remaining and migrating gives rise to the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), as they follow the flow of karma to enter all realms of existence.
The fifth layer concerns the moment of taking birth through the force of karma. At that time, the six sense organs share the same basis, with the eight consciousnesses as their nature;
yet, as various objects form the organs, there arise distinctions of separation and lack of form, as well as distinct forms. Because their nature is fundamentally the same, they are joined together;
because their functions are different, they turn away from one another. Thus, being both the same and different, they possess no fixed standard, and by this intermingling of sameness and difference—
Weaving delusions, one forms the turbidity of life; the eight consciousnesses maintain the continuity of the physical and mental aggregates throughout a single lifetime, which constitutes "life.
These five layers of confusion obscure the true nature, such that seeing, hearing, cognition, and awareness remain far removed from those of the Tathāgata.

Now, if you wish to cause this seeing, hearing, cognition, and awareness to reach far toward the virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, then that upon which they depend must serve as the basis for fundamental cultivation.

The causal conditions must be examined with care; one must necessarily select and eliminate the root of birth-and-death—the empty, floating, and deluded consciousness—and rely upon the nature of the non-arising, non-perishing, perfect, and profound stillness to accomplish this merit.
This is precisely what is meant later by "if one discards arising and ceasing and maintains the true permanence.
By returning to maintain this profound stillness, although there is no intentional turning back of delusion, delusion naturally subsides and recedes of its own accord, until—

The coarse afflictions having been previously subdued, the fundamental awakening appears to return to the stage of the first faith; this is the attainment of the fundamental luminous awakening, which possesses the nature of being without birth or extinction.

This is the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Only then does it become the true mind of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*). From this point on, one is able to perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the resultant ground (*phala-bhūmi*).

As for the "resultant ground," the stages of abiding (*vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), and orientation (*mukha*), as well as the stages of equality (*samatā*) and wondrous subtlety (*prakarṣa*), are all the resultant ground. Now, by means of...
Clarifying water is likened to this: one must clarify water using a still vessel, which serves as a metaphor for clarifying the mind by relying upon wondrous stillness.

As sand and soil naturally settle and clear water naturally appears, it symbolizes the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions. When the mud is removed and pure water remains, it symbolizes the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance.
Upon reaching the permanent severance of fundamental ignorance, the characteristics of clarity become purely refined, and all [phenomena] are [seen as such].
When transformations are seen as non-existent and afflictions no longer arise, all are in accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of nirvana;
just as water that has become entirely clear will show no sign of turbidity regardless of how much it is stirred, this marks the ultimate consummation of the work of cultivation and realization.
The second meaning is that those six faculties of cognition become simultaneously purified.
Regarding the second definitive meaning, one should carefully discern the root of afflictions:
the karma that has manifested before sentient beings since beginningless time and moistens future existence is entirely affliction; yet, as for the karma thus produced—
As for who truly creates that which is moistened and brought into birth, and who truly receives it—this is entirely the fault of the fundamental source.
Therefore, one must first know where this fundamental source resides before one can subdue all delusions and advance toward the state of Tathāgata.
It is just as a person in the world who unties a knot must first know the location of that knot before [proceeding].
That which is able to know and that which is understood are merely what is called the "fundamental. What is this? It is your six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

Because these six organs exist, they draw in the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) from without and give rise to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) within. These internal and external evil thieves are able to plunder the family treasure, whereby the true nature (*tathatā*) is lost.
Once the true nature is lost, one sinks and drowns in birth and death (*saṃsāra*); thus, one spontaneously arises within the world of sentient beings.
Bound by fetters, they are unable to transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). What is called the "sentient-being world" (*sattva-loka*)? It is the body of these sentient beings.
"World" (*loka*) refers to the sense of flux and transition; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial location. As for spatial location, there are fourteen directions:
the four cardinal points, the four intermediate directions, plus above and below. As for the categories of flux, there are three: the past, the future, and the present. (1)
All sentient beings, because this bodily form is constituted by the interweaving of manifold delusions, fully possess the meanings of the directions of front, back, left, and right.
Within the body, the meaning of "the world" (loka) is established through the sense of constant flux and non-abiding.
Because these worlds thus interact with one another, they are called the "sentient-being world. Although these positions are ten in number, the zenith and nadir have no substantial location.
While the corners have no fixed direction, there are fixed positions that can be clearly identified, namely the four cardinal directions: east, west, south, and north.

When the three periods of time intersect with the four directions, three times four results in twelve; when the four directions intersect with the three periods of time, four times three likewise results in the number twelve.
Although there are twelve, each one possesses all principles in their entirety; therefore, by...
By folding this cloth upward, one can change one into ten, change ten into a hundred, and change a hundred into a thousand;

thus, each of the six sense organs possesses twelve hundred merits. While it is generally said that the merits of the six sense organs are each complete in themselves, if we consider the capacities of those in this region, they cannot be without degrees of superiority and inferiority. For instance, as for the eye, it perceives what is before it.
Later, when one is in darkness and observes the positions around one's left and right, only two-thirds of the surrounding space can be seen;
therefore, its merit is only eight hundred. By contrast, the ear hears throughout the ten directions without anything being obstructed;
when active, it hears sounds as if they have proximity and distance, yet when still, it hears silence that is vast and boundless. Therefore, its merit is perfect.
Even if it were complete at one thousand two hundred, it would be like the nose: although there is inhalation and exhalation of breath, there is no exchange of air between them.
Exhalation can grasp fragrance but cannot perceive it; inhalation can perceive fragrance but cannot grasp it.
Thus, being deficient by one-third, its merit is only eight hundred. As for the tongue, there is no worldly or world-transcending wisdom that it cannot accommodate.
As for the statement that "some are limited while the principle is fundamentally boundless," its meritorious qualities are thus perfectly complete at one thousand two hundred.
In the case of the body, it is composed of particles that form contact; it can perceive what is adverse or favorable, but lacks this capacity when separated.

Since it possesses both [faculties] when in combination and lacks one when separated, its meritorious qualities amount to only eight hundred. As for the mind, it silently encompasses the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Because it encompasses all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms without exception, its merit is perfectly complete—amounting to one thousand two hundred [qualities].

Now, you wish to enter through practice by way of the six sense faculties, turning against the current of the flow of birth and death to trace back to the root of that flow until reaching the ground of non-arising and non-ceasing; how could this be done indifferently, without knowing what to choose?
"You must carefully examine these six sense-faculties: which possesses a nature of union and is deep, and which possesses a nature of separation and is shallow;

which is perfectly penetrating (*pariṇita*), and which is not. If you follow this perfectly penetrating faculty to turn back from delusion and return to the Truth, your merit will exceed that of one who does not follow the perfectly penetrating faculty by a factor of ten million times ten million eons. I have now fully revealed the six kinds of profound stillness and perfect penetration."
The measure of these merits is as follows: according to your own inclination, select those which you deem suitable to enter;

I shall then clarify them for you so that you may advance in your spiritual practice. For the eighteen realms are fundamentally without superiority or inferiority, and all Buddhas cultivated them to attain unsurpassed Bodhi.
However, because your faculties are inferior, you encounter many obstructions and have not yet attained perfect mastery.

Because of wisdom, one must necessarily select that which is suitable for entry and focus exclusively on a single gate; by entering deeply until delusion is exhausted and reality manifests, then all six sense faculties will simultaneously become pure.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One... [up to] ...it does not constitute perfect subtlety.”
Ānanda, having heard this teaching on reversing the flow of the desire-stream of birth and death and entering the single gate of the six purities, was unable to deeply comprehend its meaning;
therefore, he requested the Buddha to clarify it for him. The Buddha said:

"This reversal of the flow of the desire-stream of birth and death, proceeding deeply until reaching the single gate of the six purities, is not a matter for those who have merely severed coarse delusions. Now, Ānanda..."
One who realizes the fruit of *srotāpanna* has merely severed the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) still remain;

how much more so in this faculty, where there are further subtle delusions of the same essence—namely, the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*utpāda-sthiti-anyathātva-nirodha*)—how could Ānanda possibly know the measure or number of those to be severed?
What is called "entering once and becoming pure in six ways" does not mean that the faculties truly possess one or six.
If you insist that the six sense organs are fixed as one, then since the ear, eye, head, and feet each have distinct functions and do not communicate with one another, they are not fixed as one.
If you insist that the six sense organs are fixed as six, then when your ear now comes to hear the Dharma, what connection does it have with the body or the mouth?
And when the mouth comes to inquire about the meaning, the body rises to show reverence; thus, they are also not fixed as six. You should know this.

These faculties are neither one nor six; they arise solely because you have been submerged in beginningless inversion and delusion, whereby you falsely give rise to the concepts of "one" and "six" within the perfectly湛 (zhan—profoundly still and clear) reality.
You, as a Srotāpanna, do not enter the six sense-objects, and thus the six [faculties] have dissolved;
yet you still cling to the six faculties as a single entity. This is not yet the extinction of "one. How does this differ from an ordinary person who clings to the six?
How strange! It is just as when the great void of space combines with various vessels, we say the space is "different";
yet when the vessels are removed and one contemplates the space, we say the space is "one. How could space itself become either the same or different because of your false conceptualizations?
Furthermore, how can you seek to establish right and wrong within it? Since neither "one" nor "six" truly exist, why is it that the six sense faculties currently manifest?
Why is this? It is because the delusion arises from clinging to stillness. The wondrously perfect true nature is inherently tranquil;

however, because there are delusory objects, that tranquility becomes that which is clung to, and thus it gives rise to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Once seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing exist, one grasps at external objects, and these coalesce to form the sense organs.
Initially, they consist of subtle matter, which is called the four great elements in their pure state; once they have become coarse, [the process is complete].

As for form, it is called the four turbidities of the floating faculties; from this, through inversion, they flow outwardly in pursuit of externals, rushing headlong to form the boundless cycle of birth and death—this is the "outflow of desire.
Thus one knows that the formation of these six faculties originates in false existence;
because of the false existence of awakened clarity, they adhere to delusion and emit light. Since the six faculties are complete, they are due to delusion.

When you arouse [this awareness], you will know that phenomena, being detached from dust, have no inherent substance. You need only not follow external objects; the internal faculties can then be uprooted.
As each faculty is uprooted, you detach from clinging and settle inwardly, thereby returning to the original reality. The luminosity that is inherently present will then spontaneously manifest.
Since this is true for one faculty, the false attachments of the other five faculties should likewise be uprooted for a complete liberation. Therefore it is said: "Entering through one..."
The sixth is purity. That which is called "the manifestation of the fundamental radiance" does not arise from the cognitions produced by external objects;
its clarity does not follow the sense organs to emerge, but merely relies upon them to manifest. Since it relies upon the organs to manifest, the organs cannot restrict it;
thus, the six organs are all mutually interchangeable. One may see with the nose and hear with the eyes. Now, observe this:
For example, Aniruddha saw despite having no eyes; the dragon Upananda heard despite having no ears; the goddess of the Ganges smelled fragrances despite having no nose;
Gavāmpati knew tastes despite having a different kind of tongue; the Śūnyatā-deva perceived touch despite having no body;
and Mahākāśyapa understood through cognition despite having no mind. These individuals may have achieved such states through the cultivation of the Hīnayāna, or they may be ordinary beings.
Now, if even the retributive fruits obtained through practice cannot be confined by the faculties, how much less so for one who has manifested the fundamental luminosity?
When the various faculties are fully uprooted and the inner clarity radiates light, its efficacy does not stop at the mutual functioning of the faculties alone;
rather, all ephemeral phenomena and the transformations of the vessel-world are simultaneously melted by the light of the mind, just as ice is dissolved by hot water.
The ice, by responding to his thought, was transformed into supreme awakening.

The Buddha further feared that people might say this perfect subtlety is not inherently possessed by everyone, and thus doubt its sudden manifestation; therefore, he used a proximate matter to verify it:
"Suppose people gather and look with their eyes, and you were suddenly to close them—though there are people standing before them, the six sense organs would be dark and blank."
If one were to discern by tracing that person’s body with the hand, although the eyes do not see it, the head and feet are nonetheless discerned;
this is no different from seeing with eyes open. By verifying it through this, one knows that seeing does not depend on light, for the human being inherently possesses it.
Indeed, if seeing depended on light, there would be no seeing in the dark; only when it arises spontaneously without depending on light can it perceive all darkness.
The characteristics [of the faculties] can never be permanently obscured; it is only ordinary people who are hindered by the sense organs and their objects that they cannot perceive them constantly.
Now that the sense organs and their objects have been eliminated, why would the perfect and wondrous state not be realized?

Regarding the tongue perceiving flavors, the ancient commentary states that Gavāmpati suffered from a "cow-whistling" ailment, meaning he had a cow's tongue, yet he was able to perceive the flavors of what people ate. This explanation is not [correct].
Although there is indeed the ailment of "ox-whistling," how could it be called the ox's tongue?
I, the fool, say that one who knows flavors with a "different tongue" simply does not use the tongue yet is nonetheless able to know flavors.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One... why would one fail to achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?

This Ānanda, having understood the Buddha’s teaching that if, during the causal stage, one takes a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental practice for cultivation while seeking the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible;
and having also understood the Buddha’s teaching on being free from darkness and free from light.

Having perceived the essence and other attributes, they subsequently raise this objection: "The awakening-mind (*bodhicitta*) on the causal stage must correspond to that of the resultant stage in order to achieve the fruit.
Now, observing the state of fruition: that which is called unsurpassed right wisdom is named *bodhi*; that which is tranquil, eternal, and blissful is named *nirvāṇa*;
that which is non-deceptive and immutable is named *tathatā* (Suchness); and that which is free from faults and transcends all negation is named the Buddha.
To discern all phenomena while remaining unstained by attachment is called the *amala-vijñāna*.
To not establish even a single dharma as real while afflictions are utterly exhausted is called the *śūnya-tathāgatagarbha*.

To perfectly reflect all phenomena without discrimination is called the *ādarśa-jñāna* (Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom). Although these seven designations differ, they are all pure and unstained, perfect and complete.

That which is impartial, firm, and solid like a diamond king, and cannot be destroyed—those who hope for this fruit must necessarily take that which is eternally abiding, neither arising nor ceasing, as its cause.
Now, observing the function of the six sense organs, they have no substance apart from their objects, being just like the consciousness-mind;
how could one rely upon them as a cause to seek the fruit of the sevenfold eternal abiding? Indeed, I...
I have once advanced these faculties to illustrate them by way of the consciousness-mind, and again withdrawn this consciousness-mind to harmonize it with the faculties;
through this cycle of advancing and retreating, I have sought with subtle discernment, yet ultimately no mind or mental factors can be found.

Who, then, shall establish the cause to seek unsurpassed enlightenment? Previously, I heard the Buddha say that within the faculties, the six penetrations are exquisite, still, and perfectly luminous; now, however—
Upon examination, this lacks any real meaning and contradicts the authentic words [of the Buddha], ultimately resulting in mere frivolous discourse.

According to the Buddha, when the six sense organs are separated from their objects, they lack a substantial body; this refers to the absence of the substance of delusory attachment, not that there is no nature within the organs themselves.

Ānanda then claimed that if they lacked nature when separated from objects, this was a fallacy, and thus raised this objection. The Buddha then verified this by means of the incident of hearing a bell.
When the Buddha examined his hearing, he took the striking of the bell as the arising of hearing and the subsiding of the sound after a long time as the ceasing of hearing;

thus, he treated the sound as the act of hearing. When he examined the sound itself, he took the striking of the bell as the arising of sound and the subsiding of the sound after a long time as the ceasing of sound;
thus, he treated the sound as the object of sound. Having already treated it as hearing, he further...
To answer with sound would result in the fault of self-contradiction and incoherence, as there is no fixed certainty.
If you claim that when sound vanishes it becomes "no-hearing," then the nature of hearing itself must be severed; yet when the bell is struck again, why can it be heard once more?

It is clear that what exists or does not exist is the sound, not the hearing. If the absence of sound meant the absence of hearing, then who is it that knows the absence? That which knows is the hearing, not the sound.

Within the act of hearing, sounds arise and perish of their own accord, yet the nature of hearing itself remains constant, free from arising or perishing. You are still deluded by taking sound to be hearing;
how then can you wonder at the notion of the eternal being perceived as intermittent? This is merely your own inverted confusion and delusion to make such a claim;
you should never say that hearing lacks an inherent nature apart from the presence or absence of movement and stillness, or the states of closure and openness. Now, let us examine this.
When those who sleep soundly in the world hear the sound of pestles in their dreams, they may mistake it for a bell or a drum;
yet in their dreams, how could they recall whether things were still or moving, open or closed, unobstructed or blocked? Though their bodies are in slumber, the nature of hearing is not clouded.
This serves as an analogy to know that this nature is not merely unclouded within a dream, but even when the body dissolves and life passes away, this nature ultimately does not perish.
The eradication [of afflictions] is specifically because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have failed to awaken to the purity, subtlety, and permanence of their own nature;

thus, they cannot internally follow that which is constant while externally pursuing various delusions. Consequently, they undergo the cycle of defiled transmigration, birth after birth without end, finding no means to realize the truth.

If one can abandon that which arises and perishes, let go of external conditions, and inwardly illumine so that the six faculties cease their activity together, one will maintain alone the true and constant.

Then the constant light will naturally manifest before you. When the constant light manifests, the faculties, objects, and consciousness-mind will naturally dissolve and fall away in accordance with thought.
These three—faculties, objects, and consciousness—are dust and defilement that obscure and cloud the *prajñā*.

Now that they have dissolved, the Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright; how could one then fail to achieve unsurpassed knowledge and vision? [The section on] Rāhula striking the bell (1).
It is sufficient for the World-Honored One to inquire twice—whether it exists or does not exist—but why must he strike again to inquire a third time?

Observe carefully the subsequent refutation, which states: "If there were truly no hearing and the nature of hearing had already ceased, being like a withered tree, how would you know when the bell is struck a second time?
This inquiry into the third time is of great significance; it is not merely intended to... [The text appears to be truncated].
To examine this further, the matter of hearing the sound of pounding in a dream goes one step deeper than what preceded it.

There is a verification of sound through movement, and a verification of sound through stillness; in both cases, there is no cessation. Yet, this has not yet reached the point of transcending both movement and stillness.
Now, while one is dully dwelling in a dream, how could one be mindful of stillness or motion? Thus, one transcends both movement and stillness, and yet the nature of hearing remains uninterrupted.
Thus it is. *A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Four;
*A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Yuánxián of Yǒngquán Chán Monastery on Mount Gǔ at Fúzhōu.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, although [you have] spoken... [up to] the single path to the gate of nirvāṇa."

In the preceding chapter, the Buddha has already clearly identified the six sense-faculties as the knots and further clarified that not following external objects is the essential point for resolving these knots.

Ānanda, however, harbors a doubt: although the six faculties are indeed the knots, he fears that there must be an original source for these knots located elsewhere, and thus the essential method for untying them might not be limited to merely not following external objects. For this reason, he now sheds tears and raises [this question].

He earnestly requested instruction. The Buddha then rubbed the crown of his head with his hand, caressing and comforting him. Immediately, the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions shook in six ways;
this signifies that the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) constitutes the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), and that from these, [the obstructions] are now shaken and shattered.
From the crowns of each of the *rajas* (dust-mote) Tathāgatas, precious lights emerged; this signifies that this Dharma is...
The Unsurpassed Crown Dharma simultaneously bestows empowerment upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head;
this signifies that they preach in unison and realize in unison, with no other path. All Buddhas collectively address Ānanda, saying:

"If you wish to know that which is the root of the fetters causing you to revolve in birth and death—the innate ignorance—it is none other than these six sense organs. This indicates that the nature of these organs is itself innate ignorance.
If you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi that enables you to swiftly realize peaceful liberation and the wondrous, eternal tranquility, it is also solely these six faculties.
To say that the nature of these faculties is itself Bodhi is to speak of the fundamentally pure essence.
Although Ānanda heard the Buddha’s words, he still did not clearly understand their purport; for while the Buddhas usually teach the Dharma in brief, [the full meaning remains hidden].
Since there are eighteen realms, why do you now single out the six sense organs as being so important? Thus, harboring doubt, he questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Although the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are divided into internal and external, they all arise through the manifestation of the one mind; thus, they share a single source.
Although they share a single source, it is the faculties that act as the essential fetters: by means of them one becomes an ordinary person, and by means of these same six, one becomes a sage."
"The faculties exist, yet the objects do not accompany them"—these two phrases distinguish the objects.
"If it were the nature of consciousness, it would arise falsely due to the faculties and objects, like flowers in the sky, having no substantial reality at all;

since it is neither the root of bondage nor the essential point for liberation"—these two phrases distinguish consciousness. Yet, how could these six faculties and six objects possibly possess any reality?
How can the nature [of the faculties] be apprehended? It must first arise through the objects (*viṣaya*), and the cognition of the faculties must first manifest through that cognition.
The characteristics of these objects and the seeing [faculty] each lack self-nature; they exist only in mutual dependence, like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
You should now understand that the nature of these faculties is not reached; do not grasp them as being truly existent, nor dismiss them as non-existent.
Yet, to further maintain "non-existence" and establish these two types of cognition is precisely the root of ignorance and the knot that binds one to birth and death.

If one penetrates the nature of this very root and does not grasp at it as being existent, nor maintain the view of non-existence—this absence of these two views is the fundamentally pure essence of Nirvana.
This bondage resides solely in the root; this liberation resides solely in the root. How could anything else possibly intervene therein?
How remarkable! The Buddha spoke these verses again to clarify this point: "The true nature is empty of the conditioned. These ten lines below establish the fundamental thesis and refute attachments;

by means of analogy, they reveal that the sense organs and their objects lack inherent nature. Within the true nature, all dualistic oppositions are severed—there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned.
Conditioned phenomena are empty and do not exist, arising merely from conditions; this is illustrated through metaphor.
Like illusory phenomena, unconditioned dharmas have neither arising nor ceasing, nor do they possess substantial reality; they are like flowers in the sky.

While conditioned things can certainly be said to be empty, how could the unconditioned also be unreal? This is because when the false is rejected to reveal the true, "true" and "false" stand in opposition to one another;
since there is a "true" that exists in opposition to the false, that "true" itself becomes false, for it remains a realm accessible to discursive thought.

Therefore, since both the real and the unreal have already been negated as a pair, how could there be any sense-faculty that sees or any object-field that is seen? Within, there is no substantial nature;

it is merely like two reeds leaning against each other. The six lines below, beginning with "The untying of the knot shares the same cause," praise the fact that the untying of the knot resides solely in the sense-faculty.
This means that although this faculty is like two leaning reeds, as for the knotting and the untying, they reside only [in the faculty].
Therefore, although the gap between the sage and the ordinary person is as vast as that between clouds and mud, there are in fact no two separate paths.
This is because the nature within the intersection is neither existent nor non-existent. Those who are deluded and obscured cling to existence or non-existence;
this is precisely ignorance, the very root of birth and death. Those who have attained illumination do not cling to existence, nor do they cling to non-existence. Thus...
Since this is the essential path for achieving liberation where no nirvana exists, could there be any other cause outside of this?
The four lines of verse beginning with "The sequence of the causes for untying the knots" describe the matter of untying the knots from their source.

This means that when the knots are formed, they necessarily proceed from the subtle to the coarse through six successive layers before the characteristics of the source are fully manifested; therefore, the untying of the knots now must likewise proceed from the coarse to the subtle.

Next, through six successive stages, the roots and origins are gradually exhausted until all six knots are completely severed; then even "one" no longer stands, and one returns to the primordial state of perfect stillness.
However, as the faculties employed differ in their degree of excellence, one must select a path of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) and enter it through cultivation.
When external objects are no longer followed and one returns to the original truth, one enters the stream and achieves completion.
The four lines of verse beginning with "The subtle consciousness of the ear-dhāraṇī of Perfect Enlightenment" describe the excellence of the nature of the faculties.

Why is it that this Dharma is cultivated by relying solely on the six faculties? It is because the nature of the faculties is itself the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). *Ādānavijñāna* is an alternative name for the eighth consciousness;
this consciousness directly takes the *tathatā-gotra* (nature of the treasury) as its essence and is most subtle, such that none but a Buddha can perceive it.

One fully knows that within this intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are seeds of ignorance and perfuming (*vāsanā*) capable of producing the phenomena of boundless birth and death, like a torrential flood flowing on without ceasing.
If this consciousness is said to be real, how can it be so when it still carries and maintains the seeds of delusive habit-energies?

If it is said to be delusive, how can it be so when its essence is none other than the *tathāgatagarbha* nature? Apart from this, there is no reality; I fear that ordinary people and those of the Two Vehicles will not believe this.
Because it can be conceptually differentiated, it is neither the [right] time nor the [proper] capacity; thus, it was kept secret and not expounded.

That this sutra alone places such emphasis on this consciousness—how could it be that it treats the teachings commonly spoken with such lightness? "The self-mind grasps the self-mind"—the four lines of this verse represent the most essential point of this Dharma.
This means that because the knots of the faculties do not consist of many dharmas, their liberation likewise does not consist of many dharmas; it is simply due to...
Failing to realize that the objects of the six sense-fields are nothing but the single mind, one erroneously uses the perceiving mind to falsely grasp at the perceived objects;
