this is "the self-mind grasping the self-mind. Thus, from within the signless and non-illusory, illusory phenomena are falsely formed, and the sense organs and their objects appear distinct.
Since the former state involved false seeing that grasped at objects to produce delusive dharmas, now one simply turns [the mind back].
When the faculties are detached from objects and no longer grasp at them, then both person and phenomena are necessarily empty; even the non-illusory realm is transcended and utterly liberated.
How much more so, then, could illusory phenomena possibly be established? Thus we know that bondage is extremely easy [to incur], yet liberation is also extremely essential.
These eight lines beginning with "This is called the Wondrous Lotus" eulogize the supremacy of this Dharma; this Dharma reveals the Buddha’s knowledge.
You have shown that the essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) contains the fruit within the cause; though immersed in defilement, it is eternally pure, like a wondrous lotus flower.

The essence-nature of the unsurpassed jewel-like awakening is firm and solid; when the faculties, objects, delusions, and fetters encounter it, they are instantly dissolved, like a diamond king (*vajrarāja*).

Arising cultivation from the entirety of this nature, one maintains the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom; it is cultivation without cultivation and severance without severance, termed the "illusory samādhi" (*māyopama-samādhi*).
If you rely upon this to cultivate and advance, in the mere snap of a finger you may transcend the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) and enter the Perfect Stage (*yuanwei*).

This is called the most supreme and peerless Dharma; it is by means of this that the Buddhas of the ten directions have all emerged from birth-and-death and swiftly realized *nirvāṇa*. How can you not exert yourselves?
Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly [attained] the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Because this section [deals with] how Ānanda had not yet realized that "the six are resolved and the one is extinguished," nor understood the sequence of loosening the knots, he again requested the Buddha to provide instruction.
The Buddha then took a piece of cloth and successively tied it into six knots to illustrate this; he said that once the single cloth had been tied...
When six knots are formed, the first, second, and so on up to the sixth are clearly distinct in sequence; how could they be confused or arbitrarily renamed?
This is precisely like the six knots on a rope which are determined to be six. Only after the knots have become six does it manifest that the original cloth is one.
One can speak of "one" only in contrast to the six; if the six were all untied at once, then even... [the notion of "one" would no longer apply].
If even a single thought arises, how much more so six? When the six faculties are resolved into one, their objects likewise vanish;

the principle is the same. As for the successive formation of the six knots, what is their order? It is simply because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have failed to awaken to the nature of mind, falsely dividing it into subject and object.

Through this madness, they falsely establish objective appearances, and through these delusions, chaotic perceptions arise. From this state of frantic confusion, their knowledge and vision become false.

To give rise to the grasping of dharmas as truly existent is to give rise to delusion; if this delusion does not cease, then weariness arises. To give rise to the dust of wearied vision is to grasp at "self" and "what belongs to self.
When wearied vision gives rise to the dust, then all the various inversions of the mundane world—mountains, rivers, the great earth, birth and death, and nirvana—all manifest from this.
It is just like seeing flowers in the sky with weary eyes; how could they have any reality? Consider this according to the text.

In accordance with the establishment of the various fetters (*saṃyojana*), although the six have not been explicitly pointed out, the meaning is nonetheless very clear. The nature of the mind is the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, the sovereign minds (*cittarāja*).
When it is divided into the two portions of subject and object (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*), it becomes madness and disorder;

these are the two fetters. When cognitive vision (*jñāna-darśana*) falsely arises, one is in the stage of attachment to the true dharma (*dharmagrāha*); within this attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), there are both innate (*sahaja*) and discriminative (*vikalpika*) types, which constitute the two fetters. This is weariness.

Seeing that the ordinary person who gives rise to delusions and the person who clings to the status of a sage both possess innate and discriminative grasping—these are the two fetters—and that these six fetters originally arise from a deluded mind:
if one now wishes to untie them, how could they be resolved by any partial or expedient methods?
One must employ the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way to directly shatter that deluded mind, and only then will the fetters be resolved.
Only then can one understand that it is just as when a person in the world attempting to untie a knot cannot resolve it by pulling from the left or the right;

if one wishes to untie it, one must do so at the very center of the knot. This method of untying the knot, while appearing to belong to the realm of causes and conditions, is most subtle and wondrous, unlike the coarse phenomena of worldly conjunctions. By relying on the Buddha, one attains immeasurable wisdom.
Because it subtly illuminates what is near and brilliantly shines upon what is far, one is able to know this and speak of this.
As for these dharmas, one must necessarily select from among the six sense organs that which possesses perfect penetration.

By entering deeply through a single organ and reflecting back upon the nature of the organ rather than pursuing external objects, the wild mind can be shattered and the six knots can be untied. Once the six knots are untied, then that which was previously called—
The inverted perceptions of external phenomena, which are like flowers in the sky seen by a fatigued eye, have all been extinguished without remainder.
Since all delusions have been eliminated, what need is there to wait for the unreal? However, this knot cannot be removed instantaneously; it must proceed through stages.
Just as with the knots in a cloth, the knots were formed in sequence, so too must their untying follow that same sequence. When this faculty is first liberated, one first attains the human realm.
Emptiness is precisely the resolution of the two knots within the grasping for persons; this reverses the previous state where weary views gave rise to the dust of affliction.

As long as the grasping for phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persists, the nature of emptiness cannot yet be perfectly luminous. When the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation from phenomena, which is the resolution of the two knots within the grasping for phenomena;

this reverses the previous state where false knowledge and views were erroneously produced. Although one has attained the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—the two kinds of emptiness themselves have not yet been dissolved.

Precisely when even subtle ignorance still persists, the shadows of subject and object remain; yet, by directly attaining the simultaneous emptiness of both such that they do not arise, one immediately resolves the latter two fetters.
This is the reversal of the preceding state of madness and confusion. Reaching this point, quiescence manifests before one:

not a single dharma is seen to arise, nor is a single dharma seen to cease, and thus one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). This is precisely how the subsequent sages enter [the path].
This is the stage of Perfect Penetration. According to the ancient commentaries on this section, the "six knots" all refer to the six sense organs.
However, I [Yuyi] maintain that while the six knots are formed in succession, it cannot be said that the six sense organs are likewise formed in succession;

nor can it be said that the six knots are untied in succession, implying that the six sense organs are likewise untied in succession. The analogy and the dharma-realm are clearly not identical. Those who explain it thus [are mistaken].
To claim that "one root penetrating deeply leads to the simultaneous liberation of all six roots" as the sequential order is extremely far-fetched;

how much more so when it is already explicitly stated in this very passage that "from your beginningless [past]... clarifies the sequence of their binding, and "...this root first being liberated... clarifies the sequence of their liberation?
Why do you completely disregard these statements and rely solely on the mere coincidence of the number of the six knots and the six sense organs to establish such a sequence?

This is merely a false attachment to the names of the six knots; the scriptural text is obscure and abbreviated. Now, by analyzing the original text, the underlying meaning will become clear of itself.
Let the reader examine it closely.
[From] "Ānanda and the great assembly" ... up to "the Dharma-cause is supreme."
Ānanda had already grasped the principle of "six dissolved and one extinguished," yet he did not yet know which faculty (*indriya*) was most suitable for easy entry into practice;
therefore, he requested further instruction. The Buddha then extensively commanded the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats to each speak of the expedient means for entering the Way.
The intent of this was to reveal that all eighteen realms (*dhātu*) are methods for entering the Perfect [Way], but—
Since the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ, each has its own suitability; therefore, it is necessary to teach universally.

Kātyāyanīputra and the other six sages all extinguished the sensory dusts and united with awakening to enter perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*). Although the six sense objects belong to external appearances, they are in reality the Tathāgatagarbha mind.
If one can bring forth illumination within a single sense object, then the appearance of the object is extinguished and the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is revealed.
Kauṇḍinya was one who attained awakening through the sense-object of sound. Initially, at the Deer Park and the Cock Garden, he personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood;
when the Tathāgata turned the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, he was the first to understand it.

Because he thoroughly perceived the storehouse mind (ālayavijñāna) within the Buddha’s vocal sounds, the sense-object of sound was suddenly extinguished, his wondrous voice became subtle and perfect, and he became an Arhat.

Upānanda was one who attained awakening through the sense-object of form (*rūpa*). Initially, because he was prone to great desire, the Buddha instructed him to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as an antidote.
He first contemplated the impurity of the body's physical characteristics; subsequently, he saw only white bones.
Further analyzing these white bones down to the level of subtle dust, they returned to emptiness. Within that emptiness, he perceived the true nature of form; thus, form...

Since this [nature] and emptiness are of one single essence, how could there be two distinct dharmas? Therefore, as the sensory object of form is suddenly eliminated, wondrous form becomes secretly perfect, and one attains the state of an Arhat.
Xiangyan was one who entered through awakening to the sensory object of fragrance.

Because he followed the Buddha’s teaching that all conditioned phenomena are entirely without reality, at the moment he smelled the fragrance, he observed it with discernment and saw that this fragrance did not arise from the wood.
If birth arose from wood, what need would there be for fire? If it did not arise from emptiness, yet arose from emptiness, what need would there be for wood and fire?
If it did not arise from the smoke and fire, yet arose from the smoke and fire, why must this aloeswood be burned? Fourth, by thus investigating and exhausting [the matter], birth cannot be found;
its characteristic is fundamentally empty. How could there be coming or going? Thereby, the conceptualizing mind is dissolved, and true awakening is realized.
Having realized that the former olfactory objects suddenly ceased and the subtle fragrance became secretly perfect and pervasive, he attained Arhatship.

Bhaisajyaraja and Bhaisajyasamudgata were those who entered awakening through the sense-object of taste. Because they had been skilled physicians in past lives, they were able to taste all medicines and fully know their flavors.
By observing the cause of flavor, they saw that because flavor is intensely manifest, it is not empty and has no form that can be grasped.

Therefore, it is not that the various medicines exist [independently], for if they did not come [to the tongue], how could the gustatory consciousness know them? Therefore, it is not that the body and mind are identical [to the consciousness], for if the gustatory consciousness did not taste the various medicines, what flavor would there be?

Therefore, it is not that [the flavor] exists apart from the body and mind. When one thus discriminates and realizes that flavors are unarisen, then the sense-object of flavor is suddenly extinguished;
there remains only the single flavor of the pure, true reality (*dharmatā*), and one attains the stage of a Bodhisattva, Bhadrapāla.
Those who enter through the sense-object of touch do so by suddenly awakening to the nature of water while following the example of bathing.
Because water fundamentally lacks self-nature, and since water has no nature, the substance of the sense-object is likewise so. Thus it is said: "Neither the object nor the body is washed.

Since both water and the substance of the object are stilled, how could there be any sensation of touch in the interval? From this, one enters the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness); thus, the sense-object of touch is suddenly [penetrated].

By extinguishing subtle touch and manifesting clarity, he became a son of the Buddha and attained the stage of abiding; Mahākāśyapa was one who awakened through the entrance of the dharma-object (*dharmadhātu*).
Since the dharma-object is the shadow of the five objects grasped by the mental faculty (*manas*), it is collectively termed the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

These objects arise and perish in an instant and cannot abide for even a moment; weary of their flux and change, he cultivated the contemplation of emptiness and entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Once...

Upon attaining this samādhi, one can pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas as if in the snap of a finger; this is because the faculty of mind has ceased and the objects of the dharma are empty.

Since these dharmas are thus empty, one enters the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna), where the wondrous Dharma is revealed and all outflows (āsrava) are completely extinguished, thereby becoming an Arhat.
Regarding the sequence of the six sense-objects, what is commonly taught usually begins with form (rūpa); here, however, it begins first with... [text fragment].

Regarding the term "voice" (śabda), it is because the essence of the teaching in this [Vaipulya] method resides in the voice. This designation of "attaining arhatship" refers to the stage of the seventh faith in the Perfect Teaching;
because its severing of delusions is the same as that of the Small Vehicle, the title of "arhat" is borrowed from them, as is the case in all the sutras.
Whenever Wuxing encountered one who had attained arhatship, he invariably provided a "small" interpretation [of the term], which greatly contradicts the Buddha’s intention. This is because...
In the "Section on the Path of Vision" (*darśanamārga*), the Sūtra repeatedly censures the Two Vehicles and most clearly reveals the principles of the Perfect and Sudden;

then, in the "Section on the Path of Cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*), it further first causes them to attain the nature of perfect, tranquil, and non-arising-extinction as the fundamental cause for cultivation, which is already beyond the realm of the Two Vehicles.
Now, when it commands each of them to describe their own methods of realization and entry, how could the Buddha’s intention still lie in preaching the Lesser Vehicle?
The Buddha’s intention was not to speak of the lesser [vehicles]; how could these sages dare to present themselves as having the capacity for the provisional and inferior?

Moreover, since there were countless followers of the Mahāyāna within the assembly, what need was there for these minor sages to force their way forward? Thus we know that these sages directly manifested their realization of the ultimate truth, for they were acting in accordance with the Buddha’s secret intent.
Furthermore, the later Buddha stated that among those practitioners, there was truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority.
Knowing that the names, ranks, and magnitudes of all the sages, as well as the partial and complete dharma-gates, are all of one single flavor—perfect and real—one need not harbor further doubts.

The practice of Wuxing to arbitrarily divide them into "Great" and "Small" is a prior failure to grasp the Buddha’s intent and a subsequent defiance of the Buddha’s words; it must certainly not be followed.
Aniruddha (up to) "revolving the faculties to return to the source" is ranked first.
These five sages revolved their faculties to return to their fundamental nature and thereby attained perfect penetration.

Among the six faculties, the ear faculty is currently absent [from this list] because Avalokiteśvara is retained as the final member to correspond to the spiritual capacities of those in this region. Aniruddha [attained his realization] through the eye.
One who attains realization through the faculties was initially rebuked by the Buddha for being fond of sleep;
he wept and reproached himself, remaining awake for seven days until he subsequently lost both his eyes. The Buddha then instructed him in the *Ratnaketu-vyūha-vidyā-darśana-vajra-samādhi*, saying:
"For one who is blind, the illumination of joyful vision must employ this samādhi. The essence of this samādhi is fundamentally indestructible, yet it is capable of—"
It is called "Vajra" because it shatters heavy obstructions; this is the merit of turning back to contemplate and realize one's nature.
By revolving one's deluded vision and following that true source, deluded vision is instantly dissolved and true vision emerges from within.

Thus, one is able to see through the ten directions with perfect clarity without relying on the physical eye, thereby attaining Arhatship. Cūḍapanthaka was one who attained awakening through the faculty of the nose.

In the beginning, because he was unable to recite and uphold the teachings and lacked the quality of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), the Buddha instructed him to enter the rains retreat (*varṣā*) to regulate his breath.

He first observed the wind of the breath (*prāṇa-vāyu*), seeing it arise and perish from moment to moment until it reached its subtlest state; having exhausted the arising and perishing, they were found to have no source.

Once the wind of the breath had ceased and the mind was free of conceptualization, he attained sudden unimpededness and, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), became an Arhat. [This was] Gavāmpati.
Ti entered through awakening by means of the tongue-root. In the past, due to the karma of his speech in lightly mocking a śramaṇa, he received the retribution of being a "cow-chewer" (a ruminant).

The Buddha taught him the Dharma-gate of the single flavor of the pure mind-ground. As for what is called "single flavor," it is because one realizes that flavors are flavorless and are solely the true mark;
therefore, it is called "single flavor. This Dharma is to contemplate truly that the cognition of this flavor does not arise from the tongue.
If [the cognition] were produced from the tongue, it should not depend on the object; if it were produced from the object, it should not depend on the tongue.
Since neither can arise individually, how could they possibly do so together? If the object does not exist within the sense-field, there is no non-object either.

Where, then, does this cognition that perceives flavor come from? Once this cognition has vanished, the flavors of the sensory objects are also empty. Thus, the pure, true reality (*dharmatā*) is suddenly revealed.
Thus, he transcended all outflows (*āsrava*), left behind the realm of the physical vessel, purified his Dharma-eye, and became an Arhat.
Pindola Bharadvāja was one who attained realization through the faculty of the body. Initially, while on the road, he felt the pain of a thorn piercing his body;

reflecting upon this, he realized that there is a perception that perceives pain, yet there is also a perception of a pure mind wherein there is no perception of pain, nor even [the perception of] perception itself.
How could the awakening that awakens [to reality] exist as two distinct awakenings within a single body?

From this point, one should give rise to doubt, collect the mind, and contemplate with clarity until the body and mind suddenly become empty and all outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted; thus, the Real manifests and the delusory vanishes.

For previously, when one knew there was an awakened, pure mind, it was merely a knowledge based on inference; therefore, the delusory existed apart from the Real. Now, however, this is direct realization.
Because there is only this single awakening and nothing false exists outside of it, it is called "pure awakening. By transcending the body, one attains entry into perfect penetration.

Subhūti was one who attained realization through the faculty of the mind. Having realized emptiness and stillness over vast eons, he was not deluded upon entering the womb nor confused when separated from his previous body;
thus, he naturally remembers his births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of which he knows to be empty and still.
Not only do body and mind not exist, but all ten directions are likewise empty; this is the simultaneous emptiness of both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*).
Not only has one personally realized emptiness and stillness, but one also causes sentient beings to realize it together; this is the mutual benefit of self and others.

However, this is merely "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) and has not yet allowed for entry into the wondrous enlightenment of true emptiness. Now, having received the Buddha’s illumination, I have attained the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness and achieved [enlightenment].
The Arhat is then able to suddenly enter the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness, becoming one with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
All phenomena enter into that which is not identical to what is realized—the empty stillness where there is neither "is" nor "is-not," and which is the very attainment of true emptiness.

Turning the dharmas back toward non-existence corresponds to the preceding two phrases; this is because by reflecting back upon the nature of the sense organ of the mind, when the organ is exhausted, its nature manifests as the natural Dharma.
It returns to non-existence and enters the ocean of the nature of true emptiness.
Śāriputra immediately [attained this]... until he achieved long-lasting clarity; this is the foremost.
These six sages attained perfect penetration by tracing their awareness back to its source. This awareness and the sense organs are most difficult to distinguish.
Furthermore, the preceding five consciousnesses and the subsequent mental consciousness are often conflated; I shall now distinguish them with respect to the visual faculty.
When the eye illuminates an object, it remains unmoving for a single moment, like a mirror without discrimination—this is the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

Following that thought, there is a coarse discrimination of various characteristics that is vividly clear yet does not yet carry names or phrases—this is the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*). From this...
The sequential pointing-out and detailed analysis that exclusively calculates names and phrases is the sixth consciousness; the rest should be inferred accordingly.

Śāriputra was one who attained entry through visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*); since time immemorial, his visual consciousness has been pure, such that he could understand all phenomena upon a single sight.
This, however, was merely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). It was only upon hearing the profound principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that [he realized the ultimate].

The meaning is that awakening into the *garbha-citta* (storehouse mind) is all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; this vision is the wondrous, perfect clarity of enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), by which one attains great fearlessness and becomes a Buddha.
This eldest son [of the Buddha] first gave rise to the light of wisdom from the visual consciousness; the culmination of this light of wisdom is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Samantabhadra is one who awakened through the auditory consciousness; having long ago realized the ultimate fruit, he has now receded from his position.
To propagate the transformation [of sentient beings], they act as sons and disciples of the Dharma Kings who are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

all those who initiate the practice of Samantabhadra derive their names from this. Being able to employ the faculty of auditory consciousness to extensively discern the various capacities of beings, they manifest their bodies before anyone who initiates the practice of Samantabhadra—even if that person is located beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions—and even for those whose obstacles are so heavy that they are difficult to see, they secretly provide assistance.
He stroked their heads, providing protection and consolation so as to bring their practice to fulfillment. Tracing its fundamental cause, it originated from the illumination of the ear-consciousness;
thus, by discerning sentient beings according to their thoughts, one attains great mastery. Sundarananda was one who attained entry through the nose-consciousness;
because his mind was constantly distracted and agitated, the Buddha taught him to contemplate the white [spot] at the tip of the nose.
At first, after observing with true discernment for twenty-one days, seeing the breath like smoke is the sign that the nose-consciousness is turbid.

When pure observation becomes luminous, the interior is bright and the exterior is empty, and the smoke vanishes to become white; this is the sign that the turbidity of consciousness is gradually clearing.
When the hidden mind manifests and the turbidity of consciousness is entirely exhausted, the breath ceases and transforms into radiant light, brilliantly illuminating the ten directions.

This proves that the realization of the stage of no-more-learning and the prediction of enlightenment are all the result of the power of cessation and transformation. Pūrṇa entered the Way through the consciousness of the tongue;

since kalpas past, he has attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is fully equipped to expound the Dharma-doors with skillful means according to the capacities of beings, having attained fearlessness.
Now, encountering the World-Honored One, who instructed him in the wheel of speech to assist in propagating the Dharma-transformation, he has attained the state of an Arhat.
That is to say, when the teaching of the Dharma is pure, wisdom becomes increasingly pure. Outwardly, demons and adversaries are spontaneously subdued through the power of this teaching;

inwardly, the various outflows (*āsrava*) are naturally eliminated as wisdom is manifested. Although the teaching of the Dharma appears to involve the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), what is here called "tongue-consciousness" (*jihvāvijñāna*) refers to its spontaneous manifestation in accordance with thought, without relying on deliberation or calculation. Upāli attained awakening through the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
As for those who have entered [the path]: initially they followed the Buddha into homelessness and personally witnessed the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment;
subsequently, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, they upheld the Dharma of the precepts with purity. By this cause, they attained the tranquility of body and mind and became Arhats.

This was because they first disciplined the body and then disciplined the mind, gradually becoming able to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and develop wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, they attained all supernormal powers and benefits; this resulted from the restraint and guarding of bodily consciousness.
One who causes consciousness to cease and return to its source is like Mahāmaudgalyāyana, who attained entry through the faculty of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Initially, by hearing the profound meaning of dependent origination, he suddenly awakened to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*); his mind opened wide and he attained great penetration.

Through this, he entered the Way, and his wondrous powers of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhibala*) were universally extolled by all Buddhas. This is because when one deeply awakens to the true nature of reality, the mental consciousness...
Without arising, one returns to the wondrous stillness; through the long duration of this revolving stillness, the light of the mind is manifested and spiritual power becomes perfectly luminous.
Ucchuṣma attained samādhi, and this is the foremost.
These seven sages further share a commonality with the fundamental [teachings] in their attainment of perfect penetration.

Of the seven elements, the first five are the sense objects (*viṣaya*), while the latter two are consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the faculties (*indriya*); collectively, they do not transcend the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).

However, because the functions of these [latter ones] are so vast, they are individually accorded grand names. Thus, Ucchuṣma attained awakening through the fire element. In the past, he was driven by the fire of desire.
The blazing Buddha calls this a "mass of fierce fire" and instructs one to contemplate that all the cold and warm energies throughout the body are entirely warm touch.
Subsequently, one contemplates that this warm touch is signless and unarisen; as the body itself becomes empty, upon what could warmth abide?

When both body and mind are thus tranquil, the wondrous fire of one's nature manifests; consequently, the divine light coalesces within to form the fire of wisdom. Through this samādhi, one realizes *Arhatship*.
The Arhat further made great vows and manifested great majestic power to destroy Māra and protect the Dharma; this is what is called "the arising of the Great Jewel Flame.

He who holds the earth attained great awakening through the element of earth. Having leveled the ground throughout kalpas of accumulated effort, his meritorious deeds for the salvation of sentient beings were vast.
The Buddha then instructed him in the method of leveling the mind, saying: "The ground is not level because the mind is not level; it is the mind that is uneven."
If one can penetrate this principle and no longer hold views of differentiation, then the earth will naturally be without unevenness.
From this, one realizes that one’s own mind is fundamentally equal; whether it be the body or the world, all atoms lack intrinsic nature and appear only through false discrimination.
Since there is but the single true reality, how could there be any mutual obstruction? By this means, even [the touch of] a blade...

The soldier likewise had no contact with anything; having realized that all phenomena are entirely devoid of self-nature, he attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and provisionally took the lesser fruit.
Later, hearing the various Tathāgatas preach the wondrous Lotus Sūtra—the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—he was the first to realize it and became a leader.
In this stage, the dust of the earth was suddenly eliminated as he perfectly accorded with the *garbha-citta*. Thus spoke Candraprabha.
The Water-Element Mahābhūta is that which enters through great awakening. In the past, he encountered the Buddha Water-Deity and practiced the contemplation of water.

Initially, he contemplated that within his own body there is only the nature of water and no other substance; next, he contemplated that outside the boundaries of the self there is likewise only the nature of water, equal and without distinction.

When this contemplation was perfected, he saw only profound, still water pervading the realms of the ten directions, and his attachment to the self was extinguished. Nevertheless, he still perceived water.

Because he had not yet attained the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*), his physical characteristics had not yet perished; thus, when [the Buddha] cited the incident of throwing pebbles at the boy, it was to show that [the boy] was being burdened by the body.
Later, upon meeting the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Penetration through Mountains and Seas, he finally attained the dissolution of the body, whereupon the perception of water suddenly vanished.
There remained only the single true emptiness, wherein both person and dharma were simultaneously extinguished, and he entered into perfect penetration.

Jingye was one who attained awakening through the wind-element (vāyu-mahābhūta). Initially, he contemplated that the movements of the world, body, and mind are all equally false conditions turned by the power of the wind.
Subsequently, he realized that these various movements are like flowers in the sky—coming and going without true existence, being entirely and uniformly illusory.
Therefore, he viewed the sentient beings of the three thousand great thousandfold worlds as being like hundreds of thousands of mosquitoes and gnats.
It is stirred within the square inch of the heart alone; by this, the marks of movement are suddenly dissolved and the nature of immovability is revealed.
Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), he beheld Akṣobhya Buddha in the eastern direction as his Dharma Prince.

As for Ākāśagarbha, he is one who attained great awakening through the element of space. Initially, under Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he obtained the "Boundless Body" (*anantakāya*); he takes the merging with space as his essential nature.

"Boundless, holding four great precious jewels in his hands," etc., means that through the contemplation of the four elements as having no basis, the wondrous wisdom becomes perfectly luminous, clearly illuminating that all phenomena within the Dharma-realm are empty.

Furthermore, "manifesting a great round mirror within one's own mind," etc., means that the single jewel-like awakening is pure and perfectly luminous; its inner brilliance emits light that brilliantly shines throughout the ten directions. These are the ten kinds.
"Light" refers to the ten wisdoms of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—from the wisdom that accords with reality throughout the three periods of time up to the wisdom that knows the infinite Buddhas.
It encompasses all lands within a single body without mutual obstruction, and divides a single body into all lands in accordance with the application of giving and action;
this is the perfection and spiritual efficacy of its wondrous function. Such supernatural powers all arise from the initial contemplation of the four [truths].

The Great [Elements] have no substance and arise entirely from the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts; since these deluded thoughts are fundamentally void, how could the four great elements exist?
Thus, there is only empty space, and with it, even the Buddha-lands vanish together. Once all delusions are extinguished, True Emptiness first appears;

only then can one attain the boundless body and manifest great spiritual powers. Maitreya was one who attained awakening through the Great Element of Consciousness; for those at the initial stage of the path, this is paramount.
The world is known as a realm of wandering; it is because sentient beings perceive objects external to the mind that they give rise to false attachments and craving.

Therefore, under the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, he taught the cultivation of *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only). Upon clearly realizing that all phenomena are merely transformations of consciousness, external longings cease within the mind.

However, this attained samādhi belongs entirely to the category of cultivated attainment (*bhāvanāmayī*) and is not an innate, natural concentration (*svabhāvika-samādhi*); it was only upon reaching the era of Dīpaṃkara Buddha that [he first realized] this.
To achieve the supreme, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the conscious mind is to enter into profound resonance with the true nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Having attained this samādhi, one perceives that boundless buddha-lands all manifest from the Tathāgatagarbha, and that immeasurable buddhas all flow forth from the Tathāgatagarbha.
Since attaining this, you have received the prediction of future enlightenment and shall succeed the Buddha in his position; how could there be anything else?

Indeed, all of this arises from the contemplation that the defiled and pure environments and beings throughout the ten directions are all transformations of consciousness and originally lack self-nature.
Next, one realizes that both the transforming subject and the transformed object are fundamentally the wondrously enlightened, luminous essence of Bodhi.

Thus, one distances oneself from the *parikalpita* (imagined) and *paratantra* (dependent) natures and enters the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). It was through this great power that Mahāsthāmaprāpta attained awakening from the sense-faculties.
It is because they encountered the Buddha, whose radiance surpasses that of the sun and moon, through the teaching of the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
What is called "recalling the Buddha" (*nianfo*) is to keep the Buddha in mind. The condition for this encounter arises from mutual recollection;

if one person is single-mindedly mindful while the other is single-mindedly forgetful, how could these two possibly be certain to meet or certain to see one another? It is solely because of that single-minded mindfulness that [the encounter occurs]. Or...
Meeting or seeing [the Buddhas] occurs because of one's single-minded remembrance; yet if one forgets, one meets them and yet does not meet them, sees them and yet does not see them.
If two people remember each other with mutual mindfulness, their paths of response and resonance intersect so that they are never separated throughout kalpas—not merely meeting once or seeing once.
The Buddhas of the ten directions pity sentient beings no less than a mother remembers her child; this is what is meant by "one person’s single-minded remembrance. The multitude...

If one turns one's back on awakening and aligns with the sensory dust, refusing to recite the Buddha’s name—like a child who flees from home—it is what is called "a single person being exclusively forgetful.
In such a case, even though the great compassion of all Buddhas regards them with heavy concern, how could they possibly encounter them?
If sentient beings recite the Buddha’s name as the Buddhas recollect sentient beings, then whether in the present or in the future, they will certainly see the Buddha.
Furthermore, without relying on external conditions, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind, and the three bodies manifest in their full perfection.

This is because for those who practice *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha), the path of resonance between the practitioner and the Buddha ensures that they will surely behold the Buddha; it is just as one who is smeared with incense will inevitably acquire its fragrance.

This consists of single-mindedly recollecting one Buddha while universally encompassing the six sense faculties, never allowing them to wander or stir; this is called "pure mindfulness," and when this mindfulness continues in succession, [the realization is attained].
What indeed exists within his entry into samādhi?

Composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánxián of Yǒngquán Chán Monastery on Gǔshān, Fúzhōu.
At that time, Avalokiteśvara... [up to] "sharing the same compassion and yearning.
This Avalokiteśvara attained perfect penetration through the faculty of hearing; his sequence should follow that of Nalanda.
Now, because this method is appropriate for the present time, I have retained it here for detailed exposition so that those who desire to practice may do so with single-minded devotion.
Hearing, contemplation, and cultivation are the general path for entering the Way; in the sūtras they are called the "three types of wisdom.

However, the meaning shown in this present sūtra is entirely distinct: "hearing-wisdom" refers to the nature of hearing within the faculty of the ear, not to the grasping or the discrimination that pursues sounds.
"Learning" refers to the wisdom of reflection, which means turning back to contemplate this very nature of hearing.

"Cultivation" refers to the wisdom of practice, which means that while the fundamental function is without effort, defilements are not separated yet are separated; while delusions are not severed yet are severed. The passage beginning with "At first, within hearing...
correctly details the process of learning, reflecting, and cultivating. "Within hearing" refers to the faculty of hearing, specifically the profound, perfect, and non-arising, non-ceasing nature.
This faculty of hearing usually flows outward following sounds, which leads to endless faults and afflictions.
Now, however, it enters its source and turns back to hear its own nature, like water flowing inward, ceasing not for a single thought-moment.

Once the deluded mind is suddenly severed and one darkly accords with the Dharma-nature, the very appearance of that which is entered vanishes. When the appearance of that which is entered vanishes, that which is entered becomes still; this is stillness.

Since the truth of non-arising is fundamentally without movement, how could there be stillness? Therefore it is said that the two characteristics of movement and stillness are clearly seen as not arising;
this is because they were originally unarisen, not that they have merely ceased to exist now. Although external objects have vanished, the roots of internal fetters cannot be suddenly eliminated;
one must gradually increase through contemplative practice before the faculty of hearing and its... [object] can be [transformed].

When one hears [the teachings], both the sense objects (*viṣaya*) and the sensory faculties (*indriya*) are exhausted together. At the point where they are exhausted, both the faculties and the objects are lost, yet the illuminating awareness (*jñāna-āloka*) alone remains.

If one dwells in this state and takes it to be the true light of *prajñā*, then the cognitive object and the wisdom will remain in constant opposition, ultimately becoming an obstacle to further progress.

Therefore, one must observe until the practice reaches its peak of refinement; only then can the awakening wisdom and the heard teachings that were the object of that awakening be realized as being co-extensive.

When both emptiness and the wisdom that perceives emptiness have vanished, yet this emptiness still persists—if one clings to it as the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it remains a state of obscured darkness;
failing to open up, it ultimately becomes a hindrance that adheres to the very body.

Therefore, it is only when the wisdom of emptiness reaches its ultimate perfection that the wisdom which empties and the awareness that is emptied both cease together. Prior to this, only the objects (*viṣaya*) have been extinguished.

When the faculties arise, birth arises; when the faculties cease, awakening arises; when awakening ceases, emptiness arises—all these belong to the realm of arising and ceasing, and thus the true essence remains unmanifest.

Even when one reaches the state of emptiness, that [state] does not persist; only then do both arising and ceasing utterly cease, and the true essence of quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa) becomes clearly and vividly manifest.
This stillness is not a stillness contrasted with movement, but is the primordial stillness that is inherently unmoving. This cessation is not...

The cessation of arising is, in its essence, the cessation of non-arising; furthermore, this quiescent extinction is identical to the quiescence previously entered, though the former belonged to the stage of semblance-realization within the position of faith, while this belongs to the stage of partial realization upon entering the [Bodhisattva] positions.
As for the sudden transcendence, one transcends into the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*), where natural virtues are fully perfected and functions are without lack.
When this circulates throughout the ten directions, one attains the two kinds of sublime excellence through perfect clarity and illumination.

This chapter’s contemplative practice does not fall into the two extremes of emptiness or existence, but directly contemplates the Middle Way; it is what the preceding sutra refers to as "untying from the center of the knot.
Without the toil of severing afflictions, one simply turns back to contemplate the nature of hearing; since there is no external realm before it, coarse thoughts naturally settle first.

Next, one eliminates subtle perceptions until reaching the state of non-thought; this is precisely what the aforementioned sutra refers to as "using profound stillness to reverse that which is illusory, thereby extinguishing birth and so forth.
The entire merit of cultivation employed in this present sutra lies entirely herein; students should examine and contemplate this in detail.

"World-Honored One, from my making offerings [up to] 'bringing blessings to all sentient beings,' this is a detailed demonstration of two kinds of excellence. By what cause are these two kinds of excellent fruits obtained?

They are all obtained through the power of cultivating the practice of illusion within hearing [the Dharma], thereby accomplishing the Vajra Samādhi; for by means of this samādhi, there is no deliberate effort."
By the power of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), [the Bodhisattva] aligns upward with the compassionate power of all Buddhas to manifest the thirty-two transformations (*dvātriṃśat-kāya-vikurvaṇa*);

he may manifest the bodies of the noble fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), because when practitioners of each respective vehicle are about to perfect their own vehicle’s wisdom and principle, the Bodhisattva acts accordingly for each.
He manifests his body and preaches the Dharma to bring to perfection that which he has realized.
He may manifest the body of a lord of the two realms of form and desire, or the body of Śakra or one of his ministers;

He manifests in the forms of men and women who receive the teachings because sentient beings within the human realm each have their own specific requests;

When deluded thoughts cease, external objects no longer confront one, and the murderous mind naturally vanishes. This enables sentient beings who maintain this mindfulness to enter the realms of ghosts and spirits without being harmed by them.
Since deluded thoughts are that upon which ghosts and spirits rely, and killing is the very occupation of ghosts and spirits, when both are now absent, one transcends those ghostly realms;
therefore, they cannot cause harm. Fifth is the returning of the faculty of hearing to its source.

When the six sense faculties are all restored, they can cause sentient beings who recollect [this teaching] to cross over the calamities of war, as easily as slicing through water or blowing away light;
because both the faculties and their objects are stilled, who is there to be considered self or other? Thus, they cannot be harmed.

Sixth, when the hearing-perfuming gives rise to light that pervades the Dharma-realm and destroys all deep darkness, it can cause sentient beings who recollect [this teaching] to have such power that even if various ghosts are near, they cannot be seen by the eye.

Seventh, because all ghosts are shrouded in darkness, they are eclipsed by it; yet when sound is extinguished and hearing returns to its source, how could there be any delusive dust to cause sentient beings to perceive it?
Shackles and fetters cannot bind it, for since the dust is empty and does not entangle it, it cannot be bound.
Eighth, when sound is extinguished and hearing is perfectly pervasive, being naturally universal without depending on internal or external objects, it arises everywhere.
The power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) can cause those who mindfully recollect it to not be plundered by thieves;

for when there is no expectation, there is no enemy, and through universal loving-kindness, there is no resentment—thus they cannot be plundered. Ninth, by turning the hearing inward to depart from sound and form, one likewise cannot be plundered;

this can cause sentient beings who mindfully recollect it to remain far removed from sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). Since desire arises from form, when form is departed from, desire is also departed from. Tenth.
When the nature of the sound-element is perfectly pure and free from further delusory objects, then the faculties and their objects no longer confront one another;
this can cause sentient beings who contemplate it to be free from all anger, for since anger arises from confrontation, where there is no confrontation, there is no anger. Eleventh:

when the objects of perception have vanished and are without obscuration, clarity pervades the Dharma-realm and the body and mind are translucent like pure lapis lazuli; this can cause sentient beings who contemplate it...
Forever free from the darkness of delusion, for illumination can destroy darkness. Twelfth: being harmoniously integrated and unimpeded, one turns back to true hearing;
thus, while remaining unmoved at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one enters into the mundane world;

without destroying the world-systems, one reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas and succeed to their Dharma as a Prince of the Dharma (*dharmarāja-putra*), enabling sentient beings who contemplate this to seek it.

A man obtains a son to succeed to the Dharma King; this is the way of a man. At thirteen, the six sense faculties become perfectly complete, pervasive, and harmoniously integrated within the single precious awakening, such that there is nothing it does not illuminate—thus it is the Great Perfect Mirror—and nothing it does not contain—thus it is the empty Tathāgata-garbha.
Therefore, the infinite Dharma gates of all Buddhas are received and upheld in accordance with them without loss, enabling one to...
Those sentient beings who contemplate this, seeking a daughter, shall obtain one endowed with the virtues of a woman to serve, obey, and receive them. Fourteenth:

when the perfect penetration is manifested through the wondrous gateway of the ear-faculty, then the fundamental luminosity of the mind’s subtlety and the realms of the one and the many become interfused;
the original stillness and the perfected awareness are equalized, such that the names of "self" and "other" are rendered uniform. This is why it can cause sentient beings to uphold my [Dharma].

The merit of my name and that of the Dharma-princes who uphold this Sahā world—numbering as many as the sands of sixty-two Ganges Rivers—are exactly equal, for I have cultivated true and perfect penetration and realized the principle of equality. This is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness;
by providing all beings with merit, the Bodhisattva fully realizes the Dharma-realm, and thus [the merit] extends to all within that Dharma-realm.
Because birth is nowhere outside the body and mind of the Bodhisattva, there is a response to every invocation, and the attainment of blessings occurs through non-action (*anābhoga*).

Why are these four individually termed "inconceivable"? It is because their previous manifestations were adapted to capacities to extract suffering and bestow joy, appearing as though they could be reached by verbal or intellectual understanding.
Now, however, the full account of the marvelous subtlety of these manifestations is set forth; this marvel is peerless and truly cannot be conceived by thought.
The first is that, from the initial hearing of the nature, false hearing is cast off, and a single faculty returns to its source.

The source of the six sense organs is simultaneously liberated; the six organs are no longer partitioned, but are solely this single, perfectly interfused, pure, and precious essence of awakening (*bodhi*).

Since its essence is perfectly interfused, its function is naturally unimpeded; it is thus able to manifest immeasurable forms from within a single body and proclaim immeasurable mantras to rescue and protect sentient beings, thereby attaining great mastery.
The head represents the totality of the six functions, while the arms symbolize... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

The compassionate eyes that receive and embrace represent the wisdom of illuminating understanding; each, according to its original number, is expanded until it reaches eighty-four thousand, signifying that based upon the six fundamental functions, fundamental wisdom and compassion respond universally to worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) to attain great sovereignty.
Within a single body, the myriad phenomena of worldly affliction are fully endowed with both compassion and majesty, as well as meditative concentration and wisdom.

Because the eighty thousand phenomena of the realm of afflictions (*kleśa-dharmadhātu*), in both their facts and principles, have never been separate from my single, perfectly interfused, and pure essence, they can be identical and yet different, and can be one and yet many;
thus every dharma is perfectly interfused and every particle is fully endowed with all things.

Second, because one has emerged from the dust through hearing and reflection and is unimpeded, the wondrous power of spiritual transformations is entirely without obstruction throughout the ten directions.
Third, by virtue of cultivating the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing to the point of purity and non-attachment,
one is able to cause all sentient beings within the worlds where one travels to relinquish their bodies,
treasures, and jewels, seeking my compassion; for a stingy mind is the most difficult to break, yet a mind of renunciation is easily cultivated.
It is most difficult to give rise to the seeking mind, and it is most difficult to strengthen it;

that the sentient beings in the worlds you now traverse are all able to destroy stinginess and practice giving through your compassionate entreaties is truly inconceivable, brought about by such majestic spiritual power.
Fourth, because you have realized the Buddha-mind to its ultimate limit, you are already able to enter the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornments, which is a boundless treasury of jewels.

Suddenly opening up boundless merit and wisdom, he is naturally able to offer immeasurable precious jewels as supreme offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm; all their requests are fulfilled, with none left ungratified.
"The Buddha asks about Perfect Penetration" concludes the answer to the Buddha’s inquiry regarding the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination, which is precisely the realization of perfect interfusion.
The pure jewel-like awakening is the perfect mind of sovereign mastery; thus, responding to conditions through transformation, it manifests two forms of excellence and four inconceivabilities.

All of these result from the practice of "entering the stream and losing the object," whereby one reaches the state where stillness and extinction manifest before one, attaining Bodhi and spontaneously acquiring this samādhi.
It perfectly illumines the ten directions with total sovereignty, and thus is called Avalokiteśvara.
The names [of these methods] shall also pervade the worlds of the ten directions.

At that time, from the World-Honored One’s seat upon the lion throne (until) it was naturally spread and presented, the twenty-five sages had each finished describing their perfect penetration (*yuantong*). The Buddha then manifested auspicious omens to respond to them; this was the response of all Buddhas.

The simultaneous emission of jewel-light from all five limbs symbolizes that the realization of the nature is the ultimate brilliance, wherein the precious awakening is perfectly interfused and its entire substance is manifested.
As for the mutual conferral of empowerment, the crown represents the mark of perfect ultimacy; it signifies that the Buddhas realize the perfect ultimacy of the nature therein.
Within this assembly, the Bodhisattvas and Arhats—members of the twenty-five sages—are likewise drenched by the Buddha’s light.
As for their "summit," it signifies that their cultivation and realization are equal, without superiority or inferiority.

Having realized that the conditioned outflows (*sāsrava*) shall no longer arise, all dust-like defilements are cleared away, leaving nothing more to obstruct or divide.
When the chanting and hymns of the *brahman* naturally unfold and are performed, they enable the Dharma-realm to forever depart from all suffering and constantly attain wondrous bliss.
Since the profound principles and subtle benefits of the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration expounded by the Sage are as detailed as this, these manifold auspicious signs have appeared.

The essence of the source of truth is originally and inherently luminous, devoid of subject and object; yet through delusion, illumination arises, and the characteristics of the perceived manifest.
Once that which is manifested has appeared, the true nature immediately becomes hidden and empty, and awakening begins to differentiate. As emptiness manifests, the world first comes into being;
as deluded thoughts coalesce, they become the insentient realm of land, and as the deluded mind perceives, it becomes sentient beings.
These six phrases clarify the arising of delusion. Within great awakening, deluded space exists like a single bubble rising from the water.
If even the great ocean has reached such a state of subtlety that it is not real, how much more so the lands of fine dust that stand supported by space?
If this bubble suddenly vanishes, it is not that it was first non-existent and then ceased; rather, it was fundamentally non-existent from the start.

By this, one may also understand that the three realms of existence, which likewise stand supported by space, are of the same nature. These six phrases clarify that delusion is fundamentally empty, and thus it can be dissolved.
To "melt" means to melt away delusory appearances and return to the source; there is only this single nature.

Since sound falls within the realm of speech, it consists merely of names, phrases, and meanings; thus, it is partial rather than all-encompassing. Fragrance exists when combined with cognition, yet it does not exist when separated from it;
therefore, it is not constantly present. Flavor exists only after being tasted; therefore, it is not eternally uniform. As for touch, it depends upon that which is touched...

If manifested, it would lack a fixed substance; for a phenomenon established by relying on the shadows of the five sense-objects must necessarily have a fixed location, and thus could not pervade everywhere.

If the mental faculty (*manas*) is constantly muddled and confused, then despite the utmost effort in achieving stillness and clarity, one will ultimately never see its profound lucidity; thus, conceptual thoughts cannot be liberated.

This is why it is difficult for these five faculties to attain perfect penetration. Visual consciousness, for instance, is formed through the conjunction of the faculty, the object, and the environment. To the very end...

If the fundamental non-existence of intrinsic characteristics implies that things are empty and not real, then Samantabhadra’s thorough hearing of the ten directions—arising from the power of having cultivated great causes over many lifetimes—is not merely an expedient of the initial mind.
Furthermore, Sūndara’s contemplation of the tip of the nose as a means to remedy distraction is a provisional method for stabilizing the mind;
once the mind has attained stability, it becomes localized rather than universal. This is the teaching of Pūrṇa.
The Dharma is attained through awakening over vast eons; if one merely indulges in grandiloquent phrases, it is not the untainted (anāsrava).
Upāli’s observance of the precepts merely restrains the consciousness of the body;

since that which is not the body cannot be restrained, this is limited to a single person and cannot encompass the myriad dharmas—it is not the universally harmonizing wisdom of contemplation. Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers were rooted in his past lives.

Since the cause is not related to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), how much less so for the mental consciousness itself? If its recollections take all things as objects without departing from sensory realms, it remains stuck in delusion;

thus, these six consciousnesses are difficult to employ for attaining perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). If one contemplates the nature of earth as solidity and obstruction, one does not achieve thorough penetration;
this is not the nature of a sage. If one contemplates the nature of water, one does not depart from conceptual thought; this is not the essence of Suchness (*tathatā*).

Because the fire-element arises from excessive lust, one develops revulsion; yet, to contemplate it as being of the nature of fire is to remain unable to transcend discursive thought—it is not the skillful means of the initial resolve.
The wind-element is by nature movement, and movement stands in opposition to stillness—it is not the Unsurpassed Way.

The space-element is dull and insentient, entirely lacking awareness and illumination—it differs from Bodhi. The consciousness-element arises and perishes moment by moment; its substance is not permanent, and thus it is illusory.
Yet these are not the ultimate reality. Within the faculties, the fundamental mindfulness of the Buddha inherently possesses arising and ceasing;
to seek the unarisen and unceasing through that which arises and ceases is to have cause and effect diverge. This is why these seven great elements find it difficult to attain perfect penetration.

Regarding the twenty-four sages who, by means of twenty-four gates, each attained true and perfect penetration, they are now all excluded for what reason? It is because those [faculties] are... [the object].

This means that the nature of the noble ones (ārya-gotra) has nothing it does not penetrate; this is what is called the difference in speed between those of different classes, and it is not merely a matter of initial skillful means.
The intended meaning of the following passage can be understood from its context.
"I now address the World-Honored One... [until] such is my true mind."
Having previously examined various approaches in detail, hereafter we select the faculty of the ear alone. In establishing their teachings, the Buddhas truly have no fixed method;

they merely guide beings according to what is appropriate for their specific capacities. Now, because the faculties of the ear are particularly sharp among the sentient beings of this Sahā world, one must necessarily rely upon sound and hearing as the substance of the teaching.
Although the substance of the teaching comprises both sound and hearing, it is sound that—
This serves merely as a prelude; hearing it is itself the wondrous mind. All who wish to attain samādhi must enter through hearing.

This Avalokiteśvara is one who has entered through hearing; his virtuous functions are most excellent, for throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters lands as many as motes of dust, employing the power of great sovereignty to propagate the four sounds and receive those within the nine realms.
To cause them all to obtain the happiness of both the mundane and supramundane realms, one must investigate the underlying causes;
it is simply that the faculty of hearing is uniquely superior to the other faculties. Now, the functions of a person’s various faculties each have their own limitations and obstructions;

yet, when drums are struck in the ten directions, the faculty of hearing perceives them all simultaneously and completely. Thus, we know that the faculty of hearing is uniquely perfect. The eyes, mouth, nose, and body, however, function only through contact.
Only then do we know that when mental conceptions are distracted and chaotic, one cannot perceive at a distance;
yet with the ear, one hears sounds through a wall, perceiving them both near and far—thus we know that the faculty of hearing is uniquely pervasive.

Worldly people think that hearing arises when sound exists and ceases when sound is absent, failing to realize that while sound itself comes into and goes out of being, the hearing is not subject to arising or ceasing; such is the permanence of the faculty of hearing.

One knows that the nature of those five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) likewise does not arise or cease because of objects; rather, the five faculties necessarily depend upon mental deliberation (*vitarka*).

If deliberation has not yet arisen, or if it has ceased, and yet the faculty of hearing alone is able to hear the sound of a pestle within a dream, this demonstrates that the arising of deliberation and investigation (*vicāra*) is beyond the reach of the five faculties. Thus, one knows that the faculty of hearing is also unique.
It is a constant truth that, in this world, the faculty of hearing is uniquely superior;
thus, the holy teachings are proclaimed through the medium of sound so that those who hear them may all escape the cycle of transmigration. Yet, why is it that some ultimately fail to escape?

It is because they follow sounds and pursue them outwardly. Although Ānanda was possessed of great learning, he fell into perverse thoughts and was turned by external objects; how could this be otherwise?
It is not that by following the flow and conforming to sounds one sinks into delusion, nor that by not conforming to the flow one is free from delusion.
This Dharma-gate can shatter all delusions; it is called the Vajra King, the cultivation of the manifestation of nature through cultivation yet without cultivation.
It is called the inconceivable gate of illusion, the source from which all Buddhas are born, and the True Samādhi of the Buddha-Mother. Now, I...
I shall proclaim this Dharma for you; it possesses such majestic power and is a particularly effective remedy for Ānanda.

Although you have been widely learned throughout many kalpas and are able to retain the secret gates of all Buddhas, because you devoted yourself solely to much-learning without cultivating the outflows-free state, the outflows of desire were not eliminated. Thus, your accumulation of learning became a fault, and consequently—
Between enduring the calamity of Dēṅgā and following the false hearing that accords with sounds to uphold the teachings of all Buddhas, which is better:
to instead employ the wondrous wisdom of hearing to hear the very nature of one's own hearing? For this false hearing does not exist inherently;

it arises because the essence of hearing reflects sound, and as sound rolls back upon itself, it forms the faculty, thereby giving rise to the name "hearing. If one can turn back this hearing, [the root of delusion will be severed].
If one does not pursue sounds, one becomes detached from them; once detached from sounds, the sense-faculty itself perishes. What, then, remains that can be designated as "hearing"?
When a single faculty is liberated, the six faculties are liberated accordingly. Although the characteristics of the faculties are six, their nature is a single essence;
therefore, when one is liberated, all are liberated. Before the faculties have been liberated, it is like having a cataract in the eye, whereby one falsely perceives empty space.
Because flowers are illusory, the three realms appear as they do; once the root is understood, it is like eyes free from cataracts—how could there be illusory flowers in the sky?
Thus, the realms of dust and defilement are suddenly extinguished. Once these realms of dust are extinguished, there remains only this single, perfect, and pure jewel-like awakening.

When the aspect of purity deepens and the power of awakening’s illumination extends ever further, within this tranquil illumination, empty space is but a single bubble. How much more so, then, [the conditioned world]?
Therefore, when we look back upon the world, it is truly like a dream-event; how could there be a real Ḍākinī within a dream who could retain your form?
Now, let me clarify this further with another analogy: suppose there were a skilled illusionist who, by means of incantations and arts, could conjure up various men and women;
though they move about in a multitude, they are in reality all merely the mechanism of a single incantation.
The pulling and moving [of the mind] is like this: once the mechanism has ceased, everything ceases together, and all illusions are found to have no inherent nature.
Now, applying the Dharma to this: True Suchness (*tathatā*) possessing the function of responding to conditions is like a skillful illusionist;
its transformation into the eight consciousnesses is like a magical incantation; and its combination with the six sense objects to divide into the six sense organs is like creating various illusions.
The male and female faculties, though numbering six, are but a single refined spirit, just as men and women, though distinct, are but a single incantation.
Once the substance of this single refined spirit is shattered, the six faculties are simultaneously liberated;

it is like when the single incantation ceases, all illusory forms of man and woman vanish together. Upon reaching this state, defilements dissolve away with every thought, leaving only the pure body of awakening.
This wondrous, perfect, and luminous clarity—if residual dust has not yet been exhausted, one still dwells within the stage of training;

if the dust is exhausted and the clarity reaches its ultimate limit, that is the Tathāgata’s supreme fruition. Since the Tathāgata’s supreme fruition is entered suddenly through this very gate, is it not the most concise and the most easy?
I now exhort you all: you must simply be able to turn back this mechanism of inverted hearing and return [to its source].
Hearing its intrinsic nature means that this very nature becomes the unsurpassed path of true and perfect penetration; it is simply this.
For this gate is the direct road by which all *tathāgatas* as numerous as motes of dust enter *nirvāṇa*; therefore, there are no causes cultivated or fruits realized that do not pass through it.
I too have entered by this way—how could it be for Avalokiteśvara alone? As for other dharmas...

The gates are not such that everyone can practice them with equal success; for instance, the loss of sight by Aniruddha and the sensation of thorns by Pindola were both instances of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power being bestowed upon them. Thus, they abandoned worldly afflictions through these very circumstances.

Furthermore, the Dharma-hearing of Samantabhadra and the preaching of the Dharma by Pūrṇa were the result of profound resolve cultivated over vast eons—how could these be explained as being within the reach of shallow minds?
Therefore, I only wish for the Tathāgata to bestow his grace so that sentient beings of future generations may have no doubts regarding this gate.
For this gate is easy to accomplish through its skillful means and is fit to be taught to Ānanda and those submerged in the final age of decadence;
its efficacy surpasses that of others. Thus, with a heart of truth, I have made this selection.
Ānanda adjusted his robes... [continues] until the end of the sixth fascicle.
Ānanda, I make this request because I fear that in the final age, the faculties and natures of sentient beings will be inferior and their habitual defilements will necessarily be deep;

as the Dharma-spells move further away from the Buddha and false teachings increase and blaze, it will be difficult to achieve success in the cultivation of perfect penetration. Therefore, I request that you gather your mind and bring peace.

The method for establishing the *bodhimaṇḍa* is employed to bring it to completion. The Buddha first answers the question regarding the gathering of the mind by citing the "Three Determinate Meanings," namely:
precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These three characteristics are mutually dependent causes; if even one is lacking, [enlightenment] cannot be achieved.

To aspire toward the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state must necessarily proceed from these. Although the two aspects of concentration and wisdom have already been extensively explained, one must apply effort and advance in their practice.

While within the rear *maṇḍala*, if one observes the precepts, one should first restrain the mind before the front *maṇḍala* to serve as the expedient means for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Although the categories of precepts are many, when speaking of their root, they are merely four: lust, killing, stealing, and lying.
First, regarding the precept against lust: lust is the cause of birth and death; if one does not sever lust, [one cannot attain liberation].
One must absolutely not engage in sexual misconduct; even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra.
Therefore, those who cultivate meditation must sever lust. Even if one strives to sever it within both body and mind, there is nothing that can truly sever it;
only then may the Way of Bodhi be hoped for. Second is the precept against killing: taking life is the cause of birth and death. If one does not sever killing, one will certainly...

One must not engage in such practices; for even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits. Therefore, those who cultivate meditation must certainly sever the taking of life.
If one does not wear or consume the physical parts of sentient beings, one will no longer wander through the three realms.
Why is this? Because by wearing or consuming their physical parts, one creates the conditions for inseparable connection with them; thus, the mind [is bound].
Furthermore, by not coveting or seeking, one does not become entangled with those [objects of desire]; thus, distancing oneself from the three realms constitutes true liberation.
Third, regarding the precept against stealing: since stealing is a cause of birth and death, if one does not sever stealing, it is absolutely impossible to escape [samsara].
Even if one possesses great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before them, they will inevitably fall into deviant paths; therefore, a practitioner of dhyāna must certainly abandon theft.
If one can truly be without greed for food or clothing, give rise to no arrogance, harbor no resentment, and renounce both body and mind, then one may certainly attain true samādhi.
Regarding the fourth precept against false speech: falsehood is the cause of birth and death;
if one commits a great lie—claiming to have attained what one has not attained, or claiming to have realized what one has not realized out of greed for offerings—[the consequences are grave].
One who forms attachments and views becomes a demon that will surely extinguish the seed of the Buddha; therefore, those who practice dhyāna must sever delusion.

This is because the practice of dhyāna requires one to be held accountable for an upright mind and not to permit hypocrisy. If one falsely claims to have attained the dharmas of a superior person, it is not only useless, but will lead to downfall.
Furthermore, cause and effect must correspond: if the causal mind is not upright, the resulting fruit will be retribution.

The winding nature of causes arises from the mind; if the mind were direct, the result would necessarily not be circuitous. How could one who seeks to realize Bodhi do so while still harboring delusions?
Burning one’s fingers before the Lamp-Kindled Buddha was able to repay past debts—a feat difficult for the world to believe.
One must possess great shame and remorse and give rise to a firm and fierce resolve; furthermore, one must allow the mind to merge with wondrous contemplation and proceed directly toward Bodhi.
With this single lamp and single finger, I offer them to all the holy ones, hoping thereby to repay their kindness and extinguish my debts.
