thus, this grasping appears to be partially dissolved, which is why it is said to be "half-subtle. Furthermore, regarding the various non-Buddhist heavens of the Non-conceptualizers (*asaṃjñin*), ancient expositions based on the sūtras and śāstras all hold that when the karma of these non-Buddhists is exhausted, they must inevitably fall from there and be reborn in the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

However, upon examining this current sutra, the character "from" (從) clarifies that [the state] arises from that [preceding stage]. If one were to interpret it as "non-arising," it would be highly contradictory.
Now, if we infer this through reasoning, the sutra refers to those who do not ascend to birth because they lack the conceptual thought (*saṃjñā*) necessary to apply further cultivation.
Nevertheless, in the latter half of the kalpa for this heaven, conceptual thought arises again; perhaps this is because they fear they will subsequently fall back down.
When their power is exhausted, they are extinguished in emptiness; because of the obstacle of the body, they are reborn in the intermediate state (*antara-bhava*), where such beings ought to exist.
As for the statement that they are "not born," this refers to the general principle.
These are included within the realm of animals among the three realms.

This clarifies the realm of the asuras. "Asura" here is translated as "non-deva," meaning that while their merit and power are equal to those of the devas, they lack deva-like conduct because of their excessive anger.
Among the three realms, they exist only within the desire realm; there are four types in total.
Those who ascend to this realm from the ghost realm by the power of protecting the Dharma subsequently dwell in the air, utilizing their supernormal powers of movement.

Those born from eggs are categorized within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*); if they descend from the celestial realms (*deva-loka*) to come here, their dwelling place is adjacent to the sun and moon.
Those born from a womb are categorized within the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*);

if there are those capable of wielding worldly power whose influence reaches far and wide, who are almost entirely without fear, and who constantly vie for authority with Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Great Kings—[they are of this latter category].
These are born from transformation and are subsumed within the celestial realm (*deva-gati*). Furthermore, there is another class of inferior asuras who are born from moisture;
they dwell in the depths of the great ocean, with their mouths submerged in the watery caverns, roaming through the void by day and returning to their aquatic abodes at night.

These are subsumed within the animal realm (*tiryagyoni-gati*) due to their moist-birth origin. According to this fourfold classification of asuras, their power of merit appears to place them prior to the celestial realm.
Regarding those listed last after the realm of the immortals (*asura*), it is because they are subsumed within the four realms of existence.

As for the latter two types, the Sūtra does not state their place of origin; however, by inferring from reason, they may have been degraded from the realm of the gods, or perhaps there are those who, having accumulated merit through their conduct among humans such that they could have been reborn in heaven, fell into these realms solely because they failed to sever their anger.
Thus, from the hells up to what the Demon King Māra speaks of, this summarizes the preceding seven realms of existence (*gati*).
One does not know how many tens of millions of times one has ascended and descended, wandering through these seven realms;
clinging to them all as real, one fails to realize their falsity. Now, when we examine them closely, these seven realms are all states of delusion and conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
These characteristics arise from deluded thoughts and lead to rebirth; they further give rise to karma through deluded thoughts—how could these be inherent to the fundamental mind?
The fundamental mind is wondrous and eternally quiescent, perfect and eternally pervasive, luminous and eternally illuminating.

It is attained not through grasping or rejecting, nor through cultivation or realization. The seven realms of existence within this mind are exactly like flowers in the sky appearing in the great void.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of dwelling-attachment, nor is there even a hair’s breadth of a conceptual thread;

yet now, it is manifest that those who undergo this saṃsāra do so none other than because they take the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—as their very root. Because of the existence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, there is also the non-existence of them;
with their existence, one falls downward, and with their non-existence, one ascends upward. Existence and non-existence thus correspond to one another.

Seized by these, one revolves through the seven realms of existence. If one can manifest the true samādhi, then this fundamentally wondrous and eternally quiescent essence is devoid of both being and non-being;
the karmic causes of the three realms do not bind it, duality is extinguished, and the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle is no longer dwelt upon.
How, then, could there be any talk of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct? Because sentient beings [fail to realize this]...
If one cuts off these three [defilements], each giving rise to private karmic activities, although individuals differ from one another, they follow along according to their kind;
thus, wherever there is a commonality of retribution, it is produced solely by a single delusion. Therefore, those who wish to cultivate Bodhi must first eliminate these three delusions.
If these three are not eliminated, even if one falsely attains supernatural powers through the effort of conditioned phenomena, one will ultimately fall into the realm of Māra.
If one takes the Way as a pretext to falsely investigate with worldly wisdom and creates karma by means of supernatural powers, one will only increase in delusion and inevitably fall into ruin.
Such a person is truly to be pitied; how could this be the fault of the original Bodhi?
That which accords with this is the correct teaching, while that which contradicts it is the teaching of Māra. Students must know how to distinguish between them.

At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his teaching from the Dharma-seat—having previously shown the seven realms of existence and finding no one to pity or save—and as the assembly remained silent without question, the Buddha turned his golden countenance once more to speak of demonic affairs:
"How is it that those who practice dhyāna often give rise to demons? Demons are capable of killing."
The life-force of wisdom robs one of the wholesome Dharma; its harm is not slight. If one does not clarify this in advance, one fears falling into its turmoil.
Yet, these demonic activities are so subtle that none but a Buddha can know them exhaustively. Other people are not only unable to know them, but they cannot even ask about them.
Therefore, that the Buddha speaks of his own accord without being questioned is his ultimate, profound compassion for all who wish to proceed toward unsurpassed Bodhi.
Those who cultivate the True Samādhi while still within the stage of contemplative practice have not yet extinguished the five aggregates;
thus, demonic activities will inevitably seize the opportunity to arise. If one cannot discern them, the purification of the mind will not be correct, and one will fall into false views.
Mistaking various demonic realms for reality and considering a mere fragment of attainment as sufficient, one will ultimately sink into ruin, like the monk Wuwen.
How deeply regrettable this is! Yet, what is the reason that meditation provokes demonic interference?

It is because the sentient beings of this world possess a fundamental awareness and a mental essence that are no different from those of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Because they are deluded regarding the principle, they fail to realize the oneness of the *dharmatā*.
To perceive any sign of objective existence is called ignorance; once such signs are perceived, they cling to them and refuse to let go.
This is what is called "love. Because of this, delusion becomes increasingly pervasive and suddenly manifests throughout space. As that delusion does not cease, it eventually forms the world-systems;
thus, these impure worlds are all established upon the stubborn, deluded, and false imaginings [of the mind].
That space which arises within the mind is merely like a single fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the sky; how much more so, then, is the case with the world-systems?

What solidity can there be in empty space? Therefore, if a single person were to discern and manifest True Suchness (tathatā) and return to their original essence, all delusions would instantly dissolve.
Even empty space would perish, let alone a land, which could not fail to shatter.
Yet this samādhi shares the same awakening as the minds of all bodhisattvas and arhats, being like space itself.
When space is unified, that place becomes profoundly still and naturally free from any shaking.

However, since those Māras, ghosts, spirits, and ordinary devas are composed entirely of delusion, when the Real inclines upon the delusory, their palaces collapse and the great earth quakes and splits apart;

thus, among all beings—whether moving on water or land, or soaring through the air—there are none who are not struck with terror. This is the supernatural power of the deluded ordinary beings within this state.
Those who lack these [faculties] do not perceive the cause of this transformation and corruption.

If the various Māra kings, each possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), were all to know its cause, how could they long remain attached to the dust and toil (*rajas-kleśa*) while allowing you to destroy their abode?
Therefore, they have all come from among the various samādhis to harass you. Although they are greatly enraged, their power is fundamentally no match for that dust and toil of mine.

Abiding in wondrous enlightenment, the heterodox cannot oppose the orthodox, nor can the delusory oppose the real; it is like wind blowing against light or a blade cutting through water—they do not touch at all.
It is also like adding ice to hot water: the ice will surely melt away before long. Furthermore, those who rely merely on their own supernatural powers come from the outside;
their power is but a guest. Since the host-mind is already empty, how could they enter directly? They must wait for their opportunity as guests.

At such a juncture, if the practitioner is as if lost and their correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) becomes slightly lax, the guest spirits will find an opportunity and give rise to demonic realms.
If one can remain firm in *dhyāna* and awaken to their falsity, then even demons cannot cause harm.

When the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) dissolve and clarity returns, demonic affairs will suddenly cease; for those various evils are entirely composed of the five aggregates and are all sustained by dark, turbid energy.

Now, with my brilliance, I shall illuminate their darkness; is there anything that will not be destroyed? If you cannot awaken to the falsity of it all, you will surely become but a child of Māra or a man of Māra.
That the *mārīcī* mantra of Matangi possesses meager power is because it can only destroy one of your precepts;
that your mind has not yet reached the point of total ruin is because the matter is still minor. Nevertheless, it remains something to be feared.
If this were so, how could the power of that Māra be compared to that of Mātangī?

It can cause you, who are about to ascend the body of precious enlightenment, to suddenly suffer a fall—just as a high minister close to the Son of Heaven might suddenly be seized and confiscated, reduced to ruin beyond redemption.
What kind of harm would such a thing inflict? According to this, the root of these demonic affairs is...
Among those who practice regarding the five aggregates, most are unable to escape [disturbances].

However, if from the very beginning one can personally awaken to the mind that is neither born nor extinguished and take this as the fundamental cause for cultivation, further using the precepts as a defense and mantras as protection—then how could demonic affairs arise?
Even if demonic affairs should suddenly manifest, they will surely be dissolved and extinguished; one will not be disturbed or confused by conditioned phenomena.
As for those who have fallen into ruin, it is because they previously lacked these three [qualities] and instead practiced the cultivation of perfect penetration based on false analogical knowledge.
Ānanda, you should know that from the time you sat [in meditation] until you achieve the Unsurpassed Way...
The following clarifies the demonic activities of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Demons do not come of their own accord; they take root in the five aggregates.

As long as one aggregate has not been destroyed, ten kinds of objects will appear. Since the five aggregates are destroyed in succession, the demonic activities manifest in succession. Herein, first is the clarification of destroying the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
When the practitioner first sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and practices the cultivation of "returning the hearing," with every thought uninterrupted, then—
Discriminative coarse thoughts naturally dissolve and vanish; once all thoughts have ceased, the essence that is free from thought naturally becomes entirely brilliant and lucid, alert and unclouded.
Because this essence is detached from objects, it does not shift with movement or stillness; because this essence is detached from thought, recollection and forgetfulness are as one.
Abiding within this state, one enters deeply into right concentration, wherein the essential nature is wondrously pure and the concentrated mind is serene.

This reveals that the light of the mind has not yet emerged and wisdom has not yet arisen; thus, it is like a person with clear vision situated in profound darkness—this is the realm of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

If one attains the radiant emergence of the mind’s light such that there is no longer any obscuration, then like a person with clear vision seeing clearly throughout the ten directions, the aggregate of form is exhausted, and one may thereby transcend the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpakaṣāya*), which is established upon form.
Observe the origin of these forms: they are produced by solidified false imaginings; they possess no true reality and are not indestructible.

Now, as a practitioner within this aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), through the power of contemplation, refines their investigation until they reach the point where the aggregate is about to be broken but has not yet been broken;

at that juncture, ten states may arise, or suddenly, while in meditative concentration, one may perceive that the four great elements of the external environment are no longer dense and the body [is likewise affected].

The ability to emerge from obstructions arises because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) compels the radiance of the mind to overflow into the objective field, whereby the field before one becomes empty and spacious.

Alternatively, while in meditative concentration, one may suddenly see that within this body there is no obstruction, such that one can pick out intestinal worms (*krmi*) from inside the body while the physical form remains intact;
this is because the power of meditative concentration compels the radiance of the mind to overflow into the physical body.

Therefore, the physical body becomes empty and cavernous. When some attain this emptiness both within the body and externally toward objects, the soul, the vital breath, the will, and the spirit no longer abide in their original locations;
they interpenetrate one another, alternating as guest and host, and engage in mutual discourse.

One may hear a solitary voice speaking from mid-air, or hear the Dharma being expounded simultaneously throughout the ten directions. This arises because seeds of past hearing have been perfumed, which now, through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),...
Through the intense arousal of power, the spirit and soul were eventually entrusted to manifest as the sound of the Dharma.

Alternatively, when this mind was lucid and radiant, one suddenly saw the entire earth turn entirely golden; all its inhabitants were Tathāgatas, with a thousand Buddhas surrounding the seat of Vairocana, and a hundred billion lands floating upon lotuses.
This arose from having previously heard the holy teachings, whereby the defiled mind was awakened by spiritual insight; such is the nature of this mind.

This was discovered through the investigation of radiance. Sometimes, while in meditative concentration, one suddenly perceives the empty space of the ten directions as having the color of the seven treasures or a hundred treasures, each simultaneously filling all space without obstruction or confusion.

This occurs because, through excessive application of the mind in observation and restraint, one suddenly transcends the ordinary state, appearing to realize the perfectly interfused and unobstructed Dharma-realm.
When this state manifests, one may close one's eyes in the middle of the night and perceive strange objects within a dark room, yet the original objects in the room remain perfectly distinct.
This occurs because the mind is tranquil, subtle, and dense, its radiance clarified and undisturbed by external objects;
thus, it can penetrate the profound darkness. Alternatively, when this mind pervades all things with pervasive emptiness and fusion, suddenly the four limbs become like blades of grass.

Even if one’s body were at the mercy of burning or being hewn down, it would never experience sensation, nor would it suffer any injury. This is because the mind is all-pervasive, empty, and harmonious;

thus, one's own body and external objects are entirely tranquil. The five sensory objects dissolve together and the four great elements are cast aside, leaving a mind of pure concentration that cannot be harmed or touched by external things.
Or, when the power of the pure mind reaches its peak, one may suddenly behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.

The lands where ordinary beings and sages dwell together appear with vivid clarity; this arises because one’s long-standing habituation of revulsion toward impurity and delight in purity has accumulated as seeds of thought, which now manifest as a sacred realm through the power of meditative concentration.

Alternatively, during the middle of the night, one may see people and their surroundings in distant places from afar and even hear their speech; this occurs because the power of contemplation compels the mind, causing its refined radiance to fly forth.

Therefore, there are many instances of obstructed vision. Sometimes, when one’s investigation reaches its ultimate refinement, demonic activities manifest; suddenly, within meditative concentration, one sees the physical form of a spiritual teacher undergo transformation.
This is because an evil spirit has entered the mind, causing the arising of delusive visions. Or, one may preach the Dharma without cause, penetrating subtle meanings with apparent mastery;
this is because a celestial Māra has entered the mind, causing the arising of frantic wisdom. These are the ten kinds of states mentioned above.
All these manifestations arise from the interaction between the practitioner’s power of contemplation and the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Although there is a difference between the first nine, which are wholesome states, and the last one, which is a demonic state, if one gives rise to thoughts of them being holy and becomes attached to them, demons will surely take advantage of this to falsely claim that one has attained sainthood;
it is certain that such a person will fall into the Avīci Hell. When the aggregate of form is exhausted, one is able to transcend it.

Regarding the "impurity of the kalpa" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), most ancient commentaries explain it in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). If this were the case, the "exhaustion of the aggregates" (*skandha-kṣaya*) would merely be a state of suppression rather than severance;

how could there be the meaning of "transcending the impurity"? Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "Beholding the minds of all Buddhas is like images appearing within a clear mirror," which clearly refers to the stage of "semblance-principle" (*tulya-nimitta*).
Moreover, the Sūtra says: "The capacity for birth is shattered, and the deep channels of karmic retribution are stirred."

That one "should suspend [the fetters] completely" is a clear textual proof that one does not undergo further segmentation and is truly entering the stage of faith; how can you say it is merely "subduing" rather than "severing"?

If one were to explain this as being merely "similar," then the exhaustion of the aggregates would be a severance rather than a subduing, and only then would the meaning of "transcending the turbid world" apply.
However, in the subsequent passage concerning the fifty kinds of demons, with the exception of those belonging to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, all others are said to be "offenses."
"Since one who commits a great falsehood falls into the Avīci Hell, how could there be anyone who has entered into faith and transcended the turbid world yet still possess such a fault?

Wuxing therefore interprets the opening passage on the five aggregates as a definitive explanation (*nirdeśa*) to accord with the meaning of 'transcending the turbid world,' while he interprets the passage on the fifty kinds [of offenses]—
excluding those pertaining to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— as a provisional explanation (*neyārtha*) to accord with the fact that there are indeed those who fall."
Although the text is consistent throughout its beginning and end, these two interpretations are merely forced accommodations and are not entirely satisfactory.

Furthermore, both Jiaoguang and [the author] judge this to belong to the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), stating that because practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) do not seek actual realization, they remain at the preceding stages and thus both possess the danger of falling back.

This is merely a speculative assertion lacking support from the sūtras or śāstras; moreover, what is called "sudden" refers not only to sudden awakening but also to the capacity for sudden [realization].
Although one does not formally take up the realization of cessation, the afflictions are nonetheless severed of their own accord; how could this be merely relying on a hollow insight?

If you claim that those prior to the stages of "Abiding" (zhùqián) all fall into error, then since their views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) must be unsevered and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) must be unexhausted, by what standard can one judge their entry into the stage of Faith (*śraddhā*)?
Most contemporary interpreters merely provide literal glosses of the text, yet their preceding and succeeding arguments contradict one another—this is truly lamentable.
I shall now provisionally rely on the explanation of Wu-xing and await further refinement by those of superior intelligence.
That good man cultivates samādhi (up to) the accomplishment of the unsurpassed path.

This clarifies the destruction of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Previously, when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) was not yet exhausted, it was as if one were in deep darkness with nothing to be seen;
now that the aggregate of form is exhausted, one is able to see the minds of all Buddhas, like reflections appearing in a bright mirror.

This is merely the manifestation of a semblance-principle, for true realization has not yet been attained, as there remains the aggregate of sensation acting as the recipient of experience. Since this [aggregate] exists...
Because one cannot perceive or employ [the body], it is like a person under a spell whose hands and feet remain intact yet cannot move;

this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). If the mind can detach from the body and look back at its own face, entering and exiting at will without any obstruction, then the aggregate of sensation is exhausted.
That which depends upon sensation to establish the turbidity of perception (*saṃjñā-kaṣāya*) can then be transcended from this point onward.
Contemplating the origin of feeling, one sees that it is formed by empty, luminous, and deluded thoughts; it has no reality and cannot be destroyed.

When a practitioner, within the aggregate of feeling, is pressed by the power of contemplation—neither having yet broken through nor being about to break through—it gives rise to ten kinds of objects.
Or, while in meditative concentration, a great radiance may arise, and there may be things perceived as manifestations; knowing these to be not truly functional, he disregards them.

If you suppress the mind and suppress it too forcefully, the seeds of agitation, sorrow, and grief will arise, producing boundless compassion. Even upon seeing a mosquito or a gnat, you will pity them as if they were your own infant.
If you realize this is not right, it will subside of its own accord after a short time. If you take this to be "sainthood," the demon of compassion has taken possession of you;
you will weep at every person you meet, inevitably losing right concentration and falling into ruin. Or, within meditative absorption, [compassion] may become excessive...
When signs manifest before one, one attains an unprecedented sense of great inspiration; this inspiration becomes excessive, leading to extreme agitation.

The seeds of *māna* (self-conceit) give rise to infinite heroic resolve, claiming equality with all Buddhas and asserting that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment.
If one realizes this is erroneous, it will naturally subside after a short time. If one takes it to be holy, a mad demon has taken possession; such incomparable *māna* will inevitably lead to ruin.
While in right concentration, one may fall into ruin. Or, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has not yet been broken through, there is nothing gained by advancing;

when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has already dissolved, there is no place to retreat to. One falls into a state between these two poles, where all is vast and nothing is seen. Because of this lack of vision, a great desiccation arises;
memories sink deep without dispersing, and one takes this for a sign of diligent progress. This results from an imbalance in the power of concentration.

If one excels yet lacks the wisdom of self-illumination, and realizes this error, there will naturally be no fault from others. However, if one considers oneself a sage, the demon of recollection (*smṛti-māra*) will attach itself;
by constantly dwelling on such thoughts morning and evening, one will surely lose right concentration and fall into ruin.

Or, within meditative absorption, if the power of wisdom is excessively intense, one may become fixated on the superiority of one's own nature and suspect oneself to be Vairocana. This arises from [a lack of...]
If one can constantly and critically examine whether one is immersed in views and knowledge, and realizes their error, one will naturally be free from the blame of others;

yet if one considers oneself a sage, one becomes subject to the demons of inferiority and complacency. Claiming for oneself that one has attained the Unsurpassed Way, one will surely lose right concentration and fall into ruin.
Or, while in meditative absorption, because new realizations have not yet been attained, the old mind has already perished; thus, one surveys the two temporal limits.
Suddenly, hardships arise within me, giving rise to boundless anxiety as if sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison;
I constantly seek to cast off my life to attain early liberation. This is due to the fault of excessive diligence in cultivation, which agitates the seeds of remorse and affliction.
If one realizes this is erroneous, there will naturally be no blame from others. If one considers oneself a sage, then the demon of anxiety will possess them, causing constant self-lamentation.
They may rejoice in their own death, or they may be constantly sorrowful and unable to bear seeing others; they will inevitably lose right concentration and fall into ruin.
Or, within the meditative state of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), they may give rise to a mind of attachment and delight in its purity and stability;

this stirs up the seeds of restlessness (*auddhatya*) so that great joy arises which they cannot restrain. This occurs because, having initially attained pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), they lack the wisdom to self-restrain themselves.

If one realizes that this is not the self, there will naturally be no blame from others; yet if one considers this to be sainthood, the demon of joy will possess them, leading to frivolous laughter, singing, and dancing.
Believing they have attained unimpeded liberation, they will inevitably lose right concentration and fall into ruin.

Or, while in a state of meditative absorption, they may perceive the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) manifesting; becoming satisfied with such minor attainments, they suddenly give rise to groundless arrogance and rely upon it.

If one already surpasses others, even the rank of a Buddha is still considered light by them, let alone the Two Vehicles; this arises from suddenly giving rise to a sense of superiority and lacking the wisdom to save oneself.
If one realizes this is wrong, there will be no fault in oneself nor blame in others. If one considers oneself a sage, the demon of great conceit (māna-māra) will attach itself to them;
they will fail to pay homage to stupas and temples, destroy scriptures and images, and will surely lose right concentration to fall into ruin. Or, in some cases...

Within the clarity and brilliance of perfect concentration, one is further able to give rise to wisdom that momentarily accords with principle; as cognition merges with principle, they do not conflict or resist one another.
Because there is no conflict or resistance, immeasurable pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) subsequently arises, and body and mind become harmoniously adjusted.

This is called "realizing the state of an Arhat" and attaining great self-mastery. Through this wisdom, which momentarily accords with principle, the aggregates of sensation and all sensory objects are free from heaviness and turbidity.
Because of delusion, one attains a state of lightness and purity; yet if one realizes this is not [the ultimate], there will naturally be no fault from others.

If one considers this state to be "sainthood," then the demon of attachment to lightness and purity will possess them; they will claim to have attained sainthood and never seek further progress, just like the monk who had heard nothing.
They will inevitably lose right concentration and fall into ruin. Or, within the meditative state of the *vedanā-skandha*, one may again achieve clear awakening and attain...
If one clings to this luminous emptiness and tranquil nature as being devoid of even a single dharma that can be grasped, one will consequently fall into nihilism, denying cause and effect.
If one realizes this is erroneous, there will naturally be no fault in others. If, however, one considers this state to be the holy, then a "demon of emptiness" will take possession;

such a person slanders the observance of precepts as being for the Lesser Vehicle, claiming that since the Mahāyāna realizes emptiness, what need is there for any observance or violation? Consequently, they come to utterly destroy their monastic discipline (*vinaya*).
If one errs for oneself and leads others astray, one will surely lose right concentration and fall into ruin.

Or, while in a state of concentration, one may attain a nature of empty clarity and develop a deep attachment to it, giving rise to boundless craving. When this craving reaches its peak, it triggers the seeds of greed, ultimately provoking mad desire.

This occurs because the meditative state is so harmonious and pleasant that one lacks the wisdom to maintain self-restraint. If one realizes this is erroneous, there will be no fault in oneself or others. If...
If one considers these to be holy, the demon of desire will attach itself; taking desire as the Way, it teaches and transforms through lustful conduct in groups of hundreds and thousands.
Thus, one deludes oneself and deludes others, inevitably losing right concentration and falling into ruin.

These ten kinds of phenomena that appear above are all manifestations resulting from the interaction between the practitioner’s power of contemplation and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

When that son of good family cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is exhausted—up until the attainment of the Unsurpassed Way—this clarifies the destruction of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
Previously, while the aggregate of sensation was not yet exhausted, the body was subject to grasping; therefore, the mind did not depart from the body.
Once the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, the body is no longer subject to grasping; therefore, the mind departs from the body, and its dwelling and movement become free.
From this point on, there arises the distinction between ascending through the stages of sainthood and attaining the *manomaya-kāya* (body born of mind).

As for the *manomaya-kāya*, it means being born according to one's will, swift and unimpeded. Although you have not yet attained it, since the *skandha* of sensation has already been shattered, the cause for it exists;
it is just like a person in sleep who utters words in a dream: though they have no conscious awareness, the speech produced forms a rhythmic cadence that is heard by those nearby.
The listeners all understood his words: "This is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

If it is like a clear mirror from which dust has been removed, so that there is no longer any obscuration, then the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) will be revealed here. When one clearly perceives the beginning and end of the cycle of birth and death for a particular class of beings, the aggregate of perception is exhausted;
thus, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa*), which relies upon perception for its establishment, can be transcended from this point. Observe the origin of perception."
This is merely that which is formed by the fusion of deluded thoughts; it has no true reality and cannot be destroyed.

Now, when the practitioner has exhausted the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) and no more perverse thoughts arise, they dwell within this perfect samādhi of the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate).

As they are about to break through but have not yet done so, they may give rise to ten kinds of demonic activities. Alternatively, their mind may crave perfect luminosity, whereby they sharpen their intense contemplation and become greedy for it.

Those who seek such skillfulness, their marvelous essence being already perfected, will find their subtle functions naturally manifest. Yet, if they harbor a mind of longing and seeking, this immediately creates a point of vulnerability for the heterodox;
thus, demons gain the opportunity to fly their spirits into people, preaching the Dharma and displaying supernatural powers for them.

All of this serves to cater to their fondness for cleverness and seeking, causing their minds and wills to become deluded, increasing their lust and breaking their precepts, until they ultimately meet with royal punishment.
Yet, that one enters Avīci Hell is entirely due to seeking such skillfulness with a single thought as the stepping-stone.

Alternatively, if the mind loves to wander and be dissolute, it will cause one’s refined thoughts to fly away as it greedily seeks out experiences. Whether walking, standing, or dwelling in meditative concentration, what harm is there in traveling and paying homage?

However, if one’s deluded emotions are dissolute and negligent, they will merely waste right mindfulness; thus, Māra seizes the opportunity to cause his refined essence to fly and attach itself to people.
For their sake, he preached the Dharma and manifested supernatural powers (ṛddhi), doing nothing but catering to their fondness for wandering and seeking;

he caused their minds and wills to become deluded, increasing their lust and breaking their precepts, until they ultimately incurred the King’s punishment and entered the Avīci Hell—all because of that single thought of wandering and seeking, which served as the ladder for these misfortunes.
Alternatively, there are those whose hearts love the subtle and profound principles, such that they clarify their refined reflections and greedily pursue them.

To harmonize with the principle of silent illumination through the forgetting of artifice, the truth naturally merges in mystery; yet, to conceive a thought of seeking or hoping for it instead becomes the root of delusion.

Thus, demons find their opportunity, instantly flying their essence to possess a person to preach the Dharma and manifest supernatural powers, doing nothing but catering to the seeker’s preferences and desires.
This causes the person’s will to become confused and increasingly aligned with transgression until, ultimately, they incur the king’s punishment.
To enter Avīci Hell, one seeks this very thing; a single thought serves as the stairway for it.

Perhaps the mind loves to exhaustively investigate the primal cause of all things, thereby refining its spirit and greedily seeking clarity. Yet the profound root of all things is something that none but a Buddha can fathom;
now, by forcibly pursuing worldly principles, one instead increases the defilements of the mind. Thus, Māra seizes the opportunity and flies his essence to possess the person.

People preach the Dharma for them, manifesting supernatural powers to cater to their fundamental desires, causing their minds and wills to become deluded, increasing their lust, and leading them to break the precepts;
ultimately, they fall into royal punishment and enter the Avīci Hell—all because this single thought of seeking is the foundation for it.
Alternatively, those whose hearts crave immediate responses may study with unceasing diligence, yet they greedily seek the hidden and the obscure.

I am moved by the fact that while their merit is profound and their conduct manifest, their responses arise from the hidden depths; yet because they harbor aspirations in their hearts, these instead become a source of heterodox deviation.

Thus, demons take advantage of this, flying their spirits to possess people to preach the Dharma for them and manifest supernatural powers—all of which serve to cater to their desires and inclinations.
This causes their wills to become deluded and confused, increasing their lust and leading them to break the precepts, until finally they encounter royal punishment and enter [into calamity].

That all [beings] may attain this state of resonance depends on a single thought as its foundation. Some, however, cherish a heart of profound stillness and seek to cultivate supernormal powers through clarity;
they thus restrain body and mind while greedily seeking tranquility. Now, when the mind is extinguished, objects are stilled; when thought moves, conditions proliferate.
To give rise to a greedy mind for stillness is called "divergent thought. Therefore, demons seize the opportunity and fly their essence [into the practitioner].
They follow others who preach the Dharma for them, manifesting supernatural powers not out of anything else, but solely to cater to their desire for stillness;

they cause their minds and wills to become deluded, leading them to claim they have realized sainthood. Ultimately, they fall under the king’s law and enter the Avīci Hell—all because this single thought of seeking stillness serves as the ladder for such a fate.
Alternatively, those whose hearts cherish subtle and hidden knowledge diligently and painfully investigate and seek it out.

Those who greedily seek supernormal powers such as the knowledge of past lives—whereby these powers would naturally manifest through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)—if they instead seek them with forced effort, it conversely becomes a perverted type.
Consequently, Māra seizes the opportunity to dispatch his agents, who possess spirits that enter human bodies to preach the Dharma for them.

These manifestations of power are nothing but a means of catering to their desire for knowledge, causing their minds and wills to become deluded; they claim to have realized sainthood, yet in the end...
Falling into royal calamity and entering hell—all of this is caused by the single thought of seeking knowledge, which serves as the stepping-stone.
Perhaps the mind loves spiritual transformations and thus investigates the causes of such changes, greedily grasping at supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).

Since the power of supernormal realms is attained only upon the departure from desire, to forcibly seize it with a greedy heart results instead in defiled attachment; thus, Māra finds his opportunity and immediately dispatches a spirit to possess them.
They attach themselves to others who preach the Dharma and manifest supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), doing nothing but catering to their desire for such powers;

they cause their minds and wills to become deluded, leading them to claim they have realized holiness (*arhatship*). Ultimately, they fall into royal punishment and enter the Avīci Hell—all because this single thought of seeking supernatural powers serves as the ladder for their downfall.
Alternatively, those whose hearts love to penetrate deeply into quiescent extinction (*śamatha*) investigate the nature of the myriad transformations.

Yet, those who greedily seek profound emptiness—whereas clarifying emptiness within form is supreme wisdom, grasping at emptiness by extinguishing form is a false view—therefore allow Māra to find his opportunity.
Māra then flies his essence into a person to preach the Dharma for them and manifest supernatural powers, doing nothing but catering to their fondness for seeking emptiness.
This causes their minds and wills to become deluded, increasing lust and breaking the precepts, until they finally commit transgressions.
It is because of these difficulties that one enters the Avīci Hell; all such pursuits of emptiness have a single thought as their foundation.

Perhaps the mind cherishes long life, and thus one undergoes arduous investigation, desiring to escape the short lifespan of the *pariccheda* (segmented) realm and hoping for the long years of the *pariṇāma* (transformative) realm.

However, if views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are not exhausted, the segmented realm will naturally perish; yet, if delusions are entirely unsevered, to force such a pursuit is but a false fabrication, whereby Māra gains an opportunity.
The spirits will immediately fly to attach themselves to humans, preaching the Dharma and manifesting supernatural powers for them, all in order to cater to their fondness for longevity;
eventually, they even cause them to indulge excessively in lustful desires, hastening their own destruction. It is certain that such individuals will fall into the Avīci Hell;
all of this is due to the single thought of seeking long life serving as the gateway. These ten types [of spirits] all arise from the power of contemplation and mental visualization.
Because the *skandhas* interact with one another, this realm appears. Regarding the old interpretation: "From that time, the celestial Māra...
is assigned to the celestial Māra, while "from his own mouth, he delights in speaking words... is assigned to the ghost-spirit Māra. This is a profound error in logic. Jiaguang (Jiaguang) says:

"The 'ghost-spirit' is precisely one dispatched by the celestial Māra; the character 'jing' (spirit/essence) in 'flying spirit' (*feijing*) belongs to the ghost-spirit, who is sent forth by the celestial Māra."
This explanation is very reasonable and may be followed.
*A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Nine;
*A Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánxián of Yǒngquán Chán Monastery on Mount Gǔ at Fúzhōu.
Regarding that son of good family who cultivates samādhi and has exhausted the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception), [up to] the pure pointing-out instruction.

This clarifies the destruction of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Previously, when the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) had not yet been destroyed, awakening was perceived as perception and sleep as a dream;
the clarity of awareness was thus muddled by them. Only when the *saṃjñā-skandha* is exhausted do dreams and waking thoughts vanish.

Awakening and sleep become one, and the clarity of awareness is empty and still, no longer bearing the coarse shadows of external objects. When facing the myriad phenomena, it is merely like reflections appearing in a mirror, without any clinging.

Departing leaves no trace; it is merely a void that receives illumination and responds. When this is so, the old habits of floating thoughts have already vanished, and only the true essence is revealed.
This is the root-source of birth and death. This root-source serves as the common foundation for the twelve classes of beings to arise together.
Since it has now been disclosed, one can see it exhaustively; however, sentient beings each possess distinct seeds of their own.

The source of the life-force has not yet been fully penetrated; this is the foundation of common birth, pure yet turbulent, serving as the pivotal hub for the movement and cessation of sense-objects and consciousness.
This is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

If this flickering nature of clarity-and-turbulence is extinguished and enters into profound stillness—like waves upon water transforming into clear, still water—then the *saṃskāra-skandha* is exhausted, and the multitude [of afflictions]...
That which is established upon the basis of the turbidity of birth can be transcended from here. The source of contemplative practice is formed by subtle and hidden delusions;

it is not something truly real that cannot be destroyed. If practitioners, within the meditative concentration of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), maintain a clear and upright mind, the ten kinds of celestial Māras will find no opportunity, and they will then be able to investigate and break through it.
The twelve categories of birth within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) are here revealed as their fundamental source.

If a person contemplates that profound, pure, yet restless, perfect source and is able to give rise to ten kinds of false wisdom, or if they engage in conceptual calculations regarding that perfect source, they will fall into the two heterodox theories of non-causality.
First, this person perceives that there is no cause for the fundamental nature; this occurs because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has become fully manifest.

Riding upon the eight hundred merits of the faculty of the eye, one can see all sentient beings within eighty thousand kalpas as they transmigrate according to their karma, dying here and being born there;

yet, because the power of his supernormal faculties does not reach beyond eighty thousand kalpas, he sees nothing in the darkness before that point and thus reckons that since eighty thousand kalpas ago, sentient beings have arisen spontaneously without cause. This constitutes falling into false views and becoming lost to right awakening.
Second, these people perceive that the end has no cause;

because they see that the arising of various species has no cause, they conclude that for eighty thousand kalpas all sentient beings have been spontaneously so and without change—just as humans give birth to humans, birds to birds, crows are naturally black and cranes naturally white—and by using prior cases to infer subsequent ones, they maintain this view. Thus...
I calculate that there is fundamentally no awakening at the beginning, nor is there any matter of achieving the roots of awakening at the end; thus, this "end" is without cause.

Of these two types of non-Buddhists, the former merely perceives the cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) of sentient beings but does not perceive its causes—the distinct karmic seeds and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
the latter does not even perceive the existence of cyclic existence, but merely observes that sentient beings arise through the production of their own kind, and therefore acts [accordingly].
Regarding this calculation, those who engage in speculative reckoning within the context of the perfect and eternal fall into the four heterodox theories of universal permanence.

The first is as follows: when this person’s practice reaches the manifestation of the *skandha* of formation (*saṃskāra-skandha*), they perceive that the locus where the mind and its objects arise is entirely devoid of cause.

Consequently, they develop supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) through which they can know the continuous succession of the arising and ceasing of the mental states of sentient beings throughout twenty thousand kalpas; they then take this to be [the truth].

First, regarding "permanence": this refers to the practitioner of the Human Vehicle who, through the clear observation (*abhisamaya*) of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, perceives that the fundamental nature of the four great elements is eternally abiding;

from this, they give rise to the notion that the nature of the four great elements of sentient beings throughout forty thousand kalpas is likewise constant, and thus they reckon it to be permanent. Second, regarding "permanence":

this refers to the practitioner of the Human Vehicle who, through the clear observation of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, perceives that the fundamental nature of the eight consciousnesses is unchanging; from this, they give rise to [the notion of permanence].

Fourth, by means of supernormal knowledge, one can perceive that the consciousness-nature of sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas is eternally abiding; thus, one reckons it to be permanent.

Furthermore, once this person has exhausted the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formation (*saṃskāra-skandha*) becomes manifest; they falsely claim that birth-and-death belongs to perception, and now that perception is exhausted, the aggregate of formation is therefore the principle of non-birth-and-non-death, which they reckon to be permanent. These four [cases] are all instances of not seeing through the aggregate of formation.

Because of arising and ceasing, there arises this attachment; or, those who engage in conceptual calculations regarding self and others fall into the four inverted views of the non-Buddhists, specifically the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.

First, such a person uses a tainted mind to contemplate the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the ten directions; they take these to be the transformations of false consciousness rather than reality, and thus they cling to them.
They conceive of a divine self (*ātman*) and reckon that this self pervades the worlds of the ten directions, being concentrated, luminous, and unmoving;

yet all sentient beings undergo birth and death within the heart of this self. From this, they reckon that which is the unmoving self to be eternal, while those who undergo birth and death to be impermanent.
Furthermore, when these people universally observe lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and see those undergoing the destruction of a kalpa, they consider them to be non-existent.
Fourth, they commonly regard that which does not perish throughout the kalpas as permanent;

these people falsely calculate that their own mind is subtle and secret, difficult to perceive, like a minute particle that wanders through the ten directions without ever changing or shifting, while the bodies it produces arise and perish in an instant.
Thus, they take this unchanging nature to be permanent and the arising-and-perishing body to be impermanent. Fourth.
This person, once the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, perceives the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as a constant flow;
they then reckon this constant flow of formations to be permanent. Furthermore, they reckon the cessation of sensation and form to be impermanent.

These four reckonings are all, in total, impermanent, yet they falsely divide them into permanence and impermanence—this constitutes a perverse attachment. Alternatively, there are those who engage in conceptual speculation regarding various states or stages.

Falling into the four heterodox theories of finitude: first, this person observes the constant flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and falsely calculates that there is a point of interruption in the past and future, which they call "finitude" (*antavān*);
they then regard the present continuity as being uninterrupted, which they call "infinite" (*anantavān*).
Second, this person contemplates eighty thousand kalpas and sees that prior to those eighty thousand kalpas there was a void silence, devoid of sight or hearing, which they call "non-existence."
Third, for eighty thousand kalpas there have been sentient beings called "those with limits.
These people reckon that their own cognition, which is able to pervade all sentient beings, is their own nature and is therefore infinite;

yet they reckon that although those beings currently appear within the scope of their own cognition, they do not see or know the cognition of those beings, and thus that cognition belongs to the nature of those others and is finite. Fourth, these are...
People calculate that within the bodies of all sentient beings there is both half-birth and half-extinction, and that the world is likewise;

thus, they take the half-born as finite and the half-extinguished as infinite. These four views all arise from falsely distinguishing between existence and non-existence, and are therefore false attachments.
Or, those who give rise to conceptual calculations regarding knowledge and vision fall into the external [paths].
The four kinds of delusions regarding the Path are: the immortality of indecisive equivocation (*amarā-vikṣepa*), and pervasive false theorizing.

First, there is the person who contemplates the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the source of transformation. Observing that phenomena are not uniform, they consequently give rise to divergent interpretations, asserting that things are both changing and constant, both arising and ceasing, both increasing and decreasing, and both existent and non-existent. When someone comes to question them, they provide a response that stands between two extremes. Self-...

Second, this person confuses their speech so that the listener does not know what is being said; because they observe only the place where the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) perishes from moment to moment, they realize only its non-existence.
Thus, when someone comes to question them, they say only "it is non-existent" and have nothing further to say.

Third, this person observes only the place where the *saṃskāra-skandha* arises from moment to moment, and thus realizes only its existence. Therefore, when someone comes to question them, they say only... [existence].

Regarding the fourth of these remaining points where nothing further is said: this person contemplates the arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as neither uniform nor singular, seeing both existence and non-existence.
Since the object they perceive is already fragmented, the mind that perceives it is likewise distracted.

When someone comes to question them, they answer by saying "existence" is precisely "non-existence," and then say "non-existence" is not "existence. Thus, their own words mutually contradict one another as they resort to evasive and deceptive speech.

It is impossible to exhaustively investigate these four cases, as they are all alike. Because one fails to perceive the entirety of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), deluded and erroneous conceptualizations arise, leading to such attachments.
Alternatively, those who form conceptualizations regarding the inexhaustible flow [of existence] fall into the views of external paths concerning the existence of signs after death;
their resolve is inverted, and they take the continuous flow of the aggregate of formations as the cause for their conceptualizations of inexhaustibility.
The three—form, feeling, and perception—are established in dependence upon volitional formations and are likewise all inexhaustible. Some claim that form is the self;
some claim that the self contains form; some claim that form belongs to the self; and some claim that the self exists within form.

One applies these four reckonings to feeling, perception, and volitional formations as well, resulting in sixteen modes of reckoning, all of which maintain that after death the four aggregates do not perish.
Furthermore, based on this calculation, one holds that both afflictions (*kleśa*) and bodhi are both inexhaustible and do not obstruct one another;
for since afflictions arise from the aggregates (*skandha*) and bodhi is realized through the aggregates, both are inexhaustible.

However, since the nature of the aggregates tends toward extinction moment by moment, how could they possibly endure long after death? Therefore, this calculation constitutes a false attachment. Or, regarding what was previously extinguished...

Those who engage in conceptual calculation regarding form, sensation, and perception fall into the path of externalists; their resolve after death is characterized by the absence of marks and is inverted.

Because they perceive that the first three aggregates (skandhas) have all ceased, they conclude that although the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) still exists, it is identical to grass and trees and cannot even be perceived while alive.
Since it cannot be found even in the present, how could it possibly exist after death? Thus, both cause and effect would be non-existent, leading to a state of total nihilism.
Furthermore, based on these eight kinds of signlessness, they recklessly calculate that both the cause and fruit of *nirvāṇa* are entirely empty.

They claim that because the cause and fruit of *nirvāṇa* are cultivated in dependence upon the present aggregates (*skandha*) and realized in dependence upon the future aggregates, and since the aggregates themselves are ultimately unobtainable, how could there be cultivation or realization?

Thus, they say they are "all empty. However, cause and effect are clearly manifest, and the retribution of karmic response is not false; how can one dismiss them as non-existent? Therefore, this [view] is...

To calculate this as being either existence or non-existence is a false attachment. There may be those who see the activity-aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) as persisting while the aggregates of form, sensation, and perception have ceased;

they dualistically calculate both existence and non-existence, and their own essential natures thus contradict one another. Such persons fall into the heterodox paths and, after death, give rise to the "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" inverted doctrine.

Within the cessation of form, sensation, and perception, they perceive the activity-aggregate as existing yet not existing; within the persistence of the activity-aggregate, they perceive form, sensation, and perception.

To claim that [the self] is non-existent yet not non-existent, and that the four aggregates are neither existent nor non-existent—thus forming eight aspects collectively—is to grasp at any single condition and thereby form such attachments.
Furthermore, based on these collateral speculations, one claims that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, and that their reality or unreality is indeterminate.

However, although the substance of delusion is empty, it becomes existent through the transformation of karma; how then could they both be "neither"? Therefore, this speculation constitutes a false attachment.

If there are those who speculate that after the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there is no further place for rebirth, such persons fall into the seven nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists;
or they may speculate that the body of humans or devas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is annihilated; or they may speculate that it is annihilated when desire is exhausted in the first dhyāna;

or they may speculate that it is annihilated when suffering is exhausted in the second dhyāna; or they may speculate that it is annihilated in the extreme bliss of the third dhyāna; or they may speculate that it is annihilated in the fourth dhyāna and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If one abandons and extinguishes [the aggregates] until they reach their ultimate limit, such that both the present and the future are simultaneously extinguished, how could they arise again?
Since the outflows within the seven limits all proceed from the transformation of karma, how could they constitute a state of annihilation? Therefore, this calculation is a false attachment.

Alternatively, if there are those who speculate regarding the arising of subsequent existences after the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), such persons fall into the five theories of nirvana held by non-Buddhists. Or...
Some perceive the clarity and brightness of the heavens of desire as nirvana; some perceive the departure from sorrow in the first dhyāna as nirvana;

some perceive the absence of suffering in the second dhyāna as nirvana; some perceive the ultimate bliss in the third dhyāna as nirvana; and some perceive the simultaneous disappearance of both suffering and pleasure in the fourth dhyāna as nirvana.
These five are all states of rebirth within the tainted heavens; when their retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of saṃsāra, and thus they are not the true [nirvana].
Because of this, such false conceptualization constitutes a perverse attachment. These ten types of perverse wisdom mentioned above all arise from the power of contemplation;
because the aggregates (skandhas) interact with one another, these attachments are produced, and their downfall is certain.

When that good man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted—up to the point where he does not encounter byways—this clarifies the destruction of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). If the aggregate of formations is exhausted, then the generative mechanisms of the twelve classes of beings are shattered;
the mainstays of the paths of rebirth and the deep channels of karmic retribution are all severed and no longer continue, and the celestial nature (*dharmadhātu*) is about to...
As clear as the crowing of a cock at dawn when the east has already begun to brighten, the habit of agitation has been stilled;
thus the six sense faculties become empty and tranquil, no longer wandering or dissipated. Because they do not wander, both the internal and external become profoundly limpid and bright.

Because the internal and external are profoundly limpid and bright, both the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are simultaneously lost, and one enters that which is nowhere to enter. Reaching this state, one can deeply penetrate the reception of sentient beings.
The source of life is traced by observing its origin and grasping its course; thus, one does not fall into the summoning and drawing forth of categories of beings.
Indeed, the common source of birth throughout the worlds of the ten directions has now been attained; it is revealed and no longer kept secret—this is called the realm of the *vijñāna-skandha*.

If, within the concentration of the *vijñāna-skandha*, one can further refine and polish the six sense faculties so that their opening and closing become free and mutually responsive, [one transcends this stage].
When one uses purity to make the body and world transparent like lapis lazuli, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted;

that which constitutes the turbidity of life, which depends upon consciousness for its establishment, can from this point be transcended. One observes that the origin of consciousness is formed by formless, illusory conceptualization;
it has no true reality and is not something that can be destroyed. Now, although the practitioners have already emptied the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), even so—

It is said: although birth and death have been extinguished, the *vijñāna-skandha* has not yet been shattered; subtle birth and death still persist, meaning that the essence of this quiescent extinction has not yet reached perfection.

If a practitioner can give rise to ten kinds of "mad" insights at this stage—such as temporarily attaining the integration of the sense-faculties so they are no longer obstructed within meditative contemplation, and being able to harmonize with the enlightened nature of the ten directions and enter the Perfect [Reality]—[then progress is made].
Originally, this refers to the cessation of activity returning to the manifestation of consciousness as such.

If one takes that which is returned to as being truly permanent and establishes it as a true cause, then because that cause has something upon which it depends, one falls into the category of the Sāṃkhyas. This is because a true cause is non-existent, while "that which is depended upon" is merely delusion.
Now, if one establishes consciousness as the cause, then the mind has something attained and the fruit has something to which it returns; this contradicts [the principle of non-attainment].
Those who, while possessing perfect penetration, turn their backs on *nirvāṇa* and give rise to the seeds of external paths are as follows:

if they take the consciousness to which they have returned as the essence of the self (*ātman*), and seeing that all phenomena are transformations of consciousness, they claim, "I am able to produce all sentient beings and worlds," they falsely grasp at being the agent while in reality they are not the agent;
they thus fall into the category of Maheśvara, for each [of these paths] has its own distinct destiny.

There is a realm with continuity that arises from collective karma; if one is able to give rise to the proliferation of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), thereby violating perfect penetration and turning one's back on *nirvāṇa*, one will be born among the gods of Great Pride (*mahāmāna*) who possess the seed of the "pervasive-perfection" (*piānyuán*). "Pervasive-perfection" means that the essence of the self pervades the entire realm of space.

If, regarding the consciousness that has turned toward its object of refuge, one falsely identifies it as the producer of one's own body and the ten directions of empty space, then— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.)
To form the conception that these are truly eternal is to be ignorant of the truth of non-arising and unaware of the delusion of birth and extinction;
to reckon what is impermanent as permanent is to fall into the category of the *Īśvara* gods.

By establishing a causal basis for dependence, one produces the fruit of false conceptualization, thereby contravening perfect penetration and turning one's back on *nirvāṇa*. This gives rise to the seed of "inverted perfection. As for inverted perfection:
Inverting [the truth], one takes that [insentient matter] to be all-pervasive and capable of producing a self.

If, regarding the consciousness of what is known, one reckons its cognitive essence to be all-pervasive throughout everything—claiming that grasses, trees, sentient beings, and humans are no different from one another and revolve in mutual cycles—this is a false attachment to the existence of cognition where there is actually no cognition;
it is precisely to fall into the category of the Pāṭhas and Sainikas. As for the sentient and the insentient:
Although they are equally transformations of consciousness, since the seeing and the perceived are already distinct, how could both possess cognition?

Your current calculation that perfect cognition serves as the cause results in the false fruit of empty delusion; it violates universal penetration and turns its back on Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.
"Inverted cognition" means the inversion of taking non-cognition to be cognition. If, within the state where the six sense-faculties are universally fused and mutually functional, for even a moment—
Having attained conformity with causes and their mutual fulfillment, they falsely reckon that all dharmas are capable of perfect transformation and the production of supreme fruits.
Consequently, some seek the light of fire, others delight in the purity of water, some cherish the circulation of wind, and others observe the formation of dust;
each venerates these objects as the established cause for cultivation and regards them as permanent. This is the deluded attachment to that which can produce [results].
If one truly cannot give rise [to the Way], one immediately falls among the ranks of the Kāśyapas and the Brahmins;
that is to say, having lost the fundamental mind, they falsely follow external objects to establish the causes for deluded seeking and the fruits of deluded hope.

Thus they violate perfect penetration and turn their backs on Nirvāṇa, giving rise to the seeds of inverted transformation. "Inverted transformation" means being inverted by taking those [external objects] as the agents of transformation. If...

Within the perfectly bright and lucid essence of consciousness, one calculates that the luminosity therein is empty and still; thus, one destroys all dharmas and takes their eternal extinction as the object of pursuit.
Taking this—which is not truly a place of refuge—to be a place of refuge, one falls among the Śūnyatā-devas (the "Empty-Space" devas) and their like.
This consciousness merely appears to be extinguished but is not truly extinguished; yet, by clinging to it as real, one establishes what is false.
To take that which lacks cause and produce the fruit of annihilation is to contradict perfect penetration and turn one's back on Nirvana, thereby generating the seed of nihilism.

If one reckons the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-ghana*) to be perfect and eternal, desiring to preserve the body so that it remains as solid and enduring as the essence of consciousness—never decaying or passing away—one falsely deems it worthy of attachment when in truth it is not; such a person immediately falls into the abyss of Āsura.

Such beings take the physical body—which is illusory and fundamentally impermanent—to be their life-essence. By clinging to this, they seek to solidify a body that is inherently fragile and pursue a fruit of long-term confinement;
thus, they turn away from perfect penetration and背离 (violate) Nirvana, giving rise to deluded seeds that prolong rebirth.
If one instead regards consciousness as the life-essence, it then communicates with external objects: when objects arise, consciousness persists; when objects cease, [consciousness likewise ceases].
Because they fear the extinction of consciousness, they instead retain the dust of worldly toil and extensively transform the realm of desire for their own amusement.
By grasping at consciousness as the true sovereign while it is in fact not the true sovereign, they fall into the class of the *ṭakkirāja* spirits;

they perversely give rise to false thoughts, taking the intense dust of desire as the cause and its flourishing as the fruit. Thus, they contravene perfect penetration and turn their backs on Nirvana.

These are those who give rise to the seeds of celestial and demonic states. Because they perceive that the karmic habits within the manifest life-source are not uniform, they differentiate among them—discerning what is essential and what is coarse, what is true and what is false—and become stuck in the cycle of cause, effect, response, and stimulus.
Thus, they turn their backs on the path of pure non-cultivation and non-realization; this is merely knowing suffering and severing it.

Having gathered the evidence for cessation and cultivated the path, they no longer advance further, but instead fall among those such as the śrāvakas of fixed nature and the bhikṣus who have heard nothing.
This is because the profound stillness of the consciousness-aggregate (vijñānaskandha) is not true nirvāṇa; their pursuit of perfect purity ultimately leads to the fruit of stagnant quiescence.
Thus, they oppose universal penetration and turn their backs on nirvāṇa, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness. If one contemplates this...

If this consciousness, being perfectly pure and luminously aware, exhausts its depth and subtlety and establishes itself as Nirvana without proceeding further, it falls into the category of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas who do not turn their minds back toward enlightenment. For this perfect purity and luminous awareness is not true Nirvana;
it is merely an attachment to the harmony of perfect awakening that results in the stagnation of a tranquil clarity, thereby contravening universal penetration and turning one’s back on Nirvana.
"Born of attachment to the perfection and clarity of awakening, one does not transform it into the seed of perfect manifestation.

"Not transforming it into perfect manifestation" means that while one maintains this perfection and clarity of awakening, one is unable to give rise to the transformative activity of great compassion. These ten aforementioned types of deluded interpretations all arise because the power of contemplation and the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) interact;
thus, such attachments are produced. For the most part, these are seeds of former habitual attachments stored within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which now, due to [contemplative practice]...
To be stirred by this and, in accord with one's prior inclinations, to recognize it as the true ground of rest and repose—how profound is the calamity!
Externalists and ordinary worldlings ultimately fall into the Avīci Hell, while Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas finally stagnate at the minor fruits; how deep indeed is their transgression!

This Dharma-gate, from the past through to the final instructions [of the Buddha], summarizes the preceding text to demonstrate the merit of its transcendent realization and the power of its protection.

This Dharma-gate for discerning the five aggregates is not only what those in later generations should know in advance; it was also [taught by] the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past.
There is no way to attain the opening of the mind without relying on this method;
whenever a *skandha* has not yet opened, one must rely on this dharma-gate to discern and avoid being deluded by the ten kinds of demonic realms. Only then can that *skandha* be eliminated.

This applies to all [skandhas] from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Once the *vijñāna-skandha* is exhausted, the various faculties will function interchangeably, and one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
From within this mutual functioning, one can directly transcend into the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), the Vajra-dry-wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*);

yet, there is still something to be attained. Through this dry wisdom, the refined essence of perfect clarity gives rise once more to wondrous transformation, which dissolves and incinerates subtle ignorance until not even a hair’s breadth remains—just like a lapis lazuli gem containing the moon. Thus, one again transcends the stages of faith, practice, and abiding.

If one directly enters sublime enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and returns to the state of non-attainment, then is this method of discerning demons not indeed a great skillful means for entering sublime enlightenment?
However, this is beyond the reach of the intellectual power of other sages;

rather, it is the Buddhas who, through the wisdom within meditative concentration, bring forth clear and distinct awareness so that practitioners may recognize demonic realms as they manifest before them.
At that time, one will immediately be able to recognize [the truth] and thereby wash away the defilements of the mind, so as not to fall into perverse thoughts.

Consequently, all demons will be extinguished without remainder, allowing one to proceed directly to Bodhi; even those of the two vehicles who are inferior may advance toward Great Nirvana without any further confusion.
If, however, sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age are dull-witted and do not understand the practice of *dhyāna*, [they will fail].
Furthermore, you should not listen to or distinguish the demonic teachings that delight in practicing samādhi, for fear of falling into error or loss;
rather, simply exhort them to single-mindedly uphold my Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Dhāraṇī.

If they are unable to recite it, simply transcribe it in the meditation hall or carry it upon their person, and even Māras will be unable to disturb them. This is the ultimate practice of the Tathāgata.
This realization is not comparable to the illusory city on the way; it is the final model for posterity and not a discourse of incomplete teaching from the initial stage.
You all should revere and follow it, and must not treat it with negligence.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat... [up to] "he does not crave the three realms.

From this point downward, Ānanda requests the Buddha to further clarify the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which serves to develop the meaning left unexhausted in the preceding text.
First, he asks about the deluded thoughts that give rise to the five aggregates; next, he asks about the sudden and gradual methods for their elimination.
Question: Regarding the depth and shallowness of the limits of the five aggregates, the Buddha said:

"This essence is the wondrously luminous fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), which is all-pervading and pure, leaving no room for anything else. How could there be birth and death, defilements, or even empty space?
It is only due to the arising of deluded thoughts that these falsely produce the various vessel-worlds within the original fundamental awakening. From this...
