The true is inherently existent yet suspected of being lost; the false is inherently empty yet clung to as real. This is like the case of Yan-ruo, who in his delusion mistook his own head for a reflection.

Thus, it can be known that the five aggregates are rooted in false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Yet, the reason people suffer from stubborn attachment and cannot break through it is the fault of such false calculation.
Now, since the false is fundamentally without cause, how could one possibly engage in erroneous calculation? By means of this, [the nature of the aggregates] is revealed.
Not knowing that there is no cause, one reckons it to be a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); not knowing that there is a causal condition, one reckons it to be spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
Now, the essential nature of empty space arises from delusion regarding existence and thus still belongs to the realm of illusory birth.
Since it is entirely illusory, upon what basis can one deliberate? To speak of "causal conditions" or "spontaneity" is nothing more than false conceptualization. If one were able to know this...
If one admits that false existence has an origin, it must be said to arise from causes and conditions; yet, since its origin is not known, how can there be causes and conditions?
How much less, then, can one postulate a "self-nature"? Therefore, the Tathāgata taught that the five aggregates share the same root in false imagination (*vikalpa*);

they have no true reality that can be grasped or conceptualized. As for what is called the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) being rooted in false imagination, it is because your body originally arises from—
When one's parents desire to meet and unite, yet you instead cast thoughts of love and hatred upon them, only then can the life-force be transmitted.
Once these three types of thought are firm, the body is subsequently formed. As I previously stated: when one thinks of sour things, saliva flows;
when one thinks of climbing a height, the legs ache. There is no actual presence of sour things or the act of climbing a height, yet saliva flows.
The numbness of the feet arises from being of the same category as delusive thought. If the body were not of the category of delusion, how could delusive thought be able to produce such a resonance?

Thus we know that this present physical body is precisely what is called "the delusion of solidity. Regarding what is said that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is fundamentally based on delusive thought:
it is like when one's mind imagines standing atop a high precipice; though this is not actually real, the feet truly [experience the sensation].
The experience of sourness and astringency arises entirely from empty reception; because this reception is capable of manifesting clarity, it subsequently moves the physical body.

Thus, one knows that the present two types of sensation—beneficial and detrimental—are precisely what are called "empty, luminous, and deluded thoughts. As for what is meant by saying that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is fundamentally based on deluded thought:
it is because your perception is able to direct your body, causing the body to act in ways that do not conform to the nature of non-perception; how else could it move according to your will?
When the mind arises that takes on various shifting images, its forms correspond with its thoughts, merging into a non-dual state.
To know that what is presently perceived as a thought or a dream is merely the movement of deluded emotion is what is called "merging into delusive conceptualization.

This is what is meant by saying that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is fundamentally based on delusion; for within this body, the nature of transformation is subtle, hidden, and secret.
The physical form shifts its basis daily, yet one is never conscious of this movement. If this movement were not you, how could it be that your body shifts?
If it were truly you, why would you yourself not be conscious of it? Whether it is you or not you is entirely indeterminate; how, then, can there be any real meaning in it?
Know that the present formations (saṃskāras) do not cease for even a single moment; this very state is what is called the "subtle and hidden delusion."

That which is called "perception" (saṃjñā) refers to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), which is fundamentally rooted in false conceptualization (vikalpa). Because this consciousness is subtle and refined, the world generally regards it as permanent.
This consciousness does not depart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; if it were truly essential and genuine, it should not be defiled by habitual tendencies.
Consider now what you saw in the past: after many years have passed, you suddenly see that strange object again, and your memory of it remains vivid and clear.
Examining this, one knows that within this essence which is lucid and profoundly still, there is the perfuming of every thought-moment; how could there be any room for calculation?
One should know that this stillness is not ultimate reality, but is subject to arising and ceasing—like a rapid torrent of water appearing tranquil from a distance.

If it were not such a state of ideation, how could it receive these deluded habits? This ideation must be eliminated through the mutual functioning of the six sense organs; only when their opening and closing are mastered will it be extinguished.

The ear is that which knows; the present seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—these various consciousnesses are formless and void, and this is precisely what is called "subtle, refined, and inverted conceptualization.
Viewed from this perspective, although the five aggregates differ in their refinement or coarseness, shallowness or depth, they are, in essence, all produced by deluded thoughts;
how could they be inherently present within the true mind? Furthermore, if you wish to know more about these five...
Regarding the depth of the realms (*dhātu*): one must know that both form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are the limits of form, for emptiness is also termed a single manifest color (*varṇa*).
Both contact (*sparśa*) and separation are the limits of sensation (*vedanā*), for separation is precisely the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Both memory and forgetfulness are the limits of perception (*saṃjñā*), for forgetfulness is the stillness of perception. Both arising and ceasing are the limits of formations (*saṃskāra*), for the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) proceed in succession.

The transition [of the stages] is collectively termed "activity" (*caryā*). Because consciousness enters into a state of profound stillness (*zhan*) and merges with true stillness, this stillness is also called the "limit of consciousness.
This union of the true and the deluded is precisely what is named the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*).

If a student can understand the depth and shallowness of these five layers of causal realms, they will be able to know the boundaries for the elimination of each of the five types [of afflictions], thereby avoiding confusion and intermixture.

Furthermore, if you wish to know the sudden or gradual nature of the elimination of these five [aggregates], I have previously clarified that the elimination of the five aggregates all possesses a sequential order.
This is because, when discussing their arising, consciousness comes first and form last;
however, when discussing their elimination, form comes first and consciousness last. Nevertheless, this [distinction] refers only to arising and elimination.
It is only fitting that it be thus; if one were to insist on this interpretation alone, how could one know what is false? One must understand that principle is realized suddenly (*tun-wu*):
since all phenomena arise from the mind and are produced by deluded thoughts, when thought is itself non-thought, all [delusions] are instantly exhausted.

Because there is fundamentally no delusion within true nature, it is said that "through awakening, they are eliminated together. However, if we speak of specific matters (*shi*), they certainly cannot be removed all at once.
Because the false dharmas of the five aggregates differ in their coarseness and subtlety, it is the nature of things that the coarse elements are eliminated first;
although the practice of understanding and application involves sudden severance, there is nonetheless an internal sequence. Therefore, I said that they are exhausted through successive stages.

When I previously showed you the method of the *kapāsa* cloth, you should have known that the substance of the cloth is one, and that the six knots arise due to binding. Since the principles of suddenness and gradualness are thus clear, what remains unclear that you must inquire about once again?
"Now you already know that the five aggregates have the five false imaginings as their root source.
You should convey this meaning to future generations so that practitioners may recognize their falsity and develop a deep sense of weary detachment.
Knowing that there is true *nirvāṇa*, they will not falsely give rise to attachment toward the false causes and effects of the triple world. The section on the True Doctrine ends here.
The arising of the five aggregates is in reality devoid of sequence; it is a simultaneous transformation within a single thought-moment.

However, because they are distinguished by their coarseness or subtlety, there appears to be a succession. In the contemplative methods of the Perfect and Sudden, severance is likewise not sequential;
yet when the practice reaches its fruition, the coarse defilements naturally fall away first. This principle is something practitioners must understand.
Ānanda, if there were another person who— [from here until] "paid homage and departed"—
this subsequent section on the dissemination (*pravartana*) praises the merit of upholding this sutra and exhorts its circulation for future generations.
If there were someone who offered the seven treasures, filling the entirety of space in the ten directions, to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, and served them;
If one makes offerings without a single day being in vain, then one’s wealth and treasures will be most extensive, the field of merit most supreme, and the resolve of the mind most diligent;

how could the resulting merit and virtue have any limit? Ānanda, the fact that by giving seven coins to the Buddha one obtained the status of a Wheel-Turning King serves as a reverse illustration, from which the greatness and benefit of this merit can be known. Thus the Buddha said: [The Buddha then spoke: "There is..."
If a person commits all four grave offenses and ten heinous crimes, they will inevitably fall into the various Avīci hells throughout the ten directions in a mere instant.

However, if one can, with a single thought, propagate this Dharma-gate within the Age of Dharma-Decline to instruct those of later learning, their karmic offenses will be extinguished at that very moment.
Not only will their sins be eradicated, but they will even be able to transform the sufferings of hell into [liberation].

The merit obtained in the Land of Peace and Bliss surpasses that of the former person not merely by a hundredfold or a thousandfold, but reaches a point where even calculation and analogy cannot reach it.
Now, if even karma of the most heavy kind can be transformed in a single thought-moment and result in such extraordinary merit, what is the reason for this?
It is truly because making material offerings to the Buddha ultimately remains within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*) and does not yet enter [the path of liberation].

This sutra is inconceivable in its doctrine, principle, practice, and fruition; even a single word or half-phrase enters the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), and merely hearing it once provides the seed for Buddhahood. Therefore, the merit of propagating this sutra is beyond measure.
Even if one cannot propagate it, merely being able to uphold and recite it allows one to reach Bodhi directly, free from demonic obstacles; such is its merit.

Furthermore, how could even an exhaustive eon suffice to describe it all? Thus, whether the members of this holy assembly were of shallow or deep capacity, they each received the benefits of the Dharma according to their own measure of realization.
Together they attained the perfectly wondrous True Mind, ultimately returning to the supreme fruit of fruition;
neither karma could entangle them nor Māra disturb them—how great was their joy! Their vow was for its universal circulation.
Needless to say, this is even more so after one has withdrawn from the ritual.
*The Concise Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Ten.
